passages.title: Superconductivity
passages.text:
A
Superconductivity is the ability of certain materials to conduct electric current with exactly zero electrical resistance once cooled below a specific temperature known as the critical temperature. In an ordinary conductor such as copper, some electrical energy is always lost as heat because electrons collide with vibrating atoms as they move; in a superconductor below its critical temperature, this resistance vanishes entirely, and a current set flowing in a closed superconducting loop can, in principle, continue circulating without any external power source for as long as the material remains cold enough.

B
The phenomenon was discovered in 1911 by the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, three years after he had first succeeded in liquefying helium, a technical achievement that allowed him to cool materials to within a few degrees of absolute zero. While measuring the electrical resistance of solid mercury at these extremely low temperatures, Onnes observed that the resistance dropped abruptly to an immeasurably small value at 4.2 kelvin, a result so unexpected that he initially suspected a fault in his equipment. Onnes received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1913, awarded for his work on the properties of matter at low temperatures, including this discovery.

C
A full theoretical explanation did not arrive until 1957, when the physicists John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, and John Robert Schrieffer proposed what became known as BCS theory. According to this theory, below the critical temperature electrons can overcome their mutual electrical repulsion and pair up, forming what are called Cooper pairs, through a subtle interaction mediated by vibrations in the surrounding crystal lattice. These paired electrons move through the material collectively, in a coordinated quantum state that cannot lose energy in the small increments that would normally cause resistance, allowing the current to flow without any dissipation. The three physicists shared the 1972 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.

D
For decades after Onnes's discovery, every known superconductor required cooling with liquid helium, an effective but expensive coolant. That changed in 1986, when Georg Bednorz and Karl Müller discovered a class of ceramic materials, now called high-temperature superconductors, that became superconducting at temperatures far higher than BCS theory had led physicists to expect. Certain compounds in this family superconduct above 77 kelvin, the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, a far cheaper and more abundant coolant than liquid helium, opening the door to more practical applications. Bednorz and Müller were awarded the 1987 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery, remarkably only a year after they first published it. Despite this progress, a complete theoretical explanation for why these ceramic materials superconduct at such comparatively high temperatures remains elusive, and no material yet superconducts at ordinary room temperature under everyday pressure.

E
Superconducting materials are already central to several important technologies. The powerful electromagnets used in magnetic resonance imaging scanners and in particle accelerators such as the Large Hadron Collider rely on superconducting coils to generate magnetic fields far stronger than conventional electromagnets could sustain without melting. A related property, known as the Meissner effect, causes a superconductor to expel any magnetic field from its interior, which allows a magnet to be levitated stably above a superconducting surface, a principle exploited in some experimental high-speed trains. Researchers continue to search for materials that superconduct at higher temperatures and lower pressures, since a room-temperature superconductor would allow electricity to be transmitted over long distances with no loss to resistance, a change that could transform the efficiency of electrical grids worldwide.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức vật lý phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Nuclear Fusion
passages.text:
A
Nuclear fusion is the process by which two light atomic nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy in the process. It is the reaction that powers the Sun and almost every other star: at the Sun's core, immense pressure and a temperature of around fifteen million degrees Celsius force hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium, converting a tiny fraction of their mass directly into energy according to Einstein's equation relating mass and energy. This same reaction, if it could be reliably reproduced and controlled on Earth, promises a source of electricity that produces no greenhouse gases during operation and leaves behind none of the long-lived radioactive waste associated with conventional nuclear fission power stations.

B
Fusion is difficult to achieve because atomic nuclei carry a positive electric charge and therefore repel one another strongly at close range. Overcoming this repulsion requires heating a fuel, typically a mixture of the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, to temperatures of well over one hundred million degrees Celsius, several times hotter than the core of the Sun itself, since Earth-based reactors cannot rely on the Sun's crushing gravitational pressure to assist the reaction. At such temperatures the fuel exists as a plasma, an electrically charged gas in which electrons have been stripped from their atoms, and no solid container could survive direct contact with it.

C
The most widely pursued approach to containing this plasma is a device called a tokamak, a doughnut-shaped chamber first developed by Soviet physicists in the 1950s, which uses powerful magnetic fields to hold the superheated plasma in place without it touching the chamber walls. An alternative approach, known as inertial confinement, instead compresses a small pellet of fuel using an array of extremely powerful lasers fired simultaneously from multiple directions, heating and compressing it so rapidly that fusion reactions occur before the pellet has time to fly apart. In December 2022, researchers at the National Ignition Facility in the United States announced that a laser-driven fusion reaction had, for the first time, produced more energy than the lasers had delivered to the fuel pellet, a milestone known as fusion ignition.

D
The largest tokamak project currently under construction is ITER, an international collaboration involving the European Union, the United States, China, Russia, India, Japan, and South Korea, being built in southern France. ITER is designed to produce ten times more fusion energy than the external power required to heat its plasma, though it is intended purely as an experimental device to demonstrate the physics and engineering involved, not to generate electricity for the grid. Construction has faced repeated delays and cost overruns since the project began in the early 2000s, and the first fusion experiments using its full deuterium-tritium fuel mixture are not expected until the following decade.

E
Even if ignition and sustained plasma confinement are achieved reliably, converting fusion energy into usable electricity presents its own engineering challenges, including designing materials able to withstand years of intense neutron bombardment and developing practical methods for extracting the heat released and using it to generate steam for conventional turbines. For these reasons, most experts caution that commercial fusion power stations, if they prove feasible at all, are unlikely to supply significant amounts of electricity before the middle of the twenty-first century. Nonetheless, the recent progress at facilities such as the National Ignition Facility has renewed optimism, and a growing number of privately funded companies are now pursuing fusion alongside the large government-backed projects that have historically dominated the field.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức vật lý phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Neutron Stars
passages.text:
A
A neutron star is the collapsed core left behind after a massive star explodes as a supernova, packing more mass than the Sun into a sphere typically only about twenty kilometres across. The result is by far the densest kind of object in the universe apart from a black hole: a single teaspoon of neutron-star material would weigh roughly as much as a mountain on Earth. The extraordinary density arises because the star's gravity has crushed protons and electrons together until they merge into neutrons, the particle that gives the object its name.

B
Neutron stars form only from stars significantly more massive than the Sun, typically between about eight and twenty times its mass. When such a star exhausts the nuclear fuel in its core, the core collapses catastrophically while the star's outer layers are blown outward in a supernova explosion. If the collapsing core is not massive enough to continue collapsing all the way into a black hole, the collapse instead halts once the neutrons themselves resist further compression, a quantum mechanical effect known as neutron degeneracy pressure, leaving behind the extraordinarily dense object that remains.

C
Many neutron stars spin extremely rapidly, a consequence of the original star's rotation being concentrated into a far smaller volume, in the same way a spinning skater speeds up when pulling in their arms. Some rotate hundreds of times per second. A neutron star that emits regular beams of radio waves from its magnetic poles, sweeping past Earth like a lighthouse beam as the star rotates, is called a pulsar. Pulsars were discovered in 1967 by the astronomer Jocelyn Bell Burnell, then a graduate student, who noticed a remarkably regular radio signal and briefly wondered, along with her colleagues, whether it might be a message from an extraterrestrial civilisation before the true explanation was established. The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery was awarded to her supervisor, Antony Hewish, a decision that has remained controversial among many astronomers ever since.

D
Neutron stars also possess magnetic fields far stronger than any that can be produced artificially on Earth, trillions of times stronger than the Earth's own magnetic field. A small subset of neutron stars, called magnetars, have magnetic fields stronger still, powerful enough that, according to some calculations, a magnetar as close as the Moon could wipe the data from every credit card on Earth. Magnetars occasionally release enormous bursts of X-rays and gamma rays, thought to be caused by sudden readjustments in their intensely stressed magnetic fields and crusts, sometimes described informally as starquakes.

E
When two neutron stars orbit one another closely, they gradually spiral together, losing energy through the emission of gravitational waves, until they finally collide and merge. In August 2017, such a merger was detected simultaneously by LIGO, through the gravitational waves it produced, and by dozens of telescopes around the world, which observed the resulting flash of light across multiple wavelengths, an event named GW170817. The observation confirmed that neutron-star mergers produce heavy elements such as gold and platinum through a rapid nuclear process, providing the first direct evidence that at least some of the precious metals found on Earth originated in such a cataclysmic collision billions of years ago.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức thiên văn học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Exoplanets
passages.text:
A
An exoplanet is any planet that orbits a star other than the Sun. Although philosophers speculated for centuries that other stars might host worlds of their own, the first confirmed detection of a planet orbiting a Sun-like star did not come until 1995, when the Swiss astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced the discovery of 51 Pegasi b, a gas giant orbiting extremely close to its parent star. The pair shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery, which opened a field that has since identified thousands of worlds beyond our solar system.

B
Because exoplanets lie so far away and are vastly outshone by the stars they orbit, astronomers detect most of them indirectly rather than by seeing them in a telescope image. The transit method, responsible for the majority of confirmed discoveries, looks for the tiny, regular dip in a star's brightness that occurs each time a planet passes directly in front of it as seen from Earth. The radial velocity method, used to find 51 Pegasi b, instead detects the slight wobble a planet's gravity induces in its host star, which very slightly shifts the wavelength of the star's light as it moves alternately toward and away from Earth. A smaller number of exoplanets, generally large and orbiting far from their star, have been imaged directly.

C
NASA's Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, transformed the field by continuously monitoring the brightness of more than 150,000 stars simultaneously, searching for transit dips too small to detect from the ground. Before Kepler, only a few hundred exoplanets had been confirmed; by the time the mission ended in 2018, it alone had contributed to the confirmation of more than 2,600 exoplanets, along with thousands of further candidates still awaiting confirmation. Kepler's data also allowed astronomers to estimate, for the first time, that the Milky Way likely contains billions of planets similar in size to Earth.

D
A region around a star where conditions might allow liquid water to persist on a planet's surface, neither so hot that any water boils away nor so cold that it freezes solid, is often called the habitable zone. A planet orbiting within this zone is not automatically habitable, since factors such as its atmosphere, its size, and its magnetic field all strongly influence whether liquid water could actually exist there, but the habitable zone provides astronomers with a useful first filter when searching among thousands of candidates for the planets most likely to resemble Earth. Proxima Centauri b, discovered in 2016 orbiting the star nearest to the Sun, lies within its star's habitable zone, making it one of the most closely studied exoplanets to date despite lying more than four light-years away.

E
The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, has extended the field by analysing the atmospheres of exoplanets in unprecedented detail. As a planet transits its star, a small fraction of the star's light passes through the planet's atmosphere on its way to Earth, and different gases in that atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths of light, leaving a distinctive chemical fingerprint that the telescope's instruments can detect. Using this technique, astronomers have already identified water vapour, carbon dioxide, and other molecules in the atmospheres of several exoplanets, a capability that scientists hope will eventually allow them to search for combinations of gases that could indicate the presence of life on a planet many light-years from Earth.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức thiên văn học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: CRISPR Gene Editing
passages.text:
A
CRISPR is a technology that allows scientists to alter the DNA of living cells with a precision that was unimaginable only a decade earlier, cutting a specific sequence of genetic code and either disabling it or replacing it with a new one. The name stands for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats, a rather technical description of a pattern of repeated DNA sequences first noticed in bacteria in the late 1980s, though at the time no one understood what the sequences were for.

B
The true function of these repeated sequences was only worked out decades later: they form part of a natural immune system that bacteria use to defend themselves against viruses. When a virus infects a bacterium and the bacterium survives, it stores a short snippet of the virus's genetic material within its own CRISPR sequences, a kind of genetic memory. If the same virus attacks again, the bacterium uses this stored snippet, together with an enzyme called Cas9, to recognise and cut apart the invading virus's DNA before it can cause harm. In 2012, the biochemists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that this bacterial defence system could be reprogrammed to cut any DNA sequence a researcher chose, simply by supplying Cas9 with a different guide sequence, transforming a curiosity of bacterial biology into a general-purpose gene-editing tool. The two scientists shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery.

C
In practice, researchers design a short strand of guide RNA that matches the target DNA sequence they wish to edit. This guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to the matching location in a cell's genome, where Cas9 cuts both strands of the DNA double helix. The cell's own repair machinery then mends the cut, and researchers can exploit this repair process either to disable the targeted gene, by allowing the repair to introduce small errors, or to insert a new sequence of their choosing, by supplying a template for the cell to copy during repair. Compared with earlier gene-editing techniques, CRISPR is markedly faster, cheaper, and more accurate, which is why it spread through research laboratories worldwide within just a few years of its discovery.

D
CRISPR has already been used to treat human disease. In 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved Casgevy, a CRISPR-based therapy for sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia, two inherited blood disorders, marking the first CRISPR treatment to reach approved clinical use. The therapy works by editing a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body to switch on a gene that produces a form of haemoglobin normally active only before birth, compensating for the patient's defective adult haemoglobin, before the edited cells are returned to the patient. Researchers are pursuing CRISPR-based treatments for a wide range of other genetic conditions, though each new application requires years of testing to confirm both safety and effectiveness.

E
The power of CRISPR has also raised serious ethical questions, most sharply illustrated in 2018 when the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced that he had used CRISPR to edit the genomes of human embryos, resulting in the birth of twin girls with an edited gene intended to confer resistance to HIV. The announcement was met with near-universal condemnation from the international scientific community, both because the safety of the edits had not been adequately established and because editing embryos changes DNA in a way that can be inherited by future generations, a step regarded by most researchers as crossing an ethical line that ordinary gene therapy in adult patients does not cross. He was later sentenced to prison in China, and the episode prompted renewed international debate over how, and whether, editing of the human germline should ever be permitted.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: mRNA Vaccines
passages.text:
A
An mRNA vaccine works on a principle quite different from that of traditional vaccines, which typically introduce a weakened or inactivated form of a pathogen, or a piece of one of its proteins, to train the immune system. Instead, an mRNA vaccine delivers a set of genetic instructions, in the form of messenger RNA, that directs a person's own cells to manufacture a harmless fragment of a viral protein themselves. The immune system then learns to recognise this self-made protein as foreign and mounts a defence against it, a response that will later protect the person if they encounter the actual virus.

B
Messenger RNA is a molecule that cells naturally use to carry genetic instructions from DNA in the nucleus to the protein-making machinery elsewhere in the cell, so the basic biological process an mRNA vaccine relies on is not new. What was new, and what took decades to perfect, was finding a way to introduce synthetic mRNA into cells without it being destroyed almost instantly by the body's defences or triggering a damaging inflammatory reaction. The biochemist Katalin Karikó spent much of her career pursuing this goal, often with little institutional support, before she and her collaborator Drew Weissman discovered in 2005 that modifying one of the chemical building blocks of the synthetic mRNA allowed it to evade the immune system's early defences long enough to do its work. The pair were awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this discovery.

C
A second technical obstacle was delivering the fragile mRNA molecule into human cells intact, since RNA on its own breaks down within minutes if injected directly into the bloodstream. The solution that made mRNA vaccines practical was to encase the molecule inside a tiny sphere of fat known as a lipid nanoparticle, which protects the mRNA during its journey and helps it fuse with a cell's outer membrane, releasing its genetic cargo directly inside. Refining these lipid nanoparticles to be both safe and efficient at delivering their payload occupied much of the practical development work behind the first mRNA vaccines.

D
These decades of preparatory research meant that when the COVID-19 pandemic began in early 2020, mRNA vaccine developers could move with unusual speed. The genetic sequence of the SARS-CoV-2 virus was published in January 2020, and within weeks the pharmaceutical company Moderna had designed a candidate vaccine targeting the virus's spike protein, the structure the virus uses to attach to human cells. Pfizer and the German company BioNTech developed a second mRNA vaccine along similar lines. Large clinical trials later that year showed both vaccines to be more than ninety percent effective at preventing symptomatic COVID-19, and both received emergency authorisation before the end of 2020, an extraordinarily short interval for a new vaccine technology that would ordinarily have taken years longer to reach that stage.

E
Because an mRNA vaccine can be redesigned simply by changing the genetic sequence it carries, rather than by developing an entirely new manufacturing process, researchers can, in principle, update it far more quickly than most conventional vaccines when a virus mutates. Beyond infectious disease, the same underlying technology is now being investigated for use against cancer, where a personalised mRNA vaccine could theoretically instruct a patient's own cells to display fragments of proteins unique to their tumour, prompting the immune system to attack cancer cells specifically. Several such cancer vaccines are currently in clinical trials, though, as with any new medical technology, it will take years of further testing before their safety and effectiveness in this new application can be confirmed.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Telomeres
passages.text:
A
A telomere is a stretch of repetitive DNA sequence found at each end of a chromosome, acting somewhat like the plastic tip on the end of a shoelace that stops the lace from fraying. Without telomeres, the ends of chromosomes would be indistinguishable from the broken DNA produced by damage, prompting a cell's repair machinery to fuse chromosomes together or trigger an unnecessary alarm response, either of which would be catastrophic for the cell. In humans, telomeres consist of the same six-letter DNA sequence repeated thousands of times over.

B
Each time a cell divides, the enzymes responsible for copying its DNA are unable to fully replicate the very end of each chromosome, so a small portion of telomere is lost with every division, a phenomenon known as the end-replication problem. Over many rounds of division, telomeres shorten progressively until they become too short to protect the chromosome effectively, at which point the cell typically stops dividing altogether, entering a state called senescence, or self-destructs through a controlled process called apoptosis. This limit on the number of times a normal human cell can divide is known as the Hayflick limit, named after the biologist Leonard Hayflick, who first described it in 1961.

C
Not all cells are bound by this limit in the same way. An enzyme called telomerase can rebuild the repetitive sequence at the end of a chromosome, effectively resetting the countdown, and it is highly active in certain cell types, including stem cells and the cells that produce sperm and eggs, allowing these cell lineages to divide far more often than an ordinary cell without accumulating dangerously short telomeres. Telomerase was discovered in 1984 by Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider, working with Jack Szostak, and the three shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on how telomeres and telomerase protect chromosomes.

D
Most cancer cells reactivate telomerase, or use an alternative mechanism to maintain their telomeres, which is one of the reasons they can divide indefinitely rather than being restrained by the Hayflick limit that governs ordinary tissue. This observation has made telomerase an attractive target for cancer treatment: drugs designed to inhibit telomerase might, in principle, cause cancer cells to resume shortening their telomeres and eventually stop dividing, though translating this idea into an effective and safe therapy has proved considerably more difficult in practice than the underlying concept suggests, and no telomerase inhibitor has yet become a routine part of cancer treatment.

E
Telomere length has also attracted attention as a possible marker of biological ageing, since telomeres in many tissues tend to shorten as a person grows older, and several studies have linked unusually short telomeres, for a person's age, to a higher risk of certain age-related diseases. However, the relationship is far from a precise clock: telomere length varies considerably between individuals of the same age and is influenced by genetics, chronic stress, and lifestyle factors such as smoking, so measuring telomere length cannot reliably predict how long any particular individual will live. Commercial tests that claim to reveal a person's "biological age" from a telomere measurement remain scientifically contentious, and most researchers in the field caution against treating such results as more precise than the underlying science actually supports.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Epigenetics
passages.text:
A
Epigenetics is the study of changes in gene activity that do not involve any alteration to the underlying DNA sequence itself, yet can still be passed on when a cell divides. The word combines the Greek prefix epi-, meaning "on top of" or "in addition to", with genetics, capturing the idea that a layer of regulation sits above the genetic code, switching individual genes on or off without rewriting the code itself. Every cell in a person's body carries essentially the same DNA, yet a liver cell and a skin cell look and behave completely differently, a puzzle that epigenetics helps to resolve: the difference lies not in which genes are present but in which genes are switched on.

B
One of the best-studied epigenetic mechanisms is DNA methylation, in which a small chemical tag called a methyl group is attached to specific locations along the DNA strand, generally acting to silence the gene nearby. A second major mechanism involves modifications to histones, the proteins around which DNA is tightly wound to fit inside the cell's nucleus; chemical tags added to histones can loosen or tighten this winding, making the DNA in that region more or less accessible to the cellular machinery that reads genes and switches them on. Together, these mechanisms allow a cell to maintain a stable pattern of gene activity appropriate to its role, a pattern that is faithfully copied each time the cell divides.

C
Epigenetic patterns are not fixed for life. Diet, stress, exposure to toxins, and other environmental factors have all been shown, in various studies, to alter patterns of DNA methylation in humans and other animals. One frequently cited example comes from studies of the Dutch famine of 1944 to 1945, in which children conceived during the famine were later found, decades afterward, to carry distinctive methylation patterns at certain genes compared with siblings conceived before or after the famine, alongside a measurably higher risk of certain metabolic conditions in adulthood. Such findings suggest that a mother's nutrition during pregnancy can leave a lasting epigenetic mark on her child, though researchers caution that isolating the precise contribution of epigenetics from other confounding factors in this kind of historical study is genuinely difficult.

D
Whether epigenetic changes acquired during a person's lifetime can be passed on to their children remains one of the most contested questions in the field. In most cases, the epigenetic marks present in sperm and egg cells are stripped away and reset shortly after fertilisation, a process that appears to prevent most acquired epigenetic changes from being inherited. Some studies in animals, however, have reported that certain epigenetic marks appear to survive this resetting process and influence the traits of offspring, and in a few cases, of subsequent generations as well, a phenomenon known as transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. The extent to which this occurs in humans, and how significant an effect it might have, remains an active area of debate among researchers, and claims in this area are treated with particular caution because they are difficult to distinguish from other explanations, including shared environment and ordinary genetic inheritance.

E
Because faulty epigenetic regulation is implicated in numerous diseases, including many cancers, researchers have developed a class of drugs known as epigenetic therapies, which work by inhibiting the enzymes responsible for adding or removing methylation and histone marks. Several such drugs are already approved to treat specific blood cancers, on the reasoning that reactivating genes that have been abnormally silenced in cancer cells can restore normal cell behaviour or make the cells more vulnerable to other treatments. Unlike a mutation in the DNA sequence itself, an epigenetic change is, in principle, reversible, which is part of what makes epigenetic therapy an appealing avenue for future medicine, though as with many emerging treatments its use so far remains limited to a small number of specific conditions.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Neuroplasticity
passages.text:
A
Neuroplasticity is the capacity of the brain to reorganise itself by forming new neural connections, strengthening or weakening existing ones, and, to a more limited extent, generating new neurons throughout life. For much of the twentieth century, neuroscientists generally believed that the adult brain's structure was essentially fixed once childhood development was complete, and that any brain regions damaged by injury or disease would remain permanently impaired. Research since the 1960s has overturned this view, revealing an adult brain that continues to adapt and change in response to experience, learning, and injury far more than was once thought possible.

B
At the level of individual neurons, plasticity depends chiefly on synapses, the junctions where one neuron communicates with the next. A rule often summarised as "neurons that fire together, wire together" describes how synapses that are repeatedly activated in tandem tend to strengthen over time, a process called long-term potentiation, while connections that are rarely used tend to weaken and may eventually be pruned away altogether. This synaptic strengthening and pruning underlies much of learning and memory: practising a skill repeatedly reinforces the specific pattern of neural connections involved, which is part of why deliberate, repeated practice improves performance more reliably than occasional effort.

C
One of the most striking illustrations of neuroplasticity comes from studies of London taxi drivers, who must memorise the layout of thousands of streets to pass a notoriously difficult licensing examination known as "the Knowledge". Brain scans conducted by the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues found that experienced taxi drivers had a measurably larger hippocampus, a brain structure closely involved in spatial memory, than a comparison group, and that the size of this enlargement correlated with the number of years a driver had spent on the job. Because the study could not follow individuals from before they began training, it could not entirely rule out the possibility that people with an unusually large hippocampus were simply more likely to become taxi drivers in the first place, but later studies that did track trainees over time found the hippocampus growing measurably as they studied for the examination, supporting the conclusion that the training itself caused the change.

D
Neuroplasticity also plays a central role in recovery after brain injury, such as a stroke. When a stroke destroys neurons in one part of the brain, nearby or even distant regions can sometimes take over some of the lost function, particularly if the person undergoes intensive, targeted rehabilitation in the weeks and months following the injury. This capacity for compensation is generally greatest soon after the injury and gradually declines over time, which is why physical and occupational therapists typically emphasise beginning rehabilitation as early as safely possible. The degree of recovery achievable varies considerably between individuals and depends on factors including the size and location of the damage, the person's age, and how promptly and intensively rehabilitation begins.

E
Although the brain's ability to change persists throughout life, most researchers agree that plasticity is generally greater in childhood than in adulthood, a difference that helps explain why young children can often recover from severe early brain injuries far more completely than adults with comparable damage, and why learning a new language tends to come more easily before puberty than afterward. Nonetheless, evidence that meaningful plasticity persists well into old age has encouraged the development of cognitive training programmes and physical exercise regimens intended to help preserve mental function during ageing, although the scientific evidence for how much benefit such commercial "brain training" programmes actually deliver remains considerably more mixed than marketing for these products often suggests.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức thần kinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Synaesthesia
passages.text:
A
Synaesthesia is a neurological condition in which stimulation of one sense automatically and involuntarily triggers a perception in a second, unrelated sense. A person with grapheme-colour synaesthesia, the most commonly studied form, might perceive the letter A as inherently red or the number 7 as inherently green, not as a memory or association they consciously construct but as an immediate and involuntary perceptual experience, much like the way most people cannot help but perceive the sky as blue. Estimates of how common synaesthesia is vary considerably between studies, ranging from roughly one in twenty people to a much smaller fraction, depending on the exact criteria and testing method used.

B
More than sixty distinct forms of synaesthesia have been documented. Besides grapheme-colour synaesthesia, other reported forms include chromesthesia, in which sounds or music evoke the perception of colour, lexical-gustatory synaesthesia, in which spoken or written words trigger specific taste sensations, and mirror-touch synaesthesia, in which watching another person being touched produces a genuine tactile sensation on the observer's own body. A single individual may experience more than one type simultaneously, and the specific associations, such as which colour a given letter evokes, tend to be highly consistent for that individual over many years but vary considerably from one synaesthete to another, with no single mapping shared by everyone.

C
Researchers generally distinguish genuine, involuntary synaesthesia from ordinary associations by testing for consistency over time: a synaesthete asked to identify the colour they associate with a given letter will typically give the same answer with a high degree of accuracy when retested months or even years later, whereas a person asked to simply invent colour associations for letters shows far less consistency on retesting. This consistency test, developed largely by the psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen and colleagues in the 1990s, provided one of the first rigorous, objective ways to confirm that synaesthetic experiences are genuine perceptual phenomena rather than a form of vivid imagination or exaggerated memory association.

D
The neural basis of synaesthesia is not yet fully settled, but the leading explanation, known as the cross-activation hypothesis, proposes that synaesthesia arises from atypically dense connections, or from insufficient pruning of connections during early brain development, between neighbouring brain regions that would normally process their respective senses in relative isolation. Supporting this idea, brain-imaging studies of people with grapheme-colour synaesthesia have found unusually strong activity, and in some cases structural differences, in and around brain regions associated with colour processing when the person views ordinary black letters or numbers, even though nothing objectively coloured is present in what they are looking at. Synaesthesia often runs in families, and twin studies suggest a substantial genetic contribution, although the specific genes involved have proved difficult to pin down.

E
Far from being purely a curiosity, synaesthesia has been reported by a number of notable artists, musicians, and writers, including the composer Franz Liszt, who reportedly asked orchestras for "more blue" or "a little pinker" sound, and the novelist Vladimir Nabokov, who described his own experience of letters and colours in some detail in his memoirs. Researchers have also found that synaesthetes, on average, perform somewhat better than non-synaesthetes on certain tests of memory, a difference some researchers attribute to the additional sensory associations providing extra memory cues, though the effect appears to be modest and does not hold for every type of memory task studied. Rather than being classified as a disorder, most researchers today regard synaesthesia simply as an unusual but harmless variation in how the brain processes sensory information.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức thần kinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Bioluminescence
passages.text:
A
Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by a living organism, resulting from a chemical reaction inside or on the surface of the organism's body rather than from any external light source being reflected. It has evolved independently many times across the tree of life, appearing in bacteria, fungi, insects, and a remarkable diversity of marine animals, and researchers estimate that the great majority of light-producing species live in the ocean, particularly in its deeper, darker regions, where sunlight barely penetrates and bioluminescence may be the dominant source of light.

B
At the chemical level, bioluminescence typically arises from the reaction of a light-emitting molecule called luciferin with oxygen, a reaction catalysed by an enzyme called luciferase, releasing energy in the form of visible light rather than heat, which is why the process is often described as remarkably efficient compared with an incandescent light bulb, most of whose energy is lost as heat rather than light. Different groups of organisms have evolved chemically distinct versions of luciferin and luciferase, evidence that the ability to produce light arose independently many separate times over the course of evolution rather than being inherited from one single common ancestor.

C
Bioluminescent organisms use their light for a striking range of purposes. Fireflies use rhythmic flashes to attract mates, with the precise pattern of flashes often specific enough to identify the species producing it. The anglerfish, a deep-sea predator, dangles a bioluminescent lure above its mouth, generated by symbiotic bacteria housed in a specialised organ, to draw curious prey within striking distance. Many small marine organisms instead use a sudden flash of light defensively, either to startle a predator, to illuminate the predator itself and make it more visible to the predator's own predators, or to release a glowing cloud that distracts an attacker while the organism escapes into the darkness.

D
The Japanese scientist Osamu Shimomura spent decades studying the jellyfish Aequorea victoria, isolating from it a protein that fluoresces green under ultraviolet light, which he named green fluorescent protein, or GFP. Working later with Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien, Shimomura helped establish GFP as one of the most widely used tools in modern biology: by attaching the gene for GFP to a gene of interest, researchers can make a specific protein glow green inside a living cell, allowing them to watch, in real time, where and when that protein is produced and where it travels within the cell. The three scientists shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work, a discovery that began with a purely curiosity-driven study of a glowing jellyfish and ended up transforming how biologists visualise the inner workings of living cells.

E
Beyond GFP, bioluminescence continues to find practical applications. The luciferase enzyme from fireflies is widely used in laboratories as a sensitive marker of biological activity, since the amount of light it produces is directly proportional to the amount of a chemical called ATP present in a sample, allowing researchers to detect the presence of living cells, including bacterial contamination on food-preparation surfaces, with remarkable sensitivity. Researchers have also investigated bioluminescent bacteria as a possible source of low-energy ambient lighting, and some cities have experimented with bioluminescent algae to illuminate footpaths, though such applications remain far less efficient and far more experimental than conventional electric lighting for the time being.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Extremophiles
passages.text:
A
An extremophile is an organism that thrives in physical or chemical conditions that would be lethal to most other forms of life, such as extreme heat, cold, pressure, acidity, or salinity. Most known extremophiles belong to the domain Archaea, single-celled microorganisms that resemble bacteria under a microscope but differ from them fundamentally at the molecular level, though extremophile bacteria, and even a handful of extremophile animals, are also known. Far from being marginal curiosities, extremophiles have reshaped how biologists think about the limits of life and about where, in the wider universe, life might conceivably be found.

B
Thermophiles, organisms that flourish at high temperatures, were first studied intensively in the hot springs of Yellowstone National Park in the United States. In 1966, the microbiologist Thomas Brock isolated a bacterium later named Thermus aquaticus from a Yellowstone spring, at temperatures that had previously been assumed too hot to support life. Some extremophiles discovered since then, dwelling around deep-sea hydrothermal vents where mineral-rich water erupts from the seafloor, survive and reproduce at temperatures above 100 degrees Celsius, a feat made possible because the immense pressure at those depths keeps the water from boiling.

C
At the opposite extreme, psychrophiles thrive in permanently cold environments, including Antarctic sea ice and the deep ocean, where temperatures hover just above or even below the normal freezing point of water. Their cells contain specialised proteins and altered cell membranes that keep essential biological processes running at temperatures that would freeze the cellular machinery of an ordinary organism solid. Other extremophiles are adapted to extremes of a different kind: acidophiles tolerate the highly acidic water found in some mining-affected streams, halophiles thrive in salt concentrations many times higher than seawater, such as those found in the Dead Sea, and piezophiles are adapted to withstand the crushing pressure found in the deepest ocean trenches, several hundred times the pressure at sea level.

D
Beyond their scientific interest, extremophiles have proved unexpectedly valuable to industry. The enzyme isolated from Thermus aquaticus, known as Taq polymerase, can withstand the repeated heating to near-boiling temperatures required by the polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, a technique used to copy specific segments of DNA millions of times over for purposes ranging from criminal forensics to diagnosing infectious disease. Before Taq polymerase became available, researchers had to add fresh, heat-sensitive enzyme by hand after every heating cycle, a tedious and error-prone process that the heat-tolerant enzyme from a Yellowstone hot spring eliminated almost entirely, making PCR practical to automate and helping to transform modern molecular biology.

E
The existence of organisms that can survive such punishing conditions on Earth has also influenced the search for life beyond it. If life can flourish in boiling, acidic, or intensely cold and salty environments on this planet, astrobiologists reason, then similarly extreme environments elsewhere in the solar system, such as the subsurface ocean thought to lie beneath the icy crust of Jupiter's moon Europa, or the briny, sub-freezing water occasionally detected on Mars, cannot automatically be ruled out as potential habitats for life. This reasoning does not prove that life exists in such places, but it has significantly broadened the range of environments that space missions searching for extraterrestrial life now consider worth investigating.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Mycorrhizal Networks
passages.text:
A
A mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between a fungus and the roots of a plant, a relationship so widespread that an estimated ninety percent of land plant species form such partnerships with at least one fungal species. The fungus extends a vast network of extremely fine threads, called hyphae, through the soil far beyond the reach of the plant's own roots, absorbing water and mineral nutrients, particularly phosphorus, and delivering them to the plant. In exchange, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis, sugars the fungus itself, lacking chlorophyll, cannot manufacture on its own.

B
Because a single fungal network can connect to the roots of several different plants at once, sometimes of entirely different species, researchers have found that these networks can effectively link separate plants together underground, a discovery that gained wide public attention following research conducted in the 1990s by the ecologist Suzanne Simard in the forests of British Columbia. Using radioactive and stable isotopes as tracers, Simard demonstrated that carbon manufactured by one tree could travel through a shared fungal network and be taken up by a neighbouring tree of a different species, evidence that resources can move between plants that are not directly connected by their own root systems.

C
Popular accounts of this research have sometimes described the resulting network using the phrase "wood wide web", drawing an analogy with the internet, and have suggested that trees use these connections to deliberately cooperate, share resources altruistically, and even communicate warnings about insect attack to their neighbours. Many mycorrhizal researchers regard some of these popular characterisations as considerably overstated relative to the underlying evidence: while resource transfer between plants through fungal networks has been repeatedly demonstrated in controlled experiments, whether this transfer represents a coordinated, cooperative system actively benefiting the wider forest, as opposed to a largely incidental consequence of a fungus feeding several host plants simultaneously to its own advantage, remains a genuinely open and actively debated scientific question.

D
Even under the more cautious interpretation, mycorrhizal fungi provide plants with tangible benefits beyond nutrient exchange. Several studies have found that plants connected to an established mycorrhizal network show improved resistance to certain pathogens and greater tolerance of drought stress, effects thought to arise partly from direct fungal assistance and partly from chemical signals that appear to travel between connected plants through the network, priming a neighbouring plant's defences before an attack even reaches it. Seedlings that establish a mycorrhizal connection early in life also tend to survive at higher rates in many forest ecosystems than seedlings that fail to do so, which has practical implications for forestry and ecological restoration projects that plant seedlings without accounting for the state of the soil's existing fungal community.

E
The economic and ecological importance of mycorrhizal fungi has led to growing interest in applying them deliberately in agriculture, where intensive tillage, fertiliser use, and pesticide application can all damage or destroy naturally occurring mycorrhizal networks in farmland soil. Commercial mycorrhizal inoculants, containing fungal spores intended to be applied to seeds or soil, are now marketed to farmers and gardeners with claims of improving crop yields and reducing the need for chemical fertiliser, though independent trials have produced decidedly mixed results, working well in some soils and crops and showing little measurable benefit in others, a reminder that the practical value of mycorrhizal relationships, like much else in soil ecology, depends heavily on the specific conditions in which they are applied.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Genome Sequencing
passages.text:
A
Genome sequencing is the process of determining the complete order of the four chemical letters, adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine, that make up an organism's DNA. The human genome contains roughly three billion of these letters, and reading them out in order, base by base, was for decades one of the most ambitious technical challenges in the whole of biology, requiring not only new chemistry but new computational methods capable of assembling millions of short, overlapping fragments back into a single, continuous sequence.

B
The technique that made large-scale sequencing possible was developed in 1977 by the British biochemist Frederick Sanger, who devised a method, now known as Sanger sequencing, that could reliably read several hundred DNA letters at a time. Sanger had already won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1958 for unrelated work on protein structure, and the sequencing method earned him a second Nobel Prize in 1980, making him one of only a handful of people ever to receive the award twice. Sanger sequencing remained the dominant sequencing technology for roughly three decades and was the method used to complete the first draft of the human genome.

C
The Human Genome Project, an international collaboration launched in 1990 and involving research centres across the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, and China, set out to sequence the entire human genome using Sanger's method, applied on an industrial scale across dozens of laboratories working in parallel. The project, originally expected to take fifteen years, produced a working draft in 2000 and declared a essentially complete sequence in 2003, two years ahead of its original schedule, at a total cost of roughly three billion dollars, a substantial sum that nonetheless amounted to only about one dollar for each letter of DNA sequenced.

D
Since the Human Genome Project concluded, a family of newer techniques collectively known as next-generation sequencing has driven down the cost of sequencing a human genome with extraordinary speed, from the roughly three billion dollars spent on the original project to under a thousand dollars for a single genome today, a decline considerably steeper than the improvement typically seen in computer processing power over a comparable period. These newer methods work by simultaneously sequencing millions of short DNA fragments in parallel rather than one at a time, then relying on powerful computer algorithms to reassemble the fragments in the correct order by matching where they overlap, a task that would be utterly impractical to perform by hand given the scale involved.

E
The plummeting cost of sequencing has moved genomics rapidly from a purely research tool into clinical medicine. Sequencing a patient's genome can help identify the precise genetic cause of a previously undiagnosed rare disease, guide the choice of cancer treatment by revealing which mutations are driving a particular tumour's growth, and, through prenatal and newborn screening programmes, detect certain inherited genetic conditions early enough for treatment to begin before serious symptoms develop. At the same time, the growing availability of cheap, comprehensive genetic information has raised new concerns about privacy and potential discrimination, since a person's genome can reveal not only information relevant to their own health but also information about the likely genetic makeup of their biological relatives, who may never have consented to have that information disclosed.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Cambrian Explosion
passages.text:
A
The Cambrian explosion refers to a relatively sudden appearance, roughly 538 million years ago, of a striking diversity of complex animal life in the fossil record, after more than three billion years during which life on Earth had consisted almost entirely of single-celled organisms and simple, soft-bodied multicellular forms. Within a geological interval lasting perhaps twenty to twenty-five million years, brief by the standards of Earth's four-and-a-half-billion-year history, representatives of most major animal groups alive today, including the ancestors of arthropods, molluscs, and early relatives of vertebrates, appear in the fossil record for the first time, many already bearing hard shells or exoskeletons that fossilise far more readily than soft tissue.

B
Much of what is known about Cambrian animals comes from a small number of exceptional fossil deposits, called Lagerstätten, where unusually favourable conditions preserved not only hard shells but also soft tissues that are normally lost entirely to decay. The most famous of these is the Burgess Shale, discovered in the Canadian Rocky Mountains in 1909 by the American palaeontologist Charles Doolittle Walcott, which preserves an extraordinarily detailed snapshot of Cambrian marine life, including many bizarre animals with no obvious modern equivalent. A comparable, slightly older deposit called the Chengjiang biota, discovered in China's Yunnan province in 1984, has since provided further detailed evidence of the same burst of early animal diversity.

C
Several explanations have been proposed for why this diversification happened when it did, and most researchers now regard the true answer as a combination of several contributing factors rather than any single decisive cause. A sharp rise in atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels shortly before the Cambrian may have allowed animals to grow larger and support more energy-demanding tissues and behaviours than had previously been possible. The evolution of vision is thought by some researchers to have triggered an evolutionary arms race, since a predator that can see its prey creates powerful selective pressure favouring prey that can detect the predator in turn, or that develop hard defensive shells, which themselves further favour predators evolving harder mouthparts or better vision, a feedback loop that could accelerate diversification rapidly once it began.

D
The apparent suddenness of the Cambrian explosion troubled Charles Darwin himself, who acknowledged in On the Origin of Species that the abrupt appearance of complex animals, without an obvious long fossil record of simpler ancestral forms leading up to them, appeared at first glance to sit uneasily with his theory of gradual evolutionary change by natural selection. Darwin argued that the fossil record of the time was simply too incomplete to have preserved the earlier, presumably soft-bodied ancestors, and subsequent discoveries have partly vindicated this view: fossils of soft-bodied, complex, though comparatively simple, multicellular animals dating from the preceding Ediacaran period, roughly 635 to 538 million years ago, have since been found at numerous sites worldwide, suggesting that animal evolution was already well underway before the Cambrian explosion made it dramatically visible in the fossil record.

E
Rather than representing the literal sudden invention of complex animal life from nothing, most palaeontologists today interpret the Cambrian explosion as principally a dramatic increase in the rate at which animals evolved hard, readily fossilised body parts, combined with a genuine and rapid diversification of body plans that was likely already building on genetic innovations, particularly in the genes controlling embryonic development, that had arisen somewhat earlier during the preceding Ediacaran period. Under this view, the Cambrian explosion is less a mysterious violation of gradual evolution than an unusually well-preserved and dramatic record of a period of genuinely rapid, but not instantaneous, evolutionary change.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức cổ sinh vật học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Radiocarbon Dating
passages.text:
A
Radiocarbon dating is a method used to estimate the age of organic material, such as wood, bone, or textile fibres, by measuring the proportion of a radioactive form of carbon, carbon-14, that remains within it. The technique was developed in the late 1940s by the American chemist Willard Libby, who realised that living organisms continuously absorb carbon-14 from the atmosphere while alive, but stop doing so the moment they die, after which the carbon-14 already present in their tissues begins to decay away at a steady, predictable rate. Libby was awarded the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the method, which transformed archaeology by providing, for the first time, a way to assign approximate calendar ages to organic remains without relying on written historical records.

B
Carbon-14 is produced continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic rays collide with nitrogen atoms, and it exists alongside the far more abundant, stable forms of carbon, carbon-12 and carbon-13, in a roughly constant ratio throughout the atmosphere and in living organisms that exchange carbon with it. Once an organism dies, no new carbon-14 is taken in, and the carbon-14 already present decays into nitrogen at a rate described by its half-life, the time it takes for half of a given quantity of a radioactive substance to decay, which for carbon-14 is approximately 5,730 years. By measuring the remaining proportion of carbon-14 in a sample relative to the stable carbon isotopes, and comparing it against the known half-life, researchers can calculate how much time has passed since the organism died.

C
Because carbon-14 decays at a fixed, known rate, radiocarbon dating becomes progressively less precise for older samples and eventually reaches a practical limit: after roughly nine or ten half-lives, so little carbon-14 remains that it becomes difficult to measure reliably against background radiation, setting a practical upper limit for the method at around 50,000 years. This limitation means radiocarbon dating is well suited to material from within the last fifty millennia, spanning much of human prehistory, but useless for dating older fossils such as dinosaur bones, which are instead dated using other radioactive elements with much longer half-lives, or more often by dating the surrounding volcanic rock layers rather than the fossil itself.

D
An important complication is that the ratio of carbon-14 to stable carbon in the atmosphere has not remained perfectly constant over time, varying somewhat due to fluctuations in cosmic ray intensity, changes in the Earth's magnetic field, and, in recent centuries, human activity such as the burning of fossil fuels, which releases ancient carbon entirely depleted of carbon-14 into the atmosphere. To correct for these fluctuations, researchers have built detailed calibration curves by cross-checking radiocarbon measurements against material of known, independently verified age, most importantly the annual growth rings of long-lived trees, which can be counted directly, and, for material older than the oldest tree-ring records, layered deposits from lake sediments and coral. Radiocarbon dates are therefore always reported as a calibrated calendar age derived from these curves rather than as a raw, uncorrected measurement.

E
Radiocarbon dating has been applied to a vast range of archaeological and historical puzzles, from confirming the age of the Dead Sea Scrolls to establishing when humans first settled remote Pacific islands. One especially well-known application involved the Shroud of Turin, a length of linen cloth long venerated by some as the burial shroud of Jesus Christ. Radiocarbon testing carried out independently by three laboratories in 1988 dated the cloth's fibres to a range between roughly 1260 and 1390 CE, a result strongly suggesting a medieval rather than an ancient origin, though the finding has remained a subject of continued debate among some who question whether contamination or repair work on the cloth could have skewed the sample tested.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Cognitive Dissonance
passages.text:
A
Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort a person experiences when holding two or more contradictory beliefs, values, or attitudes at the same time, or when their behaviour conflicts with their own stated beliefs. The theory was introduced in 1957 by the American psychologist Leon Festinger, who proposed that this discomfort is not merely an unpleasant feeling to be tolerated but an active psychological drive, comparable to hunger or thirst, that motivates a person to reduce the inconsistency by changing one of the conflicting elements, whether that means altering a belief, changing a behaviour, or reinterpreting the situation to make the contradiction seem smaller than it really is.

B
Festinger developed the theory partly from an unusual piece of fieldwork. In the mid-1950s, he and his colleagues infiltrated a small group whose leader had prophesied that the world would end on a specific date, to observe what would happen to the group's beliefs when the prophecy inevitably failed to come true. Rather than abandoning their beliefs when the predicted apocalypse did not occur, many group members instead became more fervent believers, reinterpreting the failed prophecy as evidence that the group's faith had spared the world from destruction, a striking illustration, Festinger argued, of how people often resolve dissonance by revising their interpretation of events rather than by discarding a deeply held belief.

C
A classic laboratory demonstration of the theory, conducted by Festinger and James Carlsmith in 1959, asked participants to perform a deliberately tedious task and then to tell a waiting participant, actually an actor working with the experimenters, that the task had been interesting. Some participants were paid twenty dollars for this small deception, while others were paid only one dollar. Counterintuitively, the group paid just one dollar later reported finding the task more genuinely enjoyable than the group paid twenty dollars. Festinger explained this by arguing that the poorly paid group had insufficient external justification for having lied, and so experienced greater dissonance between their action and their true opinion, which they resolved by unconsciously convincing themselves that the task truly had been enjoyable, whereas the well-paid group could simply attribute their lie to the substantial payment and felt comparatively little need to revise their genuine opinion of the task.

D
Cognitive dissonance has since been used to explain a wide range of everyday behaviour. Smokers who are well aware that smoking is harmful to their health often report finding ways to minimise this discomfort, for instance by focusing on stories of long-lived relatives who smoked, or by exaggerating the difficulty of quitting, rather than simply quitting outright, since these mental adjustments reduce the dissonance between their behaviour and their knowledge of its risks more easily than changing the underlying behaviour does. Similarly, people who have made a difficult or costly decision, such as purchasing an expensive car, frequently seek out information confirming that they made the right choice while actively avoiding information suggesting they made a mistake, a pattern researchers describe as post-decision dissonance reduction.

E
Later researchers have refined and, in some respects, challenged Festinger's original theory. Some psychologists have argued that dissonance is best understood not as arising from any logical inconsistency in itself but specifically from a threat to a person's self-image as competent, moral, or consistent, a view known as self-consistency theory. Others have proposed that dissonance functions primarily as a signal that helps people avoid actions with genuinely harmful consequences, rather than as a general drive toward abstract logical consistency for its own sake. Despite these ongoing theoretical disputes, the basic observation that people frequently adjust their beliefs to fit their actions, rather than the reverse, remains one of the most well-replicated and widely cited findings in the whole of social psychology.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức tâm lý học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect
passages.text:
A
The Dunning-Kruger effect describes a pattern in which people with limited competence at a particular task tend to overestimate their own ability at that task, often quite substantially, because the very skills required to perform well are frequently the same skills required to recognise good performance in the first place. The effect is named after the psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger, who described it in a widely cited 1999 paper published after Kruger had noticed a newspaper report about a man who robbed banks with his face covered in lemon juice, apparently believing, wrongly, that the juice would render him invisible to security cameras.

B
In their original study, Dunning and Kruger tested university students on skills including logical reasoning, grammar, and humour, and then asked each participant to estimate how their own performance compared with that of their peers. Across all three tasks, participants who scored in the bottom quartile substantially overestimated their own ability, typically placing themselves around the fiftieth percentile despite performing considerably worse than that in reality, while the highest-scoring participants slightly underestimated their own relative standing, apparently assuming that a task which felt straightforward to them must feel similarly easy to everyone else.

C
The explanation Dunning and Kruger proposed centres on what they called a dual burden: a lack of competence at a task simultaneously prevents a person from performing it well and deprives them of the specific expertise needed to accurately judge good performance, whether their own or anyone else's. A novice chess player, for example, typically lacks not only the skill to play well but also the deeper understanding of the game required to recognise just how much stronger an expert's play truly is, making it correspondingly difficult for the novice to appreciate the full extent of the gap between their own ability and genuine expertise.

D
The Dunning-Kruger effect is frequently illustrated online using a graph showing confidence rising sharply with a small amount of initial knowledge, before dipping as a person becomes aware of the subject's true complexity, and then climbing again more gradually as genuine expertise develops, sometimes described informally as the "peak of Mount Stupid" followed by a "valley of despair". Although this graphic is a popular and intuitive way of depicting the general idea, Dunning and Kruger's original research did not actually plot confidence against increasing individual expertise over time in this way, and some psychologists have cautioned that the now-famous graph substantially overstates and oversimplifies the sequence of stages their data actually demonstrated.

E
In recent years, a number of statisticians have argued that at least part of the original Dunning-Kruger finding can be explained by a simple statistical artefact related to how the original data were compared, sometimes called regression to the mean, rather than genuinely reflecting a distinct cognitive bias unique to incompetence. Under this critique, comparing any two imperfectly correlated measurements, such as actual test performance and self-estimated performance, will tend to produce a similar pattern purely by chance, even using randomly generated data that contains no psychological effect at all. Dunning and other researchers in the original tradition have pushed back against this critique, arguing that while statistical artefacts may account for part of the observed pattern, converging evidence from other kinds of studies still supports a genuine, underlying psychological effect beyond pure statistical noise.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức tâm lý học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Game Theory
passages.text:
A
Game theory is the mathematical study of strategic decision-making among rational participants whose outcomes depend not only on their own choices but also on the choices made by others. Although the term evokes recreational games, its methods apply to a vast range of situations involving interdependent decisions, including business competition, international diplomacy, evolutionary biology, and the design of auctions, wherever the best choice for one participant depends on what other participants are expected to do.

B
The mathematician John von Neumann laid much of the field's early theoretical groundwork in the 1920s and 1930s, and the discipline was substantially developed in the landmark 1944 book Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, written jointly with the economist Oskar Morgenstern. A pivotal later contribution came from the mathematician John Nash, who in 1950 introduced what became known as the Nash equilibrium, a situation in a game in which no participant can improve their own outcome by changing only their own strategy while every other participant's strategy remains fixed. Nash shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this and related work, and his life later became widely known to the public through the film A Beautiful Mind, based on a biography of the same name.

C
Perhaps the most famous illustration in the entire field is the prisoner's dilemma, a scenario in which two individuals, arrested for a crime and questioned separately, must each decide independently whether to betray the other or to remain silent, without knowing what their accomplice has decided. If both remain silent, both receive a relatively light sentence; if both betray each other, both receive a moderate sentence; but if one betrays while the other stays silent, the betrayer goes free while the silent partner receives the harshest sentence of all. The dilemma illustrates a scenario in which each individual's own rational self-interest, considered separately, leads both toward betrayal, the Nash equilibrium of the game, even though mutual silence would objectively have produced a better outcome for both of them jointly.

D
In many real-world situations, the same interaction between the same parties recurs repeatedly over time rather than occurring only once, a variant known as the repeated or iterated prisoner's dilemma, and this repetition changes the strategic calculation substantially, since betraying an opponent in one round can provoke retaliation in future rounds. In a well-known computer tournament organised by the political scientist Robert Axelrod in 1980, in which submitted computer programs representing different strategies played the iterated prisoner's dilemma repeatedly against one another, a remarkably simple strategy called tit-for-tat, which cooperates on the first move and thereafter simply repeats whatever the opponent did on the previous move, outperformed every other, more elaborate strategy entered into the tournament.

E
Game theory has since been applied well beyond its original economic setting. In evolutionary biology, researchers use game-theoretic models to explain why cooperation and altruism can persist and even flourish among animals despite the seemingly stronger evolutionary logic favouring pure self-interest, since cooperative strategies can, under certain conditions, outperform purely selfish ones over many repeated interactions within a population. Auction designers draw on game theory to structure the rules of high-value auctions, such as those governments use to sell mobile phone spectrum licences to telecommunications companies, specifically to discourage bidders from acting strategically in ways that would otherwise depress the final price paid or distort the fairness of the outcome.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức kinh tế học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Behavioural Economics
passages.text:
A
Behavioural economics combines insights from psychology with economic theory to study how real people actually make financial and other decisions, in contrast to traditional economic models that typically assume decision-makers are perfectly rational, fully informed, and consistently self-interested. Where classical economics generally treats deviations from rational, self-interested behaviour as errors that can safely be ignored on average, behavioural economics instead treats these deviations as regular, predictable patterns of human decision-making that deserve to be studied and modelled directly, since they recur systematically rather than cancelling out at random across a population.

B
Much of the field's foundational research was conducted by the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, beginning in the 1970s. Their work identified numerous cognitive biases, systematic patterns in which people's judgements depart from what a purely rational calculation would predict, and heuristics, mental shortcuts that generally work reasonably well but occasionally lead to significant and predictable errors. One especially influential concept to emerge from this research is loss aversion, the finding that people typically experience the pain of losing a given amount of money considerably more intensely than the pleasure of gaining the identical amount, an asymmetry that helps explain a wide range of otherwise puzzling financial behaviour, including a reluctance to sell investments at a loss even when doing so would be financially prudent. Kahneman was awarded the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this research; Tversky, who had died in 1996, was ineligible, since the prize is not awarded posthumously.

C
Another central concept in behavioural economics is the framing effect, the finding that how a choice is presented, or framed, can significantly influence the decision a person makes even when the underlying options are logically identical. In a well-known illustration, people responded quite differently, in controlled experiments, to a medical treatment described as having a "ninety percent survival rate" compared with the mathematically identical treatment described as having a "ten percent mortality rate", generally rating the former description more favourably despite the two descriptions conveying exactly the same information. This sensitivity to framing has significant practical implications for how choices are presented to consumers, patients, and voters, since altering only the wording of a choice, without changing the underlying substance at all, can measurably shift the decisions people make.

D
The economist Richard Thaler extended behavioural economics into practical policy design, coining the term "nudge" to describe a small, low-cost change to how choices are presented that predictably steers people toward a particular decision without restricting their freedom to choose differently. A widely cited example involves automatic enrolment in workplace retirement savings plans: making participation the automatic default option, from which an employee must actively choose to opt out rather than actively opt in, has been shown in numerous studies to substantially raise participation rates, even though the actual financial terms on offer, and the ultimate freedom to decline, remain entirely unchanged. Thaler was awarded the 2017 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to behavioural economics, including this influential concept.

E
Governments around the world have since established dedicated behavioural insights teams, informally nicknamed "nudge units" in several countries, to apply these findings to public policy, addressing goals ranging from increasing tax compliance and organ donor registration to encouraging healthier eating and improving the uptake of government benefits that eligible citizens might otherwise fail to claim. While such interventions have generally proved to be inexpensive relative to more traditional policy tools such as financial penalties or large public information campaigns, critics have questioned both their long-term effectiveness in some domains and the underlying ethics of governments deliberately exploiting known cognitive biases to influence citizens' choices, even when the stated aims of doing so are broadly beneficial to those citizens.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức kinh tế học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).
