passages.title: The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis
passages.text:
A
The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, also known as linguistic relativity, proposes that the particular language a person speaks influences, to some degree, how that person perceives and thinks about the world, so that speakers of structurally different languages may experience certain aspects of reality in subtly different ways. The idea is named after the linguist Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf, though neither of them ever formulated a single, precise statement of the hypothesis; much of what is now called Sapir-Whorf theory was assembled and named by later scholars drawing on scattered observations in their writings.

B
Whorf's most famous, and most heavily criticised, illustration involved his claim, based on limited fieldwork, that the Hopi language of the American Southwest lacked grammatical structures for referring to time in the way English does, from which he inferred that Hopi speakers might conceptualise time altogether differently from English speakers. Later linguists, conducting more thorough fieldwork with fluent Hopi speakers, found that this claim was substantially inaccurate: Hopi does in fact possess ways of expressing temporal concepts, and the specific inference Whorf drew from his limited and, in places, mistaken data has since been widely rejected by linguists, becoming something of a cautionary tale about drawing sweeping conclusions about thought from limited grammatical observations.

C
Partly because of such early overreaching claims, a strong version of the hypothesis, sometimes called linguistic determinism, holding that language rigidly determines and limits the very thoughts a person is capable of having, has been almost universally rejected by contemporary linguists as demonstrably too extreme, not least because people can clearly think about, and later find words for, concepts their existing language does not yet have a convenient word for, and can readily translate ideas between structurally very different languages, if sometimes only with additional explanation. A much weaker version of the hypothesis, however, holding merely that language can subtly influence habitual patterns of thought and attention without rigidly limiting or determining what a person is fundamentally capable of thinking, has found considerably more support in rigorous modern experimental research.

D
One frequently cited body of supporting evidence for this weaker version comes from research on languages that use absolute directional terms, such as north, south, east, and west, for everyday spatial description, rather than relative terms such as left and right, a feature found in a number of Australian Aboriginal languages including Guugu Yimithirr. Speakers of these languages have been shown in careful experiments to maintain a remarkably precise, almost constant awareness of cardinal direction, a skill many speakers of languages relying primarily on relative terms find genuinely difficult to replicate even with deliberate effort, suggesting that habitually using a particular grammatical system for space may indeed train a distinct cognitive skill that goes well beyond ordinary language use itself.

E
Other well-studied areas of supporting evidence include research on colour perception and grammatical gender. Some studies suggest that speakers of languages with separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, as opposed to a single umbrella word covering the whole range as in English, can distinguish shades within that colour range marginally faster in controlled laboratory tasks. Similarly, in languages that assign grammatical gender to inanimate nouns, speakers have in some experiments been shown to describe those objects using adjectives stereotypically associated with the assigned grammatical gender, for instance describing a bridge assigned a grammatically "feminine" gender using words such as elegant or slender, and the same bridge assigned a grammatically "masculine" gender in a different language using words such as sturdy or strong, even though the physical object being described was, in each case, identical.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức ngôn ngữ học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The RSA Cryptosystem
passages.text:
A
RSA is a method of encryption that allows two people to communicate securely over an insecure channel, such as the public internet, without ever having to meet in advance to agree on a shared secret code. It belongs to a category known as public-key cryptography, in which each user generates a linked pair of keys, one public and one private, so that a message encrypted using the public key can only be decrypted using the corresponding private key, which the recipient keeps entirely secret and never shares with anyone.

B
The method is named after Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman, three researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who developed it in 1977 and published it the following year. Although RSA is widely regarded as one of the earliest practical public-key cryptosystems to be publicly disclosed, it later emerged that a British mathematician, Clifford Cocks, had independently devised a mathematically equivalent method in 1973 while working for the British intelligence agency GCHQ, but his work remained classified and unpublished for decades, meaning it played no role in the public development of the technology and had no influence on the wider adoption of Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman's independently discovered version.

C
The security of RSA rests on a simple asymmetry in ordinary arithmetic: multiplying two very large prime numbers together is computationally fast, taking a modern computer only a fraction of a second even for numbers hundreds of digits long, whereas taking the resulting large product and working backward to determine which two prime numbers were originally multiplied together, a process called factoring, is enormously more difficult and, for sufficiently large numbers, remains computationally infeasible using any publicly known method running on any conventional computer, even one running continuously for many years. A user's public key is derived directly from the product of two large, secretly chosen prime numbers, while the corresponding private key depends on knowing what those two original prime factors actually were, information that only the key's original creator possesses.

D
Because directly encrypting large amounts of data using RSA's underlying mathematics is comparatively slow, in practice RSA is rarely used to encrypt an entire message directly. Instead, it is typically used only to securely establish a separate, temporary shared secret key at the start of a communication session, a key that is then used with a much faster, though not itself capable of the same secure key-exchange trick, encryption method called symmetric-key encryption to encrypt the actual bulk of the data being transmitted. This combined, hybrid approach, using RSA's clever key-exchange properties briefly at the outset of a connection and a faster method for the bulk of the data afterward, is the basis of most secure web browsing today, indicated to users by a padlock symbol in their browser's address bar.

E
RSA's long-term security depends critically on the continued difficulty of factoring the very large numbers involved, and this assumption faces a genuine, though not yet realised, long-term threat from quantum computing. In 1994, the mathematician Peter Shor devised an algorithm, now known as Shor's algorithm, that would allow a sufficiently powerful quantum computer to factor large numbers dramatically faster than any known method running on a conventional computer, which would, if such a machine were ever built at sufficient scale, render RSA and several closely related cryptographic systems insecure. Because building a quantum computer powerful and reliable enough to run Shor's algorithm against real-world key sizes remains a formidable, unsolved engineering challenge, cryptographers have nonetheless already begun developing and standardising a new generation of so-called post-quantum cryptographic methods, believed to resist attack even from a sufficiently powerful future quantum computer, well in advance of such a machine actually being built.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học máy tính phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Turing Machine
passages.text:
A
A Turing machine is a simple, abstract mathematical model of computation, consisting of an infinitely long strip of tape divided into cells, each of which can hold a single symbol, together with a read-write head that moves along the tape one cell at a time, reading the symbol currently under it, writing a new symbol if instructed to, and moving left or right according to a fixed table of rules. Despite its extreme simplicity, the model, introduced in 1936 by the British mathematician Alan Turing, was designed to capture, in the most stripped-down form possible, the essential nature of what it means for a well-defined procedure to be mechanically computable at all.

B
Turing introduced the machine to answer a specific, abstract question posed by the mathematician David Hilbert, known as the Entscheidungsproblem, or decision problem: whether there exists a single, general procedure capable of determining, for any given mathematical statement, whether that statement is provable within a particular formal system of logic. Turing proved, using his machine as a rigorous mathematical tool, that no such general procedure could exist, since some mathematical questions are provably undecidable, meaning no algorithm could ever determine an answer for every possible input in every possible case. The American logician Alonzo Church independently reached an equivalent conclusion at almost the same time using an entirely different mathematical framework, and the closely related conclusions of the two men are jointly commemorated today in what is known as the Church-Turing thesis.

C
A particularly important variant Turing described is the universal Turing machine, a single machine capable of simulating the behaviour of any other conceivable Turing machine, given a suitable description of that other machine's rules encoded and provided as input data on its own tape. This concept anticipated, decades in advance, the fundamental architecture of the modern general-purpose computer: rather than requiring a distinct piece of hardware custom-built for every different task, a single, general machine can instead be reconfigured, purely by feeding it different software, to carry out an enormous range of entirely different computational tasks, a principle underlying essentially every computer in widespread use today.

D
One of the most consequential problems Turing analysed using his machine is the halting problem: the question of whether it is possible, in general, to write a single algorithm capable of correctly determining, for any arbitrary computer program and any given input, whether running that program on that input would eventually halt or instead continue running forever without ever terminating. Turing proved, using an elegant argument involving a hypothetical program applied to a description of itself, that no such general algorithm can possibly exist, a landmark result that placed a permanent, fundamental limit on what computers, no matter how fast or how cleverly programmed, can ever be made to determine about the behaviour of other computer programs.

E
During the Second World War, Turing applied his exceptional talent for abstract logical reasoning to a highly practical problem, working at Britain's Bletchley Park code-breaking centre to help defeat the German Enigma cipher machine, contributions that historians generally credit with shortening the war in Europe by a meaningful, though inherently difficult to quantify, period of time and saving a substantial number of lives as a direct result. Despite these wartime contributions, Turing was later prosecuted in 1952 under British laws that then criminalised homosexual acts, and he died in 1954 in circumstances that a coroner's inquest at the time ruled a suicide, an outcome some later biographers and historians have questioned. In 2009, the British government issued a formal public apology for his treatment, and in 2013 he received a posthumous royal pardon; the highest annual award in computer science, often described as computing's equivalent of the Nobel Prize, is named the Turing Award in his honour.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học máy tính phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Quantum Computing
passages.text:
A
A quantum computer is a machine that performs computation using the principles of quantum mechanics, storing and manipulating information not as ordinary binary bits, each of which must be either a definite 0 or a definite 1, but as quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in a quantum superposition of both states simultaneously until they are directly measured. This fundamentally different way of representing information allows certain carefully designed algorithms to explore a vast number of possible solutions to specific kinds of problems in parallel, offering the potential, for a narrow but genuinely important class of problems, to solve them dramatically faster than any conventional, classical computer ever could, no matter how powerful that classical computer might be.

B
Superposition alone does not fully explain a quantum computer's potential advantage; a second essential quantum property, entanglement, allows the states of multiple qubits to become correlated with one another in ways that have no equivalent in classical computing, so that the collective information stored across a group of entangled qubits cannot be fully described by considering each qubit's individual state in isolation. Physically realising and precisely controlling qubits has proved extraordinarily difficult in practice: current leading approaches include qubits built from superconducting electrical circuits, which must typically be cooled to temperatures colder than deep space to function, and qubits formed from individual trapped ions, held in place and manipulated using precisely tuned laser beams and electromagnetic fields.

C
A central practical obstacle facing every current approach is decoherence, the tendency of a fragile quantum state to lose its distinctive quantum properties through unavoidable interaction with its surrounding environment, an effect that current hardware can typically only forestall for a small fraction of a second before critical errors accumulate. Because of this fragility, a genuinely useful, large-scale quantum computer will likely require substantial quantum error correction, a technique that combines the information from many imperfect, error-prone physical qubits to construct a smaller number of much more stable logical qubits, though implementing effective error correction at the scale needed for genuinely useful large-scale computation remains one of the field's foremost unsolved engineering challenges.

D
In 2019, researchers at Google announced that a quantum processor they had built, containing 53 functioning qubits, had performed a highly specialised, deliberately obscure calculation, of essentially no independent practical value in itself, in around 200 seconds, a calculation the team estimated would have taken one of the world's most powerful conventional supercomputers roughly 10,000 years to complete, a claim the researchers termed quantum supremacy. Researchers at IBM subsequently disputed the specific estimate of how long a classical supercomputer would actually require, arguing that a more cleverly optimised classical algorithm could complete the same specific calculation in a matter of days rather than millennia, illustrating that comparative performance claims of this kind remain genuinely, and sometimes bitterly, contested within the field even when the underlying quantum hardware itself is not in dispute.

E
Despite this rapid, headline-grabbing experimental progress, most experts caution that today's quantum computers, often described as noisy intermediate-scale quantum, or NISQ, devices, remain far too small and far too error-prone to solve genuinely useful, real-world problems better than existing classical computers can already solve them today. Promising longer-term applications under active research include simulating complex quantum chemical and molecular systems relevant to drug discovery and battery design, a task classical computers handle exceedingly poorly precisely because those systems are themselves inherently quantum mechanical in nature, and certain narrow classes of optimisation problems in logistics and finance. Most researchers in the field estimate that a fault-tolerant, large-scale quantum computer capable of reliably delivering such practical benefits at meaningful commercial scale remains at least a decade away, and quite possibly considerably longer.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học máy tính phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Graphene
passages.text:
A
Graphene is a form of carbon consisting of a single layer of atoms arranged in a repeating hexagonal, honeycomb-like pattern, making it, at only one atom thick, the thinnest material ever isolated in a laboratory. Graphite, the common material used in ordinary pencils, is itself made up of many millions of these single atomic layers loosely stacked on top of one another, held together only weakly, which is precisely why a pencil can leave a mark on paper: pressing the pencil tip against the page shears off thin flakes of graphite, each flake made of many stacked graphene layers, that transfer onto the paper's surface.

B
Although graphene's theoretical existence had been discussed by physicists for decades, it was not successfully isolated as an actual, stable, freestanding material until 2004, when the physicists Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, working at the University of Manchester, extracted single-atom-thick flakes from ordinary graphite using an ingenious and famously low-tech method: repeatedly applying and removing ordinary adhesive tape to a piece of graphite, progressively splitting the stacked layers apart until, in some cases, only a single atomic layer remained on the tape. Geim and Novoselov shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for this achievement, a remarkably rapid interval of only six years between the initial discovery and the Nobel Prize, unusually short by the standards of physics, where major discoveries typically take many decades to receive Nobel recognition.

C
Graphene possesses an extraordinary combination of physical properties. It is roughly two hundred times stronger than steel of the same weight, while remaining remarkably flexible and almost completely transparent to visible light, transmitting more than ninety-seven percent of the light that strikes it. Electrically, graphene conducts electricity more efficiently than copper, and thermally it conducts heat away from a hot object more effectively than any other known material. This unusual combination of extreme strength, flexibility, transparency, and exceptional electrical and thermal conductivity, rarely found together in a single material, is what generated such extraordinary early excitement among materials scientists and technology companies following its successful isolation.

D
Despite this excitement, converting graphene's remarkable laboratory properties into cheap, reliable, large-scale commercial products has proved considerably more difficult in practice than initial enthusiasm suggested. Producing graphene of consistently high enough quality and purity for demanding applications such as high-performance electronics remains technically challenging and comparatively expensive at industrial scale, and many of the most ambitious early proposed applications, such as ultra-fast graphene-based computer processors intended to eventually replace conventional silicon chips, remain confined mainly to research laboratories rather than commercial products. Nonetheless, graphene has found its way into a growing, if still comparatively modest, range of niche commercial products already on the market, including specialised sporting equipment, certain smartphone touchscreen components, and additives used to strengthen composite materials in various industries.

E
Since graphene's initial isolation, researchers have identified and begun studying an entire broader family of comparably thin, two-dimensional materials with similarly striking properties, including hexagonal boron nitride, an excellent electrical insulator with a crystal structure closely resembling graphene's, and molybdenum disulfide, a two-dimensional semiconductor of particular interest for building extremely small, next-generation transistors. Researchers have also found that stacking several different two-dimensional materials together in a precisely controlled sequence, sometimes described informally as building a "van der Waals heterostructure", can produce combined materials with properties that neither individual constituent layer possesses on its own, a rapidly growing area of materials science that graphene's initial isolation in 2004 was directly responsible for opening up.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức vật lý phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Nanotechnology
passages.text:
A
Nanotechnology is the science, engineering, and application of matter at an extremely small scale, generally defined as structures measuring roughly between one and one hundred nanometres, a nanometre being one billionth of a metre, small enough that a single human hair is typically between 80,000 and 100,000 nanometres wide. At this scale, ordinary bulk materials often display physical, chemical, and electrical properties that differ markedly from how the same substance behaves in larger, everyday quantities, a consequence of quantum mechanical effects and the dramatically increased proportion of a material's atoms that sit at or near its exposed surface rather than buried deep inside its interior.

B
The conceptual foundations of nanotechnology are often traced to a 1959 lecture titled "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom", delivered by the physicist Richard Feynman, in which he speculated about the theoretical possibility of manipulating and arranging individual atoms directly, though he did not use the specific term "nanotechnology" himself, since that word was coined only later, in 1974, by the Japanese researcher Norio Taniguchi. The field did not become practically feasible until the development of specialised instruments capable of directly imaging and, in some cases, manipulating individual atoms, most notably the scanning tunnelling microscope, invented in 1981 by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, an achievement for which the two shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics.

C
Nanoparticles of gold provide a striking illustration of how dramatically properties can change at the nanoscale: bulk gold is the familiar, unreactive, yellow metal used in jewellery, but gold nanoparticles a few dozen nanometres across can appear vivid red or purple in colour and become chemically far more reactive than bulk gold, properties that depend sensitively on the precise size and shape of the individual nanoparticles involved. Medieval European artisans exploited this effect long before its underlying physical cause was understood scientifically, unknowingly incorporating gold nanoparticles into stained glass to produce vivid, stable red colouring, a technique whose true underlying physical mechanism was not correctly explained until modern nanoscience emerged many centuries later.

D
Nanotechnology has already found practical application across a wide range of industries. In medicine, engineered nanoparticles are used to deliver drugs directly and specifically to targeted cells, such as cancer cells, potentially reducing damaging side effects on healthy surrounding tissue compared with more conventional, less targeted drug delivery methods; the lipid nanoparticles central to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines are themselves a direct practical application of nanotechnology developed for an entirely different original purpose. In consumer products, nanoparticles are incorporated into sunscreens to more effectively block ultraviolet radiation while remaining transparent on the skin, into some textiles to make fabric more resistant to staining and water absorption, and into a range of electronic components to help continue shrinking the size of computer chips.

E
The rapid expansion of nanotechnology has also raised safety and regulatory questions that remain only partially resolved. Because engineered nanoparticles behave so differently from the same bulk substance, and can potentially penetrate biological barriers, including cell membranes, more readily than larger particles of an identical chemical composition, researchers have called for careful, ongoing, substance-specific study of their potential toxicity and environmental persistence, since it cannot automatically be assumed that a chemical substance considered generally safe in its familiar, bulk form remains equally safe when engineered into nanoparticle form. Most national regulatory frameworks governing chemical and consumer product safety were originally designed and written before nanotechnology existed as a mature commercial industry, and several international bodies and expert scientific panels have called for these older regulatory frameworks to be updated specifically to properly account for the potentially distinct risks that nanoscale materials, as opposed to the same substances in ordinary bulk form, may pose.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học vật liệu phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
passages.text:
A
The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek geared device, recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck near the small island of Antikythera, believed to have been used to predict the positions of the Sun, the Moon, and possibly other astronomical bodies, as well as to forecast eclipses, decades or even centuries in advance. Corroded almost beyond recognition after roughly two thousand years submerged in seawater, it survives today only as a fragmented, heavily encrusted lump of bronze, from which researchers have nonetheless managed to extract an extraordinary amount of detailed information using modern imaging technology unavailable to the divers who first recovered it.

B
The wreck itself, carrying a cargo of statues, coins, and various other luxury goods in addition to the mechanism, is generally dated to the first century BCE, and the mechanism is thought to have been built somewhat earlier, though its precise date of construction, its intended purpose in full detail, and the identity of its original maker remain subjects of ongoing scholarly debate. For decades after its discovery, the corroded, fused lump of bronze and internal gearing attracted comparatively little serious scientific attention, its true intricacy and sophistication not becoming apparent until later, more careful examination began.

C
The critical breakthrough in understanding the device came from X-ray imaging, first applied systematically to the mechanism by the British historian of science Derek de Solla Price in the 1970s, and considerably refined decades later by an international research team using advanced computed tomography, or CT, scanning technology. These imaging techniques allowed researchers to see, for the first time, the mechanism's complex internal gear-work without physically disassembling its fragile, corroded remains, revealing at least thirty separate interlocking bronze gears, arranged with a level of geometric and mechanical sophistication that had previously been assumed impossible for the ancient Greek world, comparable in intricacy, some researchers have suggested, to a mechanical astronomical clock not otherwise matched in surviving evidence for well over a thousand years afterward.

D
Detailed inscriptions found engraved on the mechanism's surviving surfaces, deciphered gradually using the same imaging technology, indicate that it could track the complex, irregular movement of the Moon across the sky using a clever gear train incorporating a deliberately offset pin-and-slot mechanism, an ingenious way of mechanically reproducing certain irregularities in lunar motion that had been recognised by Greek astronomers of the period, and could also predict the specific timing of solar and lunar eclipses using an ancient astronomical cycle known as the Saros cycle. A separate dial is believed to have tracked the four-year cycle of the ancient Olympic and other Panhellenic athletic games, an unexpectedly practical, calendrical addition to what is otherwise an overwhelmingly astronomical device.

E
No comparably sophisticated geared mechanism has ever been found from antiquity, nor does any surviving ancient text describe a device remotely resembling it in this degree of technical detail, a genuine puzzle that has led some historians to suggest that comparably advanced mechanical devices may once have been considerably more common in the ancient Mediterranean world than the surviving archaeological and textual evidence would otherwise suggest, their fragile bronze construction simply making long-term survival across two millennia extremely unlikely for all but this one fortunate exception, preserved precisely because it sank to the sea floor rather than being melted down and reused, the fate that ordinarily awaited valuable bronze objects once they became obsolete or fell out of active use.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khảo cổ học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Rosetta Stone
passages.text:
A
The Rosetta Stone is a fragment of a larger stone slab, inscribed in 196 BCE with a decree issued by a council of Egyptian priests affirming the royal cult of the young pharaoh Ptolemy V, carved in three separate scripts: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, a simplified, cursive Egyptian script used for everyday administrative purposes, and ancient Greek, the language of Egypt's ruling Ptolemaic dynasty at the time. Because all three inscriptions convey essentially the same decree, and because Greek could already be read fluently by scholars of the period, the stone offered the first genuine, reliable key that would eventually allow the long-lost meaning of Egyptian hieroglyphs to be recovered.

B
The stone was discovered by chance in 1799 by French soldiers under Napoleon Bonaparte's command, rebuilding a fort near the Egyptian town of Rosetta during Napoleon's military campaign in Egypt, and it soon attracted intense scholarly interest across Europe. Following Napoleon's eventual defeat in Egypt, the stone passed into British possession under the terms of a surrender agreement and was transported to London, where it has been held by the British Museum since 1802 and remains one of the museum's most visited single objects, though the Egyptian government has repeatedly and publicly requested its permanent return.

C
Deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, a writing system that had gone entirely unread for well over a thousand years by the time the stone was discovered, proved to be a slow, painstaking, and deeply collaborative international scholarly effort. The British polymath Thomas Young made significant early progress in the 1810s, correctly identifying that certain hieroglyphic symbols enclosed within an oval outline, called a cartouche, represented the sounds of a royal name, in this case Ptolemy, but Young ultimately reached an incorrect conclusion regarding the broader hieroglyphic writing system as a whole, wrongly believing it was used only for royal names and titles specifically rather than as a fully phonetic, general-purpose writing system capable of representing the sounds of the wider Egyptian language.

D
The definitive breakthrough came from the French scholar Jean-François Champollion, who had studied Egyptian Coptic, a later, spoken descendant language of ancient Egyptian still used liturgically by Egyptian Christians, alongside numerous other ancient and classical languages from an unusually young age. In 1822, building substantially on Young's earlier partial progress but going considerably further, Champollion demonstrated conclusively that hieroglyphs functioned as a genuinely phonetic script for ordinary Egyptian words generally, and not merely for foreign royal names transliterated into hieroglyphic symbols, a discovery that finally, and completely, unlocked the ability to read the vast body of surviving ancient Egyptian texts that had accumulated, entirely unread, over the preceding centuries.

E
The decipherment of hieroglyphs achieved through study of the Rosetta Stone transformed Egyptology from a field previously dominated by speculative, often wildly inaccurate guesswork about the meaning and purpose of ancient inscriptions into a rigorous, evidence-based academic discipline capable of reading ancient Egyptian texts directly and accurately for the first time in well over a millennium. Because of the stone's foundational importance to this transformation, the phrase "Rosetta Stone" has since entered everyday English usage as a general metaphor for any single key discovery, insight, or piece of evidence that suddenly enables the understanding, decoding, or interpretation of something that had previously seemed hopelessly obscure or entirely unintelligible.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khảo cổ học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Voynich Manuscript
passages.text:
A
The Voynich manuscript is a handwritten codex of around 240 surviving vellum pages, filled with page after page of text in an entirely unknown, unidentified writing system, accompanied throughout by elaborate illustrations of plants that do not correspond to any known real species, astronomical and astrological diagrams, and small human figures bathing in networks of interconnected pools and pipes, all rendered with a distinctive, internally consistent artistic style. It takes its modern name from Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish-American antiquarian book dealer who acquired the manuscript in 1912 from a Jesuit college in Italy, though the manuscript itself very clearly long predates him.

B
Radiocarbon dating conducted on the manuscript's vellum in 2009 placed its creation firmly in the early fifteenth century, most likely between about 1404 and 1438, a finding broadly consistent with independent stylistic analysis of its illustrations and handwriting by art historians. The manuscript's true author, its country of origin, and above all the specific meaning and purpose of its text, if the text was ever intended to carry any coherent, decodable meaning at all, remain entirely unknown despite more than a century of dedicated, often highly ingenious, scholarly and amateur attempts at decipherment.

C
The manuscript's unidentified script, now generally referred to by researchers as Voynichese, consists of somewhere between twenty and thirty distinct recurring characters, depending on precisely how variant letterforms are counted and classified, arranged into apparent words separated by clear spaces, in a manner that superficially resembles ordinary, natural written language. Detailed statistical analysis of the text has found that it does display certain measurable structural regularities genuinely characteristic of real natural languages, including consistent patterns in word length and word frequency distribution, yet it stubbornly refuses to yield to any of the conventional decoding techniques that have proved successful against every other historical cipher or unknown script previously subjected to serious, sustained scholarly attention.

D
Proposed explanations for the manuscript have ranged widely across the plausible and the wildly speculative. Some researchers argue it encodes a genuine natural language using an unusual, previously unattested writing system, possibly a lost or otherwise unrecorded language, or a known language deliberately disguised through some deliberately obscure encoding scheme. Others have proposed it is an early invented, wholly artificial constructed language, created for reasons no longer knowable to modern scholars. A more sceptical school of thought holds that the manuscript may in fact be an elaborate historical hoax, its pseudo-linguistic patterns generated through a purely mechanical process, such as a specific technique for shuffling and combining a small, fixed table of syllables, that could produce text with statistically language-like properties without the text itself actually encoding any coherent underlying meaning at all.

E
Despite the advent of powerful modern computational and statistical analysis techniques, and periodic, widely publicised claims of a definitive decipherment appearing in the media roughly once every few years, no proposed solution to the Voynich manuscript has ever achieved anything approaching broad acceptance among specialist scholars, and each new claimed breakthrough has so far been methodically scrutinised and ultimately rejected by other researchers in the field. The manuscript is now held at Yale University's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, where high-resolution digital images of every page have been made freely available online, allowing researchers and enthusiasts worldwide to continue attempting to solve what remains, more than a century after Voynich first acquired it, one of the most famous unsolved puzzles in the entire history of writing.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Library of Alexandria
passages.text:
A
The Library of Alexandria was one of the largest and most significant centres of scholarship in the ancient world, founded in the Egyptian city of Alexandria in the early third century BCE under the patronage of the Ptolemaic dynasty, the Greek-speaking rulers who governed Egypt following the death of Alexander the Great. Conceived as part of a broader research institution known as the Mouseion, dedicated to the Muses and functioning somewhat like a state-funded university and research academy combined, the library aimed at nothing less than collecting a copy of every significant text then in existence throughout the known ancient world.

B
Ancient sources describe an extraordinarily aggressive acquisition policy pursued by the library's directors, including a practice, described in several ancient accounts of varying reliability, whereby ships arriving in Alexandria's harbour were reportedly searched for scrolls, which the authorities would confiscate and copy, sometimes keeping the original for the library's own collection and returning only the copy to its original owner. Whatever the precise historical accuracy of this specific practice, which modern historians treat with some scholarly caution given the limitations of the surviving ancient sources, the library is generally agreed to have amassed a truly vast collection for its era, with ancient estimates, themselves imprecise and possibly somewhat exaggerated, ranging as high as several hundred thousand individual scrolls.

C
Contrary to the popular, dramatic image of the library's destruction in a single sudden, catastrophic fire, most modern historians now believe its decline was instead a considerably more gradual process, unfolding across several centuries and involving multiple separate, distinct episodes of damage and disruption rather than one clean, decisive event. Julius Caesar's military forces are generally believed to have accidentally set fire to at least part of the library, or to buildings closely associated with it, during fighting in Alexandria in 48 BCE, though ancient sources disagree considerably on the actual scale and severity of the resulting damage. Further, less dramatic decline is thought to have continued over subsequent centuries, driven by factors including diminishing royal patronage and funding, general political instability across the wider region, and the older, more prosaic force of simple long-term institutional neglect.

D
The library's scholarly output during its centuries of activity was genuinely substantial. Euclid, whose textbook the Elements would remain the standard introductory work in the field of geometry for well over two thousand years afterward, is believed to have worked at Alexandria, as did the astronomer and mathematician Eratosthenes, who famously calculated the circumference of the Earth with a comparatively small margin of error using nothing more than simple, careful geometric observation and reasoning, well over a thousand years before European sailors would circumnavigate the globe and thereby confirm his estimate through direct empirical means.

E
The eventual, definitive loss of the Library of Alexandria's full holdings, whatever the precise combination of causes and specific timeline actually involved, is now widely regarded by classical scholars and historians as one of the single greatest cultural and intellectual losses in the entire recorded history of Western civilisation, since a vast, genuinely irreplaceable body of ancient literature, scientific and philosophical treatises, and detailed historical records, much of it apparently never copied or preserved anywhere else, was almost certainly lost forever along with it. The library has since become a powerful and enduring symbol, invoked repeatedly across many later centuries, of both the tremendous, civilisation-shaping value of concentrated human knowledge and the profound, sobering fragility of even the largest and most carefully organised institutions dedicated to its careful, deliberate long-term preservation.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Printing Press
passages.text:
A
The printing press with movable metal type was developed in the German city of Mainz around 1440 by the goldsmith and inventor Johannes Gutenberg, whose central innovation was not the basic mechanical concept of a press, already long familiar from wine and olive presses, nor the idea of printed text itself, which had existed for centuries in East Asia using carved wooden blocks, but rather the combination of durable, individually cast, reusable metal type with an oil-based ink and a mechanical press, together forming a practical, integrated system capable of producing multiple identical copies of a text quickly, consistently, and relatively cheaply.

B
Gutenberg's most celebrated and enduring achievement was the so-called Gutenberg Bible, printed around 1455, of which roughly one hundred and eighty copies are generally believed to have been produced, printed partly on paper and partly, for a smaller number of especially prestigious copies, on the more expensive and durable material of vellum. Of these original copies, only forty-eight are known to survive today in various libraries and collections around the world, and surviving copies, on the rare occasions one has changed hands, have sold at auction for several million dollars each, reflecting both their extreme historical rarity and their foundational significance as the very first substantial book produced using movable type in Europe.

C
The printing press spread across Europe with remarkable speed following its invention: by the year 1500, only about fifty years after Gutenberg's initial breakthrough, printing presses were operating in well over two hundred and fifty European towns and cities, and it has been estimated that something in the range of twenty million individual books had already been printed continent-wide by that date, a genuinely staggering figure compared with the number of books that had been laboriously copied out entirely by hand in all the preceding centuries of European history combined.

D
This rapid, explosive expansion in the availability of printed material had transformative social and intellectual consequences that extended far beyond the technology itself. The Protestant Reformation, launched by Martin Luther in 1517, spread with unprecedented speed across Germany and much of the rest of Europe partly because Luther's writings, most notably his Ninety-five Theses, could be quickly and cheaply reproduced and widely distributed in printed form, reaching a substantially larger audience, and reaching that audience considerably faster, than any handwritten religious pamphlet realistically could have managed in the era immediately preceding printing. The printing press also gradually helped to standardise spelling and grammar within individual European vernacular languages, since printers naturally favoured consistent, uniform conventions across the many identical copies of a single work they produced, in place of the considerable regional and individual variation typically found in earlier handwritten manuscripts.

E
Historians frequently identify the printing press as one of the single most consequential inventions in the entirety of human history, credited with playing a central causal role in the later Scientific Revolution, by allowing researchers scattered across different countries to reliably share precise, accurately reproduced data and results with one another, and in the gradual, long-term rise of general literacy rates across European society, as books and other printed material slowly became cheaper and correspondingly more widely available to a much broader segment of the population than before. Although the specific claim that Gutenberg was the single, sole inventor of printing itself is sometimes qualified by historians, given the considerably earlier East Asian precedents involving both woodblock printing and, in Korea, movable metal type predating Gutenberg by roughly two centuries, his particular technological system is nonetheless generally credited with the specific, transformative impact it had on European society, culture, and intellectual life specifically.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Black Death
passages.text:
A
The Black Death was a devastating plague pandemic that swept across Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa between roughly 1347 and 1351, killing an estimated thirty to sixty percent of Europe's entire population within just a few years, making it, by most measures, the single deadliest recorded pandemic in the whole of human history. The disease is now generally attributed to the bacterium Yersinia pestis, though this precise causal identification was only conclusively confirmed through modern genetic analysis of the bacterium's DNA recovered from the teeth of medieval plague victims, work carried out in the early twenty-first century, well over six centuries after the pandemic itself had struck.

B
The pandemic is generally believed to have originated in Central Asia and to have spread westward along established, well-travelled trade routes, most notably reaching Europe in 1347 when a fleet of merchant ships arrived at the Sicilian port of Messina, unknowingly carrying rats infested with fleas that themselves harboured the plague bacterium. From Sicily, the disease spread with alarming speed across the rest of Europe, aided considerably by the dense, unsanitary conditions typical of medieval towns and cities and by the constant, sustained movement of merchants, soldiers, and travellers along established trade and pilgrimage routes throughout the continent.

C
Medieval physicians, working entirely without any concept of germ theory, proposed a wide range of explanations for the plague's cause, including the idea that it was spread through corrupted, foul-smelling air, known at the time as "miasma", and, in a deeply troubling development, the antisemitic conspiracy theory, entirely without foundation, that Jewish communities had deliberately poisoned local wells, a baseless accusation that led directly to horrific waves of violent persecution against Jewish communities across several parts of Europe during the pandemic. Medical treatments actually attempted at the time, including bloodletting and the lancing of the disease's characteristic swollen lymph nodes, generally proved entirely ineffective and were, in the case of certain treatments, actively counterproductive to a patient's chances of recovery.

D
Beyond the pandemic's catastrophic immediate human toll, historians have identified numerous significant longer-term social and economic consequences that followed. The sudden, dramatic reduction in the available labour force across much of Europe substantially increased the bargaining power of surviving peasants and skilled labourers relative to landowners, contributing over subsequent decades to the gradual decline of the feudal system of obligatory, largely unpaid agricultural labour that had previously dominated much of medieval European society. Some economic historians argue that this shift in bargaining power between labour and landowners indirectly helped lay important groundwork for the later economic and social transformations of the Renaissance period, though the precise causal weight properly attributable to the plague, relative to numerous other contributing historical factors operating over the same broad period, remains a genuinely contested question among specialist historians.

E
The bacterium responsible for the Black Death has never actually disappeared: Yersinia pestis still exists today, and isolated cases of plague continue to occur in various parts of the world, including in rural areas of the western United States, Madagascar, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, though modern antibiotic treatment, when administered sufficiently promptly after diagnosis, now makes the disease readily treatable and only rarely fatal in areas where such medical care remains reliably available and accessible, a stark contrast to the catastrophic, near-total absence of any effective treatment during the fourteenth-century pandemic.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Manhattan Project
passages.text:
A
The Manhattan Project was the codename for the United States-led research and development programme that produced the first functional nuclear weapons during the Second World War, formally established in 1942 following growing scientific concern, voiced most influentially in a 1939 letter to President Franklin Roosevelt co-signed by Albert Einstein, that Nazi Germany might be actively pursuing an atomic bomb of its own. Employing well over one hundred thousand people at its wartime peak, spread across dozens of secret research and production sites scattered throughout the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, the project represented an extraordinary, unprecedented concentration of scientific talent, industrial capacity, and government funding directed toward a single, overriding military objective.

B
The project was directed militarily by General Leslie Groves and scientifically by the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who assembled and led an extraordinary team of leading physicists, chemists, and engineers, many of them refugees who had personally fled Nazi-controlled Europe, at a purpose-built, previously nonexistent secret research town constructed specifically for the project at Los Alamos, New Mexico. The scientific and technical challenges the assembled team had to solve were genuinely immense, spanning everything from the extraordinarily difficult, resource-intensive task of separating and enriching the rare fissile isotope uranium-235 from the far more common uranium-238, to designing an entirely new class of weapon whose basic underlying physics had, until that point, existed only in abstract theoretical calculation rather than in any tested, working physical device.

C
The world's first nuclear detonation, codenamed Trinity, took place on 16 July 1945 in the New Mexico desert, producing an explosion considerably more powerful than even many of the project's own scientists had confidently predicted beforehand. Less than a month later, the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, on 6 and 9 August 1945 respectively, killing an estimated combined total of well over one hundred thousand people, the overwhelming majority of them civilians, in the immediate blasts and their direct aftermath, with substantially more dying in the following months and years from severe burns, acute radiation sickness, and a range of longer-term radiation-related illnesses and complications.

D
Japan formally surrendered on 15 August 1945, bringing the Second World War to its final conclusion, though historians continue to debate vigorously the precise relative importance of the atomic bombings, as opposed to other significant contributing factors, including the near-simultaneous Soviet declaration of war on Japan and subsequent invasion of Japanese-controlled Manchuria, in Japan's ultimate decision to surrender when and as it actually did. This question of the bombings' precise causal weight in ending the war remains one of the most extensively debated, and most persistently contested, topics in the entire historiography of the Second World War, with historians continuing to disagree substantially even after decades of subsequent archival research and analysis.

E
Several key scientists who had worked on the project, including Oppenheimer himself, later expressed significant public misgivings, and in some cases outright moral opposition, regarding the weapon's use and its subsequent, rapid post-war proliferation to other nations. Oppenheimer notably later remarked that the successful test had brought to his mind a line from the ancient Hindu scripture the Bhagavad Gita, describing himself as having become "death, the destroyer of worlds", and he subsequently opposed the post-war development of the considerably more powerful hydrogen bomb, a stance that ultimately contributed to his security clearance being controversially revoked by the United States government during the politically charged atmosphere of the early Cold War period.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Green Revolution
passages.text:
A
The Green Revolution refers to a set of agricultural research initiatives, technology transfers, and infrastructure investments occurring roughly between the 1940s and the late 1960s that dramatically increased crop yields across large parts of the developing world, most notably in Mexico, India, and Pakistan, and is generally credited with averting large-scale famines that many demographers and agricultural economists had confidently predicted, on the basis of rapid population growth outpacing food production, would otherwise strike substantial portions of Asia during that period.

B
The central figure most closely associated with the Green Revolution is the American agronomist Norman Borlaug, who spent decades working in Mexico developing high-yielding, disease-resistant varieties of wheat, including notably semi-dwarf varieties bred specifically to have shorter, sturdier stalks that could support the substantially heavier grain loads produced by increased fertiliser use without simply collapsing and falling over under that added weight, a persistent problem, known as lodging, that had previously limited how much fertiliser could be usefully applied to traditional, taller wheat varieties. Borlaug's semi-dwarf wheat varieties, once further adapted and refined for local growing conditions, dramatically increased yields when introduced to Pakistan and India during the 1960s, and he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 in explicit recognition of this contribution to global food security and the consequent prevention of large-scale famine.

C
The Green Revolution's package of innovations extended well beyond improved crop varieties alone. Its full implementation typically required substantially increased use of synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, expanded and more reliable irrigation infrastructure, and the more systematic use of chemical pesticides to protect the new, high-yielding varieties from insect damage and crop disease, together with the introduction of mechanised farm equipment in many regions. This combined technological package required considerably more capital investment than traditional subsistence farming methods had previously demanded, meaning that wealthier farmers, who could more readily afford these substantial upfront costs, often benefited disproportionately more, at least in the revolution's early years, compared with poorer smallholder farmers who frequently lacked comparable access to the credit and capital needed to fully adopt the same combined package of new technologies and inputs.

D
India provides one of the most frequently cited and dramatic examples of the Green Revolution's overall impact: the country's wheat production roughly tripled between the mid-1960s and the mid-1980s, transforming India within roughly two decades from a country that had depended heavily on substantial food imports and periodic international food aid into one that was, for the most part, self-sufficient in food grain production and, in certain years, even a net exporter of surplus grain. This dramatic transformation is widely credited with helping India avoid the kind of catastrophic, widespread famine that a number of prominent demographers and economists had confidently and publicly predicted for the country as recently as the 1960s.

E
Despite these clear and substantial benefits, the Green Revolution's longer-term environmental and social consequences have attracted considerable and sustained scholarly criticism. Heavy, sustained fertiliser and pesticide use has been linked in many regions to soil degradation over time, to the pollution of nearby rivers and groundwater through agricultural runoff, and to a marked reduction in agricultural biodiversity, since farmers increasingly concentrated cultivation on a comparatively small number of high-yielding varieties at the expense of numerous traditional, locally adapted crop varieties that had previously been grown, some of which have since become considerably rarer or effectively lost to cultivation altogether. Some economists and agricultural historians have also argued that the substantial economic benefits of the Green Revolution were not, in the end, always shared equitably among all farmers, with larger, wealthier landholders in some regions benefiting disproportionately relative to smaller, poorer farmers working comparatively marginal or less productive land.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử nông nghiệp phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Longitude Problem
passages.text:
A
For much of the age of sail, sailors navigating the open ocean could determine their latitude, their position north or south of the equator, with reasonable accuracy and relative ease, chiefly by measuring the angle of the Sun or known stars above the horizon. Determining longitude, a ship's position east or west, proved a vastly more difficult problem, since it depends on precisely knowing the difference in local time between the ship's current position and a fixed reference location, and no sufficiently accurate, reliable method existed for tracking that time difference at sea for the better part of two centuries of oceanic exploration and trade.

B
The consequences of this navigational shortfall were sometimes severe and occasionally catastrophic. In 1707, a British naval squadron, having significantly miscalculated its longitude while returning home in poor visibility, wrecked on rocks near the Isles of Scilly off the southwestern English coast, an incident that killed close to two thousand sailors in a single disaster and shocked the British public and government alike. Partly in direct response to this and other, less spectacular but still costly navigational failures, the British Parliament passed the Longitude Act in 1714, formally establishing a substantial cash prize, ultimately worth up to £20,000, a genuinely enormous sum of money for the period, for anyone who could devise a sufficiently practical and reliable method of determining longitude at sea to within a specified degree of accuracy.

C
Two broad, competing categories of solution to the longitude problem were seriously pursued during the eighteenth century. One approach, strongly favoured by many of the era's most eminent professional astronomers, relied on precisely and carefully measuring the position of the Moon relative to fixed background stars, a method requiring extensive astronomical tables, painstaking observation, and lengthy, error-prone manual calculation, but requiring no fundamentally new mechanical instrument beyond existing astronomical apparatus. The rival, mechanical approach instead required constructing an extraordinarily accurate seagoing clock, or marine chronometer, capable of reliably keeping precise time over long ocean voyages despite the ship's constant, often violent motion, significant changes in ambient temperature and humidity, and considerable variation in air pressure, a formidable and, to many contemporary experts, seemingly implausible engineering challenge.

D
The self-taught English carpenter and clockmaker John Harrison dedicated much of his working life, spanning several decades, to solving the mechanical, clock-based version of the problem, ultimately producing a succession of increasingly refined marine timekeepers, most famously a compact, watch-like device generally known as H4, which successfully kept sufficiently accurate time during an extended sea trial to Jamaica in the 1760s, comfortably satisfying the accuracy requirements originally specified by the 1714 Longitude Act. Harrison nonetheless faced years of persistent scepticism, bureaucratic delay, and outright resistance from the official Board of Longitude, several of whose most influential members had personally invested considerable professional reputation and effort in the rival, astronomically based lunar-distance method and were consequently reluctant to fully credit an unschooled tradesman's practical mechanical solution over their own preferred astronomical approach.

E
Harrison eventually received a substantial portion of the promised prize money, though only after direct royal intervention from King George III and years of additional, often bitter, dispute and advocacy on his behalf. His chronometers, and the many further design refinements and simplifications that swiftly followed from other clockmakers building on his fundamental design principles, eventually made accurate marine chronometers practical and affordable enough for widespread routine use throughout the British and other European merchant and naval fleets by the early nineteenth century, transforming maritime navigation and substantially reducing the previously severe and frequent risk of ships becoming dangerously lost or running fatally aground due to accumulated navigational error over the course of long ocean voyages.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức lịch sử khoa học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Bronze Age Collapse
passages.text:
A
The Bronze Age collapse refers to a widespread, remarkably rapid societal breakdown that struck much of the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East during the twelfth century BCE, bringing about the sudden or gradual fall of several major, previously flourishing civilisations, including the Mycenaean palaces of Greece, the Hittite Empire in Anatolia, and various New Kingdom Egyptian territories, along with the near-total disruption of the extensive, long-distance international trade networks that had previously connected these societies to one another for several preceding centuries.

B
Archaeological evidence indicates that dozens of major cities across the region were destroyed, abandoned, or both within a remarkably compressed span of just a few decades, and that literacy itself, along with monumental architecture and various other recognisable hallmarks of complex, centralised civilisation, disappeared entirely from several affected regions for centuries afterward, a phenomenon historians often term a genuine "dark age". Greece in particular experienced a documented and severe decline in population, a substantial and lasting loss of the sophisticated Linear B writing system previously used by Mycenaean palace administrators, and a pronounced simplification of material culture that persisted for several subsequent centuries before more complex, literate society gradually re-emerged.

C
Ancient Egyptian inscriptions attribute at least part of the widespread regional disruption to attacks by a loosely organised, poorly documented coalition of seaborne raiders that modern historians collectively refer to as the Sea Peoples, whose precise ethnic origin, homeland, and internal composition remain the subject of continuing scholarly debate and uncertainty. While Egyptian sources describe the Sea Peoples as a significant military threat successfully repelled by the pharaoh Ramesses III in a major recorded battle around 1175 BCE, most modern historians now regard them as more likely a consequence and visible symptom of the wider period's severe social, political, and economic instability, displaced groups set in motion by other underlying causes, rather than the primary root cause of the collapse itself.

D
Modern historians generally favour multi-causal explanations for the Bronze Age collapse rather than any single decisive event or cause. Climate scientists analysing preserved pollen samples and other environmental proxy records have found substantial evidence of a prolonged, severe drought across much of the Eastern Mediterranean region during roughly this same period, which would have significantly reduced agricultural yields and could very plausibly have triggered widespread famine, internal social unrest, and, quite possibly, the very population displacements that Egyptian sources attribute directly to the Sea Peoples. Other proposed contributing factors include a series of major earthquakes striking several key regional centres within a relatively short span of years, the systemic collapse of the tightly interconnected international trade networks upon which several Bronze Age palace economies had grown critically dependent, most notably for the reliable supply of tin needed to manufacture bronze itself, and a wave of internal social uprisings against the region's various centralised, palace-dominated political and economic systems.

E
The Bronze Age collapse is frequently cited by historians, archaeologists, and even contemporary policy analysts as a genuinely instructive historical case study in what is sometimes termed "systems collapse", the idea that several separate, individually survivable stresses, such as climate change, resource scarcity, and disrupted trade, can interact and compound one another in mutually reinforcing ways to produce a societal breakdown considerably more severe, widespread, and sudden than any single one of the individual contributing stresses could plausibly have caused on its own. Some contemporary researchers studying present-day risks to global economic and ecological stability have explicitly drawn on the Bronze Age collapse as a historical cautionary parallel when examining the potential fragility and interdependence of complex modern societies and their own tightly interconnected global systems.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khảo cổ học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Optogenetics
passages.text:
A
Optogenetics is a research technique that allows scientists to precisely switch individual neurons on or off using pulses of light, achieved by first genetically engineering the target neurons to produce light-sensitive proteins that would not otherwise be present in ordinary brain cells. Before optogenetics became available, researchers studying the brain were largely limited to comparatively blunt tools, such as electrical stimulation or targeted lesions, that typically affected many different intermingled types of neurons within a given brain region simultaneously, making it correspondingly difficult to determine which specific type of neuron, among the many present in that region, was actually responsible for producing a particular observed behaviour or physiological effect.

B
The light-sensitive proteins central to optogenetics, called opsins, were originally discovered in microorganisms such as algae and certain light-responsive bacteria, where they naturally serve to help the organism sense and respond appropriately to light in its immediate environment. Researchers, most notably Karl Deisseroth, Ed Boyden, and their respective research groups working in the mid-2000s, found that inserting the specific gene for one such opsin, called channelrhodopsin, into a mammalian neuron caused that neuron to become electrically active whenever blue light was subsequently shone directly upon it, providing an unprecedentedly precise, essentially instantaneous experimental switch for turning specific individual neurons on with a very high degree of both temporal and spatial precision.

C
To target only a single, specific type of neuron for genetic modification, out of the many different neuron types typically intermingled together within any given region of the brain, researchers combine the opsin gene with genetic techniques that restrict its expression, and thus its light sensitivity, exclusively to neurons that already naturally produce a particular other, unrelated protein unique or largely specific to that neuron type. Once the modified neurons are expressing the light-sensitive opsin, a thin optical fibre can then be surgically implanted to deliver precisely targeted pulses of light directly to that exact brain region, in an experimental animal such as a laboratory mouse, allowing researchers to switch the targeted neurons on or off with a level of precision, in both timing and location, that was entirely unimaginable using any previously available research technique.

D
Optogenetics has already substantially transformed neuroscience research. Researchers have used the technique to identify specific populations of neurons responsible for regulating a wide range of complex behaviours in laboratory animals, including aggression, specific fear responses, and various sleep-wake cycle transitions, by directly and precisely activating or silencing carefully targeted neurons and then closely observing the resulting behavioural changes in real time. In one particularly striking and widely cited experiment, researchers were able to artificially induce specific components of what appeared to be an aggressive behavioural response in mice simply by activating a very specific, carefully identified population of neurons within the hypothalamus, a brain structure previously suspected, but not definitively proven, to be centrally involved in regulating aggressive behaviour.

E
Although optogenetics remains overwhelmingly a laboratory research tool rather than an approved clinical treatment, researchers are actively exploring its potential therapeutic and clinical applications, most notably in restoring at least partial vision to certain patients with specific inherited forms of blindness, by genetically engineering surviving retinal cells that would not otherwise directly respond to light to express a suitable opsin protein instead. Early, cautiously encouraging clinical trials for this specific vision-restoration application are already under way, though optogenetic techniques intended for direct, widespread clinical use in humans still face substantial additional practical and regulatory hurdles, including the challenge of safely and reliably delivering the necessary genetic modifications to the correct human cells, and the invasive surgical requirement of implanting light-delivery devices directly and safely within living human tissue.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức thần kinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Cultured Meat
passages.text:
A
Cultured meat, sometimes also called cultivated or lab-grown meat, is genuine animal muscle tissue produced by growing animal cells directly in a controlled laboratory or industrial bioreactor environment, rather than by raising and subsequently slaughtering an entire living animal in the conventional way. The basic underlying process begins with a small sample of cells taken, typically via a comparatively minor and non-lethal biopsy, from a living donor animal, which are then placed in a nutrient-rich growth medium designed to encourage the cells to multiply, divide, and eventually mature into functional muscle tissue broadly resembling conventional meat in its basic biological composition.

B
The world's first publicly demonstrated cultured-meat hamburger was unveiled in London in 2013 by the Dutch researcher Mark Post and his research team, at a cost, for that single small patty alone, of roughly 250,000 euros, funded substantially by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, reflecting the extraordinary expense of the very earliest, still largely experimental production methods. Since that initial demonstration, production costs have fallen dramatically as researchers have refined growth media formulations, developed more efficient bioreactor designs, and identified cheaper alternative sources for various essential growth-promoting proteins, though cultured meat generally still remains considerably more expensive to produce than conventional meat from farmed animals in most current markets.

C
One particularly significant technical and financial challenge has been developing growth media that avoid using foetal bovine serum, a nutrient-rich substance extracted from unborn calves that was widely used in early cultured-meat research but is both extremely expensive and, since it still ultimately derives directly from a slaughtered pregnant animal, somewhat at odds with cultured meat's central ethical selling point of substantially reducing or eliminating direct animal slaughter for meat production. Researchers have since developed various serum-free growth media formulated instead from plant-derived or synthetically manufactured proteins, sugars, and other necessary nutrients, a development widely regarded within the field as essential for both bringing production costs down to commercially competitive levels and for cultured meat to fully deliver on its central ethical promise of essentially eliminating animal slaughter from meat production.

D
Proponents argue that cultured meat could substantially reduce the environmental footprint associated with conventional livestock farming, including its very substantial contribution to overall greenhouse gas emissions, its extensive demand for agricultural land and fresh water, and its well-documented tendency to enable and spread antibiotic resistance through the routine use of antibiotics in intensive conventional animal agriculture. Some independent life-cycle environmental assessments broadly support at least some of these claimed environmental benefits, particularly regarding land use, though the specific comparative greenhouse gas emissions of cultured meat, especially once its production is eventually scaled up to a genuinely large industrial scale, remain a matter of some continuing scientific and methodological uncertainty and disagreement, since the emissions produced depend heavily on the specific, currently unresolved question of what particular energy sources ultimately power the large-scale bioreactor facilities required.

E
Singapore became the first country in the world to approve cultured meat for direct human consumption, in late 2020, granting regulatory approval for a cultured-chicken product subsequently sold in a small number of local restaurants. Since that initial approval, the United States and several other countries have followed with their own separate regulatory approvals for various specific cultured-meat products, though the industry as a whole continues to face substantial remaining hurdles before it can realistically achieve significant, mainstream market scale, including further necessary reductions in production cost, building sufficient large-scale manufacturing capacity, and overcoming persistent, and in some markets considerable, consumer scepticism about the underlying safety, naturalness, and taste of meat grown directly from cells in a laboratory or industrial facility rather than from a conventionally raised animal.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học và công nghệ thực phẩm phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).
