passages.title: Autonomous Vehicles
passages.text:
A
An autonomous vehicle is a vehicle capable of sensing its immediate surrounding environment and navigating public roads with little or no direct, ongoing input from a human driver, relying on a combination of sensors, including cameras, radar, and often a laser-based sensing technology called lidar, together with sophisticated onboard computer software that interprets this continuous stream of sensor data in real time to identify other vehicles, pedestrians, road markings, and traffic signals, and then decides, moment by moment, how to respond appropriately.

B
The Society of Automotive Engineers has defined a widely adopted six-level scale, running from Level 0, meaning no automation whatsoever, up to Level 5, meaning full automation capable of handling literally any driving scenario a conventional human driver could handle, without requiring any human intervention or oversight under any circumstances. Most vehicles currently available for purchase by ordinary consumers offer, at most, Level 2 automation, meaning the vehicle can simultaneously control both steering and speed under certain limited driving conditions, but a human driver is still required to remain fully alert and ready to immediately retake full control at any moment, a requirement several vehicle manufacturers have been criticised for not communicating clearly enough to consumers in their marketing materials and product naming.

C
Companies such as Waymo, a subsidiary of Google's parent company Alphabet, operate a small but steadily growing number of Level 4 vehicles, commonly described as robotaxis, offering driverless rides to paying members of the public within certain carefully mapped and geographically restricted urban areas, a level of automation in which the vehicle can handle essentially all aspects of driving unassisted within its specifically defined and pre-approved operational area, without requiring any human safety driver physically present in the vehicle, but is not necessarily capable of reliably operating safely outside that carefully defined area or under unusual road and weather conditions its systems and mapping data have not been specifically designed and tested for.

D
Developing genuinely reliable autonomous vehicles has proved considerably more difficult in practice than many industry experts confidently predicted a decade ago, largely because of the sheer, effectively unbounded variety of unusual, unpredictable, low-probability situations, colloquially termed "edge cases" within the industry, that a vehicle operating in real, everyday traffic may unexpectedly encounter, ranging from a plastic shopping bag blown unpredictably across the road by a sudden gust of wind to a police officer manually directing traffic in a way that deliberately overrides standard traffic signals and posted road signs. Training a vehicle's underlying software to correctly recognise and respond safely and appropriately to the truly enormous range of such rare but individually consequential situations, many of which occur so infrequently that gathering sufficient real-world training data on them is itself extremely difficult, remains one of the central, unsolved technical challenges confronting the entire industry.

E
Autonomous vehicle crashes, though currently statistically rare in absolute terms relative to the enormous cumulative number of miles autonomous test vehicles have collectively driven, have attracted disproportionate media and regulatory scrutiny precisely because they raise novel and largely unresolved legal and ethical questions regarding liability when an autonomous vehicle's own software, rather than any identifiable human driver, is directly responsible for causing a collision. Regulators in different countries and even different states within a single country have adopted substantially different, and in some cases directly conflicting, legal approaches to testing, approving, and assigning legal liability for autonomous vehicles, and most industry analysts now generally expect the genuinely widespread, mainstream adoption of higher levels of vehicle automation to proceed considerably more gradually, and considerably more cautiously, than the more optimistic predictions confidently made throughout much of the previous decade.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học kỹ thuật phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Cephalopod Cognition
passages.text:
A
Cephalopods, a group of marine molluscs that includes octopuses, cuttlefish, and squid, possess by far the largest and most complex nervous systems found among any invertebrate animal group, a fact that has made them an object of intense and sustained scientific fascination given how evolutionarily distant they are from vertebrate animals, including humans, whose own comparably large and complex brains evolved along an entirely separate evolutionary lineage stretching back many hundreds of millions of years.

B
An octopus possesses roughly five hundred million neurons in total, a substantial number by invertebrate standards though still considerably fewer than the roughly eighty-six billion found in a typical human brain, but remarkably, only around one third of these neurons are located within the octopus's central brain proper; the remaining two-thirds are instead distributed throughout its eight arms, each of which contains its own substantial cluster of neurons capable of processing sensory information and directly controlling detailed, complex arm movements with a considerable, and only partially understood, degree of independence from the animal's central brain.

C
This unusual, highly distributed nervous system allows an octopus's individual arms to continue performing surprisingly sophisticated, coordinated tasks, such as exploring a crevice for hidden food or manipulating a small object, even when that specific arm's direct neural connection to the animal's central brain has been experimentally and reversibly severed under controlled laboratory conditions, a degree of functional autonomy essentially unheard of among vertebrate limbs, which typically become largely non-functional the moment their neural connection to the central nervous system is disrupted. Some researchers have consequently suggested that an octopus's overall cognition might be usefully understood as meaningfully distributed across its entire body, rather than being centralised almost exclusively within its brain in the way vertebrate cognition generally is.

D
Octopuses have demonstrated a genuinely impressive range of complex cognitive abilities in carefully controlled laboratory experiments, including reliably learning to navigate mazes, successfully solving multi-step physical puzzles to obtain food rewards hidden inside secured, screw-top jars, and, in several well-documented instances, apparently recognising and remembering specific individual human laboratory caretakers, in some cases directing what researchers interpreted as targeted behavioural responses, such as deliberately squirting water, at particular individual staff members they appeared to dislike or had previously found unpleasant or threatening in some specific way. Cuttlefish, close relatives of octopuses, have separately demonstrated, in one particularly notable series of experiments, an ability to delay immediate gratification, choosing to wait for a preferred food item rather than immediately accepting a less preferred one readily available sooner, a form of self-control historically associated in comparative cognition research primarily with certain relatively large-brained vertebrate species such as primates and corvid birds.

E
Cephalopod intelligence evolved along an evolutionary path entirely separate from, and largely independent of, the path that produced vertebrate intelligence, since the most recent common ancestor shared between cephalopods and vertebrates was almost certainly a comparatively simple organism lacking anything resembling a genuinely complex nervous system or brain. This makes cephalopods a particularly valuable subject for researchers specifically interested in convergent evolution, the broader biological phenomenon whereby unrelated evolutionary lineages independently evolve broadly similar complex traits, such as sophisticated cognition and problem-solving ability, in response to broadly comparable environmental pressures and survival challenges, suggesting that complex cognition of a broadly similar kind may be capable of arising through more than a single distinct evolutionary pathway across the wider animal kingdom.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức sinh học phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Ocean Acidification
passages.text:
A
Ocean acidification is the ongoing, measurable decrease in the pH of the world's oceans, caused chiefly by the ocean's continuous absorption of excess carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere primarily through the large-scale burning of fossil fuels. Since the start of the industrial revolution, the average pH of ocean surface water has fallen by approximately 0.1 units, which, because the pH scale is logarithmic rather than linear, actually corresponds to a roughly thirty percent increase in the overall acidity, or more precisely the hydrogen ion concentration, of ocean surface waters worldwide over that same period.

B
The underlying chemistry involved is comparatively straightforward: when carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater, it reacts chemically with water molecules to form carbonic acid, which subsequently dissociates further, releasing additional hydrogen ions that directly lower the water's overall pH. The ocean has absorbed, by various careful scientific estimates, somewhere between roughly twenty-five and thirty percent of all the carbon dioxide humans have released into the atmosphere since industrialisation began, a substantial buffering service that has meaningfully slowed the pace of atmospheric climate change but has come at a very real, largely hidden cost to marine chemistry and to the ocean ecosystems that depend directly upon it.

C
Increased ocean acidity poses a particular, well-documented threat to marine organisms that build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate, including corals, oysters, clams, and various species of free-floating microscopic plankton that together form the foundation of many marine food webs. As ocean water becomes more acidic, the availability of the specific carbonate ions these organisms require to construct and continuously maintain their shells and skeletons correspondingly decreases, making shell and skeleton formation measurably more energetically costly and, under sufficiently severe conditions, potentially causing existing calcium carbonate structures to begin dissolving away faster than the organism can effectively rebuild and repair them.

D
Laboratory and carefully controlled field experiments have demonstrated a range of measurable negative effects of increased acidity on various marine species, including reduced shell thickness and structural strength in oysters and other shellfish, impaired larval development in numerous fish species, and, in several particularly striking and well-studied experiments, altered, sometimes distinctly abnormal behaviour in certain reef fish, including a measurably reduced ability to detect the specific chemical scent of nearby predators, a change that would plausibly make affected fish substantially more vulnerable to predation under fully realistic, real-world ocean conditions outside the controlled laboratory setting. Coral reefs, already under severe and well-documented additional stress from rising ocean temperatures and the associated phenomenon of coral bleaching, face a genuinely serious compounding threat from acidification, since the carbonate skeleton that gives coral reefs their characteristic and ecologically essential three-dimensional structure becomes measurably more difficult for corals to build and to subsequently maintain as ocean acidity continues to rise.

E
Unlike some other, more spatially localised forms of environmental pollution, ocean acidification is a genuinely global phenomenon, since carbon dioxide readily mixes throughout the entire, interconnected global atmosphere before subsequently being absorbed into ocean water at a great many different locations across the planet, meaning that even ocean regions that are otherwise entirely pristine and free from any direct local pollution are nonetheless still measurably affected by acidification originating from fossil fuel emissions released anywhere else on Earth. Because reversing ocean acidification directly and rapidly is not realistically achievable using any currently available technology, most policy proposals for addressing the underlying problem focus instead specifically on substantially reducing the ongoing global emission of carbon dioxide, in order to slow the continuing rate of future ocean acidification, rather than on any proposed technology capable of directly restoring ocean pH to more historically typical, pre-industrial levels.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học môi trường phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Permafrost Thaw
passages.text:
A
Permafrost is ground, including soil, rock, and any ice or organic material it contains, that has remained continuously at or below zero degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years, though many extensive permafrost regions in the Arctic have in fact remained continuously frozen for many thousands of years without interruption. Permafrost underlies an estimated one quarter of all exposed land in the Northern Hemisphere, spanning large parts of Siberia, Alaska, and northern Canada, and in some particularly cold regions extends to depths of well over a kilometre below the frozen surface.

B
As global average temperatures continue to rise, permafrost across large parts of the Arctic has begun thawing at a pace that has genuinely surprised, and in some documented cases significantly alarmed, many climate scientists actively studying the region. Thawing permafrost causes the ground surface above it to subside unevenly, since the ice that had previously rigidly held frozen soil particles firmly in place gradually melts away, a process that has already caused serious, well-documented structural damage to roads, buildings, and other essential infrastructure across several Arctic settlements, in some cases requiring entire communities to be relocated to more geologically stable ground.

C
Beyond these immediate, highly visible structural and infrastructure concerns, permafrost thaw carries a considerably larger and potentially more consequential global climate implication: permafrost soils contain vast quantities of preserved organic material, chiefly the partially decomposed remains of plants, that accumulated gradually and were subsequently locked away in a stable, deeply frozen state, in many cases for many thousands of years, preventing the decomposition process from ever fully running its natural course. When permafrost thaws, microorganisms that had themselves lain dormant within the frozen ground for millennia become active once more and begin actively decomposing this long-preserved organic material, in the process releasing substantial additional quantities of carbon dioxide and methane, a considerably more potent greenhouse gas over shorter timescales, directly into the atmosphere.

D
Scientists estimate that permafrost across the Arctic collectively contains roughly twice as much carbon as is currently present in the entire Earth's atmosphere, meaning that widespread permafrost thaw has the clear potential to release a truly enormous quantity of additional greenhouse gas, substantially accelerating the pace of global climate change well beyond what is caused directly by human fossil fuel emissions alone. This phenomenon is frequently cited by climate scientists as a potential positive feedback loop, since warming causes permafrost to thaw, thawing permafrost releases additional greenhouse gases, and those additional released gases in turn cause further warming, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that could, under sufficiently severe conditions, continue to accelerate to some meaningful degree even if human-caused emissions were themselves brought under substantially better control.

E
Permafrost thaw has also unexpectedly revealed remarkably well-preserved biological remains, including the intact carcasses of woolly mammoths and other Ice Age megafauna, frozen and consequently preserved in a remarkably lifelike state for tens of thousands of years, providing scientists with an invaluable, otherwise unattainable source of ancient DNA and detailed soft-tissue anatomical information. However, thawing permafrost also raises separate, more troubling public health concerns of its own: in 2016, a notable anthrax outbreak in Siberia was directly linked by investigating scientists to the thawing of a decades-old reindeer carcass that had itself died of anthrax and had remained safely frozen and biologically inert until the surrounding permafrost thawed sufficiently to expose it, illustrating that long-dormant pathogens preserved within permafrost could, in certain specific circumstances, become an unexpected and genuinely novel public health hazard as the Arctic climate continues to warm.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học môi trường phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: Antimatter
passages.text:
A
Antimatter consists of particles that are, in a precise sense, mirror images of ordinary matter particles, sharing the exact same mass but carrying exactly opposite electric charge and certain other opposite quantum properties. The positron, the antimatter counterpart of the ordinary electron, was first predicted theoretically in 1928 by the physicist Paul Dirac, whose equations describing the behaviour of electrons unexpectedly permitted an additional, previously unanticipated solution corresponding to a particle identical to the electron in every respect except for carrying a positive rather than negative electric charge.

B
The positron was subsequently confirmed experimentally in 1932, when the American physicist Carl Anderson observed distinctive particle tracks in a cloud chamber, a specialised laboratory device used to visualise the paths of charged subatomic particles, that curved in a magnetic field in exactly the direction theoretically predicted for a positively charged particle possessing the same mass as an ordinary electron. Anderson was awarded the 1936 Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery, and Dirac himself had already separately received the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics for his earlier theoretical prediction of the positron's likely existence.

C
When a particle of matter encounters its corresponding antimatter counterpart, the pair undergo mutual annihilation, converting their combined total mass entirely into energy, generally in the form of high-energy photons, in scrupulously exact accordance with Einstein's famous mass-energy equivalence formula. This annihilation process is extraordinarily efficient at converting mass into usable energy, releasing considerably more energy per unit of mass than either conventional chemical combustion or even nuclear fission or nuclear fusion reactions, which has periodically led to popular, though currently entirely impractical, speculation about antimatter's theoretical potential as an extremely efficient future fuel or propulsion source.

D
Producing and, more importantly, subsequently storing antimatter for any meaningful, extended length of time is exceptionally difficult and correspondingly expensive in practice, since antimatter will annihilate essentially instantly upon coming into direct physical contact with any ordinary matter, including the walls of essentially any conceivable conventional storage container. Researchers instead confine antimatter particles using carefully configured magnetic and electric fields within a specialised device called a Penning trap, which suspends the antimatter in a small vacuum, keeping it held safely away from any direct physical contact with the container's ordinary-matter walls. Even with this specialised technology, only genuinely minuscule quantities of antimatter, measured in mere nanograms or even smaller amounts, have ever been successfully produced and stored by researchers worldwide, and the CERN research laboratory in Switzerland has estimated that manufacturing just one single gram of antimatter using current technology would cost several trillion dollars.

E
One of the deepest, most persistent unresolved puzzles in the whole of modern physics concerns the fundamental question of why the observable universe today appears to consist overwhelmingly of ordinary matter rather than antimatter, given that the standard, well-established theoretical models of the early universe strongly predict that the immense energy of the Big Bang should have produced closely equal quantities of both matter and antimatter in the universe's very earliest moments. Since matter and antimatter mutually annihilate one another completely upon contact, this observed, deeply puzzling matter-antimatter asymmetry implies that some subtle, currently not fully understood physical process must have very slightly favoured the production of ordinary matter over antimatter in the extremely early universe, and identifying the precise physical mechanism responsible for this small but decisive imbalance remains one of the leading open questions actively driving the entire field of particle physics research today.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức vật lý phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Space Elevator
passages.text:
A
A space elevator is a hypothetical mega-structure that would allow cargo and, potentially, human passengers to travel between the Earth's surface and orbit by riding mechanical climbing vehicles along a long, exceptionally strong cable, rather than being launched into space using a conventional chemical rocket, which currently remains by far the most expensive part of essentially any space mission. The basic conceptual idea was first proposed in a serious, technically detailed form by the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1895, inspired, according to popular later accounts, by his direct observation of the recently completed Eiffel Tower in Paris.

B
The fundamental physical principle underlying the concept relies on geostationary orbit, a specific altitude directly above the equator, roughly 35,786 kilometres above the Earth's surface, at which an orbiting satellite's own orbital period exactly matches the Earth's own daily rotation period, causing the satellite to appear to remain permanently fixed above precisely the same point on the Earth's surface at all times. A cable extending both downward from a suitably massive counterweight object stationed in geostationary orbit toward a fixed surface anchor point on Earth, and simultaneously outward beyond that same counterweight into space, could in principle remain held taut indefinitely by the combined, precisely balanced effects of Earth's gravity pulling inward and outward centrifugal force acting on the counterweight, without requiring any continuous engine power or propulsion to maintain its position and structural tension.

C
The single greatest technical obstacle preventing an actual, physically realisable space elevator from being built is straightforward but currently insurmountable material science: no material yet manufactured by humans possesses anywhere near the necessary combination of tensile strength and comparatively low density required for a cable of the enormous length involved to reliably support even its own weight under tension, let alone any additional practical cargo load riding along it. Carbon nanotubes, an exceptionally strong material discovered and characterised in the 1990s, are frequently proposed by enthusiasts and researchers as a theoretically promising candidate material, since individual carbon nanotube fibres tested under laboratory conditions have demonstrated tensile strength theoretically sufficient for the purpose, but manufacturing carbon nanotube cables of the vastly greater length, and with the very high, consistent structural quality, that an actual functioning space elevator would require remains, even today, considerably beyond current manufacturing capability.

D
Beyond the core cable-material problem, engineers have identified numerous additional serious practical challenges that would need to be solved before any space elevator could actually be built and safely operated, including safely and reliably powering climbing vehicles as they travel the enormous distance up the cable, a journey that could plausibly take several days at currently plausible climbing speeds; protecting the cable itself from micrometeorite impacts and the general hazard of increasingly abundant space debris in low Earth orbit; and managing the cable's structural interaction with severe high-altitude atmospheric winds and, at the ground anchor point itself, the additional risk posed by potential lightning strikes.

E
Despite these very substantial, currently unsolved engineering obstacles, proponents argue that a functioning space elevator, if it could ever actually be successfully built, would dramatically reduce the cost of launching cargo into orbit compared with conventional rocket-based launch, potentially by a factor of one hundred or considerably more, since a space elevator, once fully built and operational, would require vastly less energy per unit of cargo mass lifted than any chemical rocket, which must expend the overwhelming majority of its total propellant simply lifting the substantial weight of its own additional fuel. Several research groups, university engineering competitions, and at least one national space agency continue to actively study various aspects of the concept, though most experts in the field candidly agree that a fully operational, practically functioning space elevator likely remains, at an absolute minimum, several decades away, contingent above all on genuinely significant, currently unforeseen future breakthroughs in cable material science.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức khoa học vũ trụ phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Fermi Paradox
passages.text:
A
The Fermi paradox refers to the apparent, and genuinely striking, contradiction between the seemingly high statistical likelihood that intelligent extraterrestrial civilisations exist somewhere in our galaxy, given the sheer number of stars and, as researchers now know, planets involved, and the complete absence to date of any confirmed direct evidence, contact, or even indirect detectable signal from any such civilisation whatsoever. It takes its name from the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi, who is said to have posed the pointed, deceptively simple question "Where is everybody?" during an informal 1950 lunchtime conversation with fellow physicists at the Los Alamos National Laboratory.

B
The scale of the underlying puzzle becomes considerably clearer once the numbers involved are properly appreciated: the Milky Way galaxy alone contains an estimated one hundred to four hundred billion stars, a substantial proportion of which are now known, from direct astronomical observation, to host at least one orbiting planet, and the galaxy itself is roughly 13.6 billion years old, providing an immense span of time over which intelligent life, once it first arose anywhere within the galaxy, could plausibly have spread outward and colonised a very substantial fraction of it, potentially even using nothing more advanced than comparatively slow, sub-light-speed interstellar spacecraft, given a sufficiently long span of galactic time to do so.

C
Numerous, often mutually exclusive, explanations have been proposed for the apparent silence. One broad category of explanation, sometimes informally termed the "great filter" hypothesis, proposes that some extraordinarily difficult evolutionary or technological transition, a filter that most emerging forms of life or civilisation ultimately fail to successfully pass through, blocks the vast majority of potential civilisations from ever reaching the specific stage of interstellar communication or space travel required to actually be detected by others. Candidate great filters that have been seriously proposed include the specific, contingent origin of self-replicating life itself, the evolutionary transition to genuinely complex, differentiated multicellular organisms, and, more troublingly for humanity's own long-term prospects, some form of civilisation-ending technological self-destruction that might reliably occur shortly after a civilisation first develops sufficiently advanced technology.

D
Other proposed explanations do not require any single decisive filter at all. Some researchers argue that interstellar travel and long-range communication may simply be considerably more difficult, in practice, than optimistic early calculations assumed, given the immense physical distances and communication time delays genuinely involved even at the speed of light. Others suggest that intelligent civilisations might, for reasons not yet fully understood, generally prove to be comparatively short-lived relative to full galactic timescales, meaning that the specific, comparatively narrow windows of time during which any two civilisations could plausibly overlap and communicate with one another might simply be too brief and too improbably rare to have occurred yet by pure chance. A further, more speculative but frequently discussed possibility, sometimes called the zoo hypothesis, proposes that advanced civilisations may already be aware of humanity's existence but have deliberately chosen not to make contact, whether out of caution, respect for a young civilisation's own independent development, or some other motive not readily comprehensible from a purely human perspective.

E
The Fermi paradox has direct, practical relevance to ongoing efforts to search for extraterrestrial intelligence, most notably through the SETI Institute's long-running programme, established in 1984, of systematically monitoring specific ranges of the radio spectrum for any signal that might plausibly indicate deliberate artificial, rather than purely natural astrophysical, origin. Despite several decades of dedicated, sustained observational effort, no confirmed candidate signal has ever been positively identified, a persistent negative result that some researchers interpret as at least weakly supportive evidence for one or another version of the great filter hypothesis, though most researchers in the field readily acknowledge that the search conducted so far has covered only an extremely small fraction of the galaxy's total stars and only a correspondingly narrow slice of all the possible radio frequencies over which an advanced civilisation might plausibly choose to communicate.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức vật lý thiên văn phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: String Theory
passages.text:
A
String theory is a theoretical framework in physics that proposes replacing the point-like fundamental particles of conventional particle physics, such as electrons and quarks, with unimaginably tiny, one-dimensional vibrating strings of energy, so small that no experiment yet devised comes remotely close to being able to directly detect or resolve their proposed internal structure. According to the theory, the specific mode and pattern in which one of these fundamental strings vibrates directly determines which particular type of particle it appears to be to any outside observer, in much the same broad way that a single guitar string, depending on precisely how it happens to be vibrating, can produce many entirely different musical notes.

B
String theory was originally developed in the late 1960s in an unsuccessful attempt to explain the strong nuclear force, the fundamental force that binds atomic nuclei together, but was largely abandoned for that specific original purpose once an entirely different theory, called quantum chromodynamics, proved considerably more successful at explaining the relevant experimental data. Interest in string theory was subsequently revived and substantially expanded during the 1980s, once physicists realised that its underlying mathematical framework could, in principle, potentially provide a way of successfully unifying quantum mechanics, the physics governing the smallest subatomic scales, with Einstein's general theory of relativity, the physics governing gravity and large-scale cosmic structure, two extraordinarily successful theories that have otherwise stubbornly resisted every previous serious attempt at direct mathematical unification into one single, consistent framework.

C
One of string theory's most immediately striking and unusual features is its mathematical requirement of additional spatial dimensions considerably beyond the three familiar spatial dimensions of ordinary everyday experience. Depending on the precise specific mathematical version of the theory under consideration, string theory typically requires somewhere between ten and eleven total dimensions in order for its underlying equations to remain fully mathematically consistent. Proponents of the theory generally explain the fact that we do not directly perceive these additional dimensions in everyday life by proposing that they are "compactified", meaning tightly curled up into an extraordinarily small, subatomic-scale geometric shape at every single point in ordinary space, far too small for any currently conceivable experiment to detect their existence directly.

D
Despite several decades of substantial and sustained theoretical development by many leading physicists, string theory has yet to make even a single, uniquely specific, experimentally testable prediction that could clearly and decisively distinguish it from rival theoretical approaches to unifying physics, a significant and much-discussed limitation that has led a number of physicists to question, sometimes quite pointedly and publicly, whether string theory should properly be considered genuine, falsifiable empirical science in the traditional sense at all, given that a scientific theory is traditionally expected to make testable predictions capable of being proven wrong by experiment. Proponents of string theory generally respond that the theory's required extremely high energy scales, far beyond what any currently conceivable particle accelerator could plausibly ever achieve, rather than any fundamental defect in the theory's core underlying logical or scientific structure, is what has so far prevented direct, decisive experimental testing.

E
The broader mathematical framework of string theory has, regardless of its still entirely unresolved and contested status as a genuine physical theory of our actual universe, proved surprisingly and unexpectedly useful within pure mathematics itself, contributing productively to advances in several previously unrelated and quite distinct mathematical fields, including algebraic geometry and knot theory. Some physicists argue that this substantial mathematical utility alone justifies string theory's continued active study and development, regardless of whether it ultimately proves to correctly describe the actual physical universe we inhabit, while other physicists maintain that decades of research resources invested in a theory that has so far produced no directly testable predictions represents a genuinely serious and troubling opportunity cost for the wider field of fundamental theoretical physics as a whole.

— Biên soạn dựa trên kiến thức vật lý phổ thông (không sao chép nguyên văn Wikipedia).

passages.title: The Bystander Effect Reconsidered
passages.text:
A
In March 1964, a young woman named Kitty Genovese was attacked and killed outside her apartment building in Queens, New York. Two weeks later, The New York Times published a front-page story claiming that thirty-eight respectable, law-abiding citizens had watched the attack from their windows and that not one of them had called the police. The article caused a national sensation, and its central image of a crowd of indifferent spectators became one of the most widely repeated stories in the history of psychology. The editor responsible for the coverage, A. M. Rosenthal, later expanded it into a short book, arguing that the case revealed something disturbing about the coldness of modern urban life.

B
Among those who read the story were two young social psychologists, John Darley and Bibb Latané. They doubted that the witnesses were simply callous and suspected instead that the presence of so many other people had somehow inhibited each individual. To test the idea, they designed a series of laboratory experiments. In one, students talking over an intercom heard another participant apparently suffer a seizure. When students believed they were the only person who could hear, 85 per cent went for help before the seizure ended; when they believed four others were also listening, only 31 per cent did so. In a second study, rooms gradually filled with smoke, and participants sitting with two calm strangers were far less likely to report it than those sitting alone.

C
Darley and Latané proposed several mechanisms to explain these results. The first, which they called diffusion of responsibility, holds that the obligation to act is shared out among everyone present, so that each person feels only a fraction of it. The second, pluralistic ignorance, arises because people in an ambiguous situation look to others for clues about how to behave; if everyone remains outwardly calm, each concludes that nothing serious is happening. A third factor, sometimes described as evaluation apprehension, is the fear of looking foolish in public by overreacting to an event that turns out to be harmless. Together these processes seemed to explain how a large audience could produce no help at all.

D
For decades the Genovese case was presented in textbooks as the perfect real-world illustration of the effect. Yet when researchers returned to the original police files, the story began to fall apart. In 2007, Rachel Manning and two colleagues published a paper showing that there was no evidence of thirty-eight eyewitnesses. Most residents had heard only fragments of noise, few could see the attack clearly, and at least two people did contact the police. One neighbour went outside and held the victim as she was dying. The authors suggested that the tale had survived because it worked so well as a modern parable, not because it was accurate.

E
More recent work has also questioned how well the laboratory findings describe everyday emergencies. In a study published in 2019, a team led by Richard Philpot analysed more than two hundred violent disputes recorded by security cameras in Amsterdam, Lancaster and Cape Town. In nine out of ten incidents, at least one bystander intervened, typically by gesturing to calm the aggressor or physically pulling people apart. Crucially, the likelihood that the victim received help rose rather than fell as the number of onlookers increased. Although any single person may be less willing to act in a crowd, a larger crowd contains more potential helpers.

F
Psychologists have also identified the conditions under which strangers are most likely to step in. Help is more common when an emergency is unmistakable, when bystanders feel competent to deal with it, and when they share some kind of group identity with the victim. In one well-known experiment, Mark Levine invited football supporters of Manchester United to walk between two buildings, where they encountered a runner who had apparently fallen and hurt himself. Participants were far more likely to stop if the injured man wore a Manchester United shirt than if he wore the shirt of a rival club or a plain top.

G
These findings have practical consequences. First-aid instructors now teach that anyone needing assistance in a crowded place should single out one individual rather than calling for help in general terms, for example by pointing and saying, ‘You in the blue coat, phone for an ambulance.’ This simple instruction removes the ambiguity that fuels pluralistic ignorance and places responsibility on a single person. The broader lesson, many researchers now argue, is a reassuring one: the bystander effect is real, but people are considerably more willing to help one another than the legend of the thirty-eight witnesses once suggested.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học xã hội đã công bố.

passages.title: Too Much of a Good Thing?
passages.text:
A
Few ideas from behavioural science have travelled as far as the claim that too much choice is bad for us. It has been cited in business schools, advertising agencies and government departments, and it has shaped the design of everything from restaurant menus to pension schemes. The appeal is easy to understand. Most of us have stood in a supermarket aisle facing forty varieties of breakfast cereal and felt a vague sense of fatigue rather than delight. Yet an idea that seems obviously true is precisely the kind that deserves careful scrutiny, and the evidence for choice overload turns out to be considerably more complicated than its popularity suggests.

B
The story usually begins with an experiment carried out in a Californian grocery store and published in 2000 by Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper. On some days shoppers passed a tasting table offering twenty-four varieties of jam; on others, the table displayed just six. The larger display attracted more attention, with 60 per cent of passers-by stopping compared with 40 per cent at the smaller one. However, when it came to buying, the pattern reversed dramatically: about 30 per cent of those who saw the limited selection went on to purchase a jar, against only 3 per cent of those who had been offered the full range.

C
The finding was taken up enthusiastically, most influentially by the psychologist Barry Schwartz, whose 2004 book argued that an abundance of options leads not only to indecision but also to regret and dissatisfaction. Schwartz drew on an older distinction made by the economist Herbert Simon between people who try to find the best possible option, whom he called maximisers, and those who are content with something that is good enough. Maximisers, Schwartz suggested, are the chief victims of modern abundance: they invest more effort in their decisions and are often less happy with the results.

D
The jam study deserves its reputation as an elegant piece of research, but it was a single study in a single shop, and science is built on replication. When other researchers tried to reproduce the effect, the results were mixed at best. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne and his colleagues combined the data from fifty experiments on choice overload and found that, on average, the size of the effect was close to zero. In some studies large assortments discouraged people from choosing; in others they made people more likely to choose and more satisfied with what they had chosen. Rather than overturning the original result, this pattern suggested that something about the circumstances of each study determined whether a wider range of options helped or hindered the people making the choice.

E
This does not mean that the phenomenon is imaginary. A later analysis by Alexander Chernev and his co-authors suggested that the inconsistent results could be explained by identifying when overload is likely to occur. It appears to matter most when the options are difficult to compare, when people do not have clear preferences in advance, and when they are under pressure to make a decision quickly. Someone who already knows exactly which coffee they like is unlikely to be paralysed by a long list, whereas a first-time buyer of a complicated financial product may well be. Chernev's team also found that presentation matters: arranging options into clear categories, or ordering them by a single obvious criterion such as price, can noticeably reduce the sense of being overwhelmed.

F
That distinction is far from trivial, because some of the most important decisions people face fall squarely into the second category. An analysis of retirement savings plans in the United States found that each additional ten investment funds offered by an employer was associated with a fall of around two percentage points in the proportion of employees who joined the plan at all. Here, the cost of overload is not an unsold jar of jam but a lost opportunity to save for old age, and it is arguably in such cases that well-designed defaults and simplified menus can do the most good.

G
What, then, should we conclude? It would be a mistake to treat choice as a burden to be minimised wherever possible; people value freedom and variety, and many markets work well precisely because they offer both. Equally, it would be naive to assume that more options always serve consumers better. The real lesson of twenty years of research is that the effects of choice depend on context. Rather than repeating a single memorable anecdote, those who design products and policies would do better to ask who is choosing, how much they already know, and how much is at stake.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu kinh tế học hành vi đã công bố.

passages.title: The Marshmallow Test
passages.text:
A
Self-control is often described as one of the most valuable qualities a person can possess. It allows us to save money rather than spend it, to study for an examination instead of going out, and to resist the countless small temptations of daily life. For half a century, discussions of this quality have returned again and again to a deceptively simple experiment involving young children and sweets. Known popularly as the marshmallow test, it has been featured in bestselling books, television documentaries and even advertising campaigns, and it has encouraged many parents to wonder what their own children's ability to wait might reveal about their future.

B
The research began in the late 1960s at a nursery school on the campus of Stanford University, where the psychologist Walter Mischel and his students invited four- and five-year-olds into a small room. Each child was offered a choice between one small reward, such as a marshmallow or a biscuit, which could be eaten immediately, and two rewards if they were willing to wait until the researcher returned. The adult then left the room for up to fifteen minutes. Some children ate the treat almost at once; others managed to hold out for the entire period, and the researchers recorded exactly how long each child was able to wait.

C
The experiment might have remained a minor study of childhood behaviour had Mischel not stayed in touch with many of the families. Years later, when the children had become teenagers, he and his colleagues sent questionnaires to their parents and gathered information about their academic progress. The results appeared striking. Children who had waited longer in the nursery tended to be described as more competent adolescents, better able to cope with stress, and they had achieved higher scores on university entrance tests. To many observers, it seemed that a few minutes in front of a marshmallow could predict a lifetime of success. The findings, published in a series of papers in the late 1980s and early 1990s, quickly attracted attention far beyond academic psychology.

D
Mischel was at least as interested in how children waited as in whether they did. Watching through a one-way mirror, his team saw children cover their eyes, sing to themselves, kick the table or turn their chairs away from the tray. In later variations, researchers suggested different ways of thinking about the reward. Children who were encouraged to focus on its abstract qualities, for example by imagining the marshmallows as fluffy white clouds, waited considerably longer than those told to think about how sweet and chewy they would taste. Self-control, these studies implied, was not simply a fixed trait but partly a skill that could be learned.

E
The original work, however, had an important weakness: almost all of the children were the sons and daughters of Stanford staff and students, a highly educated and relatively wealthy group. In 2018, Tyler Watts and his colleagues repeated the analysis using data on more than nine hundred children from a much more varied range of backgrounds. They did find a link between waiting time at the age of four and academic achievement at fifteen, but it was only about half as strong as the earlier research had suggested. Moreover, once they took into account factors such as family income and the child's early language skills, the connection almost disappeared.

F
Other researchers have asked why a child might decide not to wait. In a study at the University of Rochester, Celeste Kidd and her colleagues first gave children a set of worn crayons and promised to bring better art materials soon. For half of the children the researcher kept this promise; for the other half she returned empty-handed. When the marshmallow test followed, children who had experienced the broken promise waited only about three minutes on average, while those in the reliable condition waited around twelve. For a child whose experience suggests that adults cannot be trusted, eating the marshmallow straight away may be an entirely rational decision.

G
Culture appears to matter as well. A study comparing children in Japan and the United States found that Japanese children waited longer when the reward was food, whereas American children waited longer when it was a wrapped present. The researchers linked this to everyday habits: Japanese children are commonly taught to wait until everyone is served before they begin eating, while American children often have to wait for birthdays or holidays to open their gifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that the marshmallow test measures not only a child's willpower but also the circumstances and customs in which that child has grown up.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học phát triển đã công bố.

passages.title: The Psychology of Waiting in Line
passages.text:
A
Waiting in line is one of the most universal and least loved experiences of modern life. We queue at supermarket checkouts, at airport security, on the telephone and, increasingly, in virtual lines on websites selling concert tickets. Richard Larson, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who has spent much of his career studying queues, once estimated that Americans collectively spend tens of billions of hours a year waiting in line. Mathematicians have long modelled how queues form and how quickly they can be cleared, but businesses have gradually realised that the length of a wait is only part of the problem. What matters just as much is how that wait feels.

B
A memorable illustration comes from an airport in Houston, Texas. Passengers there had begun complaining in large numbers about how long they had to stand at the baggage carousel. The airport responded in the obvious way, hiring extra baggage handlers and reducing the average wait to around eight minutes, which was well within industry standards. The complaints, however, continued. On closer investigation, managers discovered that passengers took only about a minute to walk from the arrival gate to the carousel and then spent the remaining time standing idle. The solution was to park arriving aircraft further from the main terminal, so that passengers had to walk roughly six times as far. Complaints fell almost to zero.

C
The Houston story illustrates one of the principles set out in 1985 by David Maister in an influential paper on the psychology of waiting. Maister argued that occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time, which explains why restaurants hand out menus to customers waiting for a table and why theme parks entertain visitors standing in line. He also observed that waits feel longer when people are anxious, when the length of the wait is uncertain and when no explanation is given for a delay. A passenger told that a train will arrive in twelve minutes is generally calmer than one left standing on a platform with no information at all.

D
Many organisations have found inexpensive ways of applying these ideas. Hotels have reduced complaints about slow lifts by installing mirrors beside them, giving guests something to look at while they wait. Telephone help lines play music and offer regular updates on a caller's position in the queue. Some theme parks deliberately display waiting times that are slightly longer than the actual figure, so that visitors who reach the front sooner than expected feel they have gained something. Such techniques do nothing to shorten the wait itself, yet they can make customers noticeably more satisfied with the same service.

E
Fairness is perhaps the most powerful factor of all. Larson has argued that what customers resent most is not delay in itself but the sense that someone else has been treated better. Few things are more irritating than choosing one of several checkout lines and watching a neighbouring line move faster. For this reason, many banks and post offices have abandoned separate lines in favour of a single snake-like queue that feeds several counters. Research suggests that the average wait is roughly the same in either system, but customers in a single queue are reassured by the knowledge that they will be served strictly in order of arrival.

F
Attitudes to queuing also vary between cultures. In some countries a disorderly crowd at a ticket window is accepted as normal, while in others jumping the queue is regarded as a serious breach of social rules and may provoke open anger. Britain is frequently described as a nation of orderly queuers, and historians have linked the habit to the rationing of food during the Second World War, when standing patiently in line became a public duty. Whether or not this explanation is correct, it shows how a queue can function as a small social system with its own unwritten code of behaviour.

G
Technology is now changing the experience once again. Many restaurants send customers a text message when their table is ready, allowing them to wait elsewhere, and some theme parks sell timed tickets that reduce the need to stand in line at all. Online systems can give customers a precise estimate of their waiting time, removing much of the uncertainty that Maister identified as a source of stress. These innovations may eventually make the traditional queue less common, but the lesson of decades of research is likely to remain relevant: people judge a wait less by the minutes it takes than by how fairly and how pleasantly those minutes are spent.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu về vận trù học và tâm lý dịch vụ đã công bố.

passages.title: In Defence of Boredom
passages.text:
A
Boredom has a poor reputation. It is associated with idleness, restlessness and, in children, with bad behaviour, and an entire industry of entertainment now exists to ensure that we never have to experience it. Smartphones in particular have made it possible to fill every spare moment, whether we are waiting for a bus, standing in a queue or sitting in a doctor's surgery. Yet a growing body of psychological research suggests that this constant escape may come at a price. Boredom, it seems, is not simply an unpleasant state to be eliminated but a signal that serves a purpose, and occasionally it may even be good for us.

B
Defining boredom is harder than it sounds. The psychologist John Eastwood, of York University in Toronto, has described it as the uncomfortable experience of wanting to engage in a satisfying activity but being unable to do so. This definition helps to distinguish boredom from mere relaxation: a person lying contentedly on a beach is not bored, whereas a person stuck in a meeting that seems pointless very often is. More recently, Erin Westgate has proposed that boredom arises from two separate problems, namely a lack of meaning in what we are doing and a mismatch between the demands of a task and the attention we are able to give it.

C
How strongly do people wish to avoid this feeling? A striking answer came from a series of studies led by Timothy Wilson at the University of Virginia and published in 2014. Participants were asked to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes with nothing to do except think. Most reported that they found the experience unpleasant. In one version, participants were given the option of pressing a button that delivered a mild electric shock, which they had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. Remarkably, around two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts.

D
If boredom is so aversive, could it ever be useful? The British psychologist Sandi Mann believes it can. In one experiment, she asked one group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers out of a telephone directory, a task chosen precisely because it was so tedious. Afterwards, they and a control group were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had endured the boring task came up with more ideas, and more original ones. Mann's explanation is that a dull activity encourages the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows the brain to make unexpected connections between ideas.

E
This interpretation fits with research on what neuroscientists call the default mode network, a set of brain regions that becomes more active when we are not focused on an external task. Activity in this network has been linked with imagination, planning for the future and reflecting on our own experiences. The important point is that these processes appear to need unstructured time in which to operate. If every gap in the day is immediately filled with messages, videos and news, the mind may rarely enter this reflective state, and some of the benefits of an idle moment may be lost without our noticing. Some researchers believe that this is one reason why good ideas so often seem to arrive in the shower or on a long walk, when attention is free to drift.

F
None of this means that boredom should be welcomed uncritically. Chronic boredom, as opposed to the passing kind, is associated with depression, overeating and risky behaviour, and nobody would recommend that a pupil in an uninspiring lesson simply learn to enjoy the experience. The more modest claim is that occasional boredom is a normal part of life and that our determination to avoid it at all costs may be counterproductive. Adults who rush to entertain children the moment they complain of having nothing to do may, with the best of intentions, be depriving them of an opportunity to develop their own resources.

G
The philosopher Bertrand Russell made a similar point almost a century ago, warning that a generation unable to endure boredom would achieve little of lasting value. Russell could not have imagined the devices that now compete for our attention, but his warning seems more relevant than ever. Learning to tolerate a few minutes of emptiness, without reaching for a screen, may be a small but worthwhile discipline. Boredom tells us that something in our situation needs to change; if we silence that message too quickly, we may never discover what we might have done instead.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học đã công bố.

passages.title: Nudging Citizens
passages.text:
A
Traditional economic theory assumed that people make decisions rationally, weighing costs and benefits carefully and choosing whatever serves their interests best. Governments that wanted to change behaviour therefore relied mainly on two tools: laws, which forbid or require certain actions, and financial incentives, such as taxes and subsidies. Over the last few decades, however, psychologists and behavioural economists have assembled extensive evidence that real people often behave in ways the textbook model cannot explain. We procrastinate, follow the crowd, stick with whatever option is presented as standard and are strongly influenced by the way information is framed. These insights have given rise to a third approach to public policy, commonly known as nudging. Since then, the approach has influenced policy in dozens of countries.

B
The term was popularised by the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein in a book published in 2008. A nudge, they explained, is any feature of the environment in which a choice is made that alters people's behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives. Placing fruit at eye level in a school canteen, rather than banning chocolate, is a nudge. Thaler and Sunstein described their philosophy as libertarian paternalism: paternalistic because it aims to steer people towards choices that improve their lives, and libertarian because everyone remains free to choose otherwise. Thaler was awarded the Nobel Prize in economics in 2017, partly in recognition of this work.

C
One of the most powerful nudges is the default, the option that takes effect if a person does nothing. Organ donation provides a well-known example. In countries where citizens must actively register as donors, the proportion who do so is often low, while in neighbouring countries with similar cultures, where everyone is presumed to consent unless they opt out, the proportion can be close to universal. Pensions offer another case. When the United Kingdom began automatically enrolling employees in workplace pension schemes in 2012, leaving them free to withdraw, participation rose sharply, because most people simply accepted the arrangement they had been given.

D
Governments were quick to take an interest. In 2010 the British government created the Behavioural Insights Team, informally known as the Nudge Unit, to apply these ideas to public services. One of its best-known projects concerned overdue taxes. Letters sent to people who had not paid were rewritten to include a simple statement that most people in their area had already paid on time. This small change, which cost almost nothing, increased the number of people paying promptly and brought in millions of pounds of additional revenue. Within a few years, similar units had been established by governments and international organisations around the world.

E
Some interventions became famous partly because they are so simple. At Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, the image of a small fly was etched into the men's urinals, giving users something to aim at, and the airport reported a large fall in the amount of cleaning required. Supermarkets have long used similar techniques for commercial purposes, placing high-profit items where shoppers are most likely to see them. Advocates of nudging argue that, since every environment influences choices in some way, it makes sense to design environments deliberately in ways that benefit the people using them, rather than leaving the outcome to chance or to commercial interests.

F
Critics raise two main objections. The first is ethical: nudges, they argue, work by exploiting weaknesses in human thinking, and governments should persuade citizens through reasoned argument rather than steer them without their full awareness. Supporters reply that most nudges are transparent and that people can easily reject them. The second objection concerns effectiveness. A study published in 2022 by Stefano DellaVigna and Elizabeth Linos compared the results of academic experiments with those of trials actually carried out by nudge units. The average effect in the academic studies was several times larger, suggesting that published research had overstated what nudges could achieve in practice.

G
A balanced view would accept that nudges are neither a miracle cure nor a dangerous form of manipulation. Many of the problems that governments face, such as climate change or rising obesity, are too large to be solved by redesigning letters or rearranging canteen shelves, and they will continue to require regulation and investment. Yet nudges are cheap and can be tested rapidly, and even modest improvements, multiplied across millions of people, may produce substantial benefits. The most sensible approach, many researchers now conclude, is to treat behavioural insights as one tool among many, to be evaluated carefully rather than adopted on faith.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu kinh tế học hành vi và chính sách công đã công bố.

passages.title: The Hawthorne Experiments
passages.text:
A
Few studies in the history of management have been quoted as often, or understood as poorly, as the experiments conducted at the Hawthorne Works, a vast factory near Chicago that manufactured telephone equipment for the Western Electric Company. Between 1924 and 1932, researchers there carried out a series of investigations into the conditions that made workers more productive. Their findings gave a name to a phenomenon that is still discussed in psychology, medicine and education today: the Hawthorne effect, the idea that people change their behaviour simply because they know they are being observed.

B
The first studies were concerned with lighting. Electricity companies of the period were keen to show that better illumination improved efficiency, and engineers set out to measure the effect precisely. In one series of tests, the lighting for one group of workers was gradually increased while a control group worked under constant conditions. To the researchers' surprise, output rose in both groups. Even more puzzling, when the lighting for the test group was later reduced to a very low level, productivity continued to climb until the workers complained that they could barely see what they were doing.

C
Intrigued, the company began a more ambitious study in 1927. Six young women who assembled small electrical components called relays were moved into a separate room, where their output could be recorded precisely. Over the following years, the researchers introduced a long sequence of changes, including shorter working days, rest breaks of different lengths and free refreshments. Almost every change was followed by an increase in output. Strikingly, when the women were returned to their original conditions, without breaks or refreshments, productivity remained higher than it had been at the start.

D
The researchers, who by then included the Harvard professor Elton Mayo, concluded that the physical changes themselves mattered less than the social situation that the experiment had created. The women worked as a close-knit team, were consulted about the changes and received an unusual amount of attention from senior staff. They felt, in other words, that someone cared about their work. This interpretation was presented in detail in a book published in 1939 by Fritz Roethlisberger and William Dickson, and it became a cornerstone of what is known as the human relations school of management.

E
A later phase of the research pointed in a less optimistic direction. In a study of fourteen men who wired telephone switching equipment, observers found that the group had developed its own informal rules about how much work was acceptable. Anyone who produced too much was mocked as a ‘rate-buster’, while anyone who produced too little was criticised for letting the others down. Output was kept at a steady level that the men themselves had agreed on, regardless of the financial incentives offered by management. Social pressure, it seemed, could restrict productivity as easily as it could raise it.

F
Curiously, the term ‘Hawthorne effect’ was not used by the original researchers at all. It was coined in 1958 by the sociologist Henry Landsberger, who used it to describe improvements in performance caused by the attention of researchers rather than by the changes they introduced. The phrase spread rapidly, and it is now routinely mentioned in medical research, where it helps to explain why patients taking part in clinical trials sometimes improve even when they receive no active treatment, simply because they are monitored more closely than usual.

G
In recent decades, however, the original evidence has been examined more critically. In 1978, two researchers re-analysed the data from the relay room and argued that most of the rise in output could be explained by factors such as stricter supervision and the replacement of two workers who had been producing relatively little. In 2011, the economists Steven Levitt and John List located the original lighting data, long thought to have been lost, and found that the supposed effect was far weaker than generally claimed. Much of the apparent improvement, they suggested, reflected regular patterns in output across the working week.

H
None of this means that being observed has no influence on behaviour. A systematic review published in 2014 concluded that research participants do sometimes change their behaviour because they are being studied, but that the size and nature of the effect vary greatly from one setting to another. Perhaps the most enduring lesson of Hawthorne is a methodological one: researchers must design their studies carefully enough to separate the effects of what they are testing from the effects of the study itself.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử quản trị học và các phân tích lại đã công bố.

passages.title: When Crowds Are Wise
passages.text:
A
In the autumn of 1906, the scientist Francis Galton visited a livestock fair in the English city of Plymouth, where visitors were paying a small fee to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and prepared. Galton, who held a rather low opinion of the intelligence of ordinary people, collected around eight hundred of the tickets afterwards, expecting to show how wildly inaccurate their guesses were. Instead he made a discovery that surprised him. Although individual estimates varied enormously, the middle value of all the guesses was within one per cent of the true weight, closer than the estimates of most of the cattle experts present.

B
Galton's observation has since been repeated in countless forms. Ask a large group of people to estimate the number of sweets in a glass jar and the average answer will often be remarkably close to the correct figure, even though few individuals come near it. On a well-known television quiz programme, contestants who were stuck on a question could ask the studio audience to vote on the answer; the most popular choice was correct around nine times out of ten, a far better record than that of the friends contestants could telephone for advice. The principle at work is simple: individual errors, if they are random, tend to cancel each other out.

C
The idea reached a wide audience in 2004, when the journalist James Surowiecki published a book on the subject. Surowiecki argued that a crowd is likely to be wise only under certain conditions. Its members must hold a diversity of opinions, each based on some private information; they must make their judgements independently rather than copying one another; and there must be some mechanism for combining their views into a single answer. In my view, it is the second of these conditions that is most often overlooked, and it explains why groups of intelligent people so frequently reach foolish decisions.

D
Consider what happens when people can see one another's opinions. In an experiment carried out at a Swiss university in 2011, participants were asked factual questions, such as the population density of Switzerland, and were rewarded for accurate answers. Some were told nothing about the answers of others; some saw the average of the group's previous estimates. Exposure to other people's views made the estimates more similar, but not more accurate. Worse, it made participants more confident in their answers. The diversity that gives a crowd its power had been eroded, yet the members felt better informed than ever.

E
Financial markets offer a dramatic illustration of the same problem. When investors make independent judgements about the value of a company, prices may reflect the available information reasonably well. When they begin to watch and follow each other, however, the result can be a bubble, in which prices rise far beyond any sensible estimate of value simply because everyone expects them to keep rising. The collapse that inevitably follows is a reminder that a crowd can be extraordinarily foolish when its members stop thinking for themselves.

F
Some organisations have tried to harness collective intelligence deliberately. So-called prediction markets allow participants to buy and sell contracts whose value depends on a future event, such as the result of an election, so that the price of a contract reflects the group's estimate of how likely that event is. Several technology companies have run internal markets in which employees bet on whether projects will be completed on time. These markets have sometimes proved more accurate than official forecasts, perhaps because employees with useful knowledge can contribute it anonymously, without having to contradict their managers in public.

G
It would be wrong, however, to conclude that crowds always outperform experts. For questions that require specialised knowledge, such as diagnosing a rare disease, the average opinion of a thousand untrained people is of little value. A crowd's judgement is only as good as the information its members possess, and averaging cannot create knowledge that nobody has. The most promising approaches, I believe, combine the two, for example by asking a number of experts to make independent estimates and then aggregating them, rather than allowing the most senior or most confident voice to dominate.

H
Galton himself drew a characteristically cautious conclusion from the Plymouth fair, suggesting that the result was more creditable to the trustworthiness of democratic judgement than might have been expected. More than a century later, that verdict still seems reasonable. Groups can be wise, but only when they are diverse, independent and properly organised. The challenge for any institution is not simply to consult more people, but to create the conditions in which their separate pieces of knowledge can be combined without being distorted along the way.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu về ra quyết định tập thể đã công bố.
