passages.title: The Montessori Classroom
passages.text:
A
Walk into a Montessori classroom and the first thing you may notice is what is missing. There are no rows of desks facing a blackboard, and the teacher is rarely standing at the front addressing the whole class. Instead, children of different ages are scattered around the room, some working alone at small tables, others sitting on mats on the floor, each absorbed in a different activity. To many visitors the scene looks unstructured, yet it is the product of a carefully designed educational philosophy that is now more than a century old and is practised in thousands of schools around the world.

B
Its founder, Maria Montessori, was born in Italy in 1870 and became one of the first women in her country to qualify as a doctor. Her early medical work brought her into contact with children who had been classified as having severe learning difficulties and who were kept in institutions with almost nothing to occupy them. Montessori noticed that they would pick up crumbs from the floor simply to have something to handle, and she became convinced that their development was being held back by a lack of stimulation rather than by any fixed limitation. When she provided them with specially designed materials, several made remarkable progress.

C
In 1907 she was invited to run a day-care centre for the children of working families in a poor district of Rome. She called it the Casa dei Bambini, or Children's House, and furnished it with tables and chairs light enough for small children to move and shelves low enough for them to reach. She introduced the materials she had developed earlier and observed carefully how the children used them. To her surprise, children as young as three would repeat a task, such as fitting wooden cylinders into holes of matching sizes, dozens of times with intense concentration, and would often choose work over the toys that were also available.

D
From these observations grew the principles that still define her method. Classes mix children across an age range of about three years, so that younger pupils learn by watching older ones and older pupils consolidate their knowledge by helping. Many of the materials are self-correcting: a cylinder will only fit into the right hole, so a child can see a mistake without being told. Children are given long, uninterrupted periods in which to choose their own activities, and the teacher's role is to observe and to introduce new materials when a child appears ready, rather than to deliver lessons to the whole group.

E
The method spread with astonishing speed. An English translation of Montessori's book appeared in 1912 and sold out rapidly, and within a few years there were Montessori schools across Europe and North America. In the United States, however, enthusiasm faded almost as quickly as it had grown. In 1914 William Heard Kilpatrick, an influential professor of education, published a critical study arguing that her ideas were outdated and offered little that was new. His criticism carried considerable weight, and the movement in America declined until the late 1950s, when Nancy McCormick Rambusch helped to revive it.

F
Whether the method actually produces better results has proved surprisingly difficult to establish. Families who choose Montessori schools may differ in important ways from those who do not, which makes simple comparisons unreliable. One of the most frequently cited studies avoided this problem by taking advantage of a lottery. In the American city of Milwaukee, places at a public Montessori school were allocated randomly among applicants, so the psychologist Angeline Lillard was able to compare children who had won a place with similar children who had applied but lost. The Montessori pupils performed better on tests of early reading and mathematics and showed stronger social skills.

G
Even so, researchers urge caution. The Milwaukee study was relatively small, and because the name ‘Montessori’ is not legally protected in many countries, schools using it vary enormously in how faithfully they follow the original approach. Some are rigorous in their use of the materials and their training of teachers; others adopt the label while retaining a fairly conventional curriculum. Supporters argue that the best evidence comes from schools that implement the method fully, and that the variation itself helps to explain why the overall research findings have been mixed.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử giáo dục và các nghiên cứu đã công bố.

passages.title: Pen Versus Keyboard
passages.text:
A
For most of the twentieth century, learning to write by hand was one of the central tasks of primary education. Children spent hours forming letters, first printing them separately and later joining them in flowing script. Today, the picture is very different. Students take notes on laptops, adults type far more than they write, and many education systems have reduced the time devoted to handwriting. In 2016, Finland stopped requiring schools to teach joined-up writing, preferring to concentrate on typing skills. Such decisions raise an obvious question: does it matter whether we write with a pen or a keyboard?

B
The question attracted wide attention in 2014, when the psychologists Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer published a study with a memorable title, ‘The pen is mightier than the keyboard’. University students watched short lectures and took notes either by hand or on a laptop. When tested afterwards, the two groups performed equally well on factual questions, but those who had written by hand did significantly better on questions that required them to understand and apply concepts. Analysis of the notes suggested a reason. Laptop users wrote more words, but they tended to record what the speaker said almost word for word.

C
Mueller and Oppenheimer argued that the slowness of handwriting is, paradoxically, an advantage. Because nobody can write as fast as a lecturer speaks, students taking notes by hand are forced to decide what is important and to express it in their own words. This process of selecting and summarising requires them to think about the material, which in turn helps them to remember it. Typists, who can keep up with the speaker, may record a great deal while processing very little. Interestingly, telling laptop users to avoid copying the lecture word for word did not solve the problem; most did so anyway.

D
Not every researcher has been convinced. When a team led by Kayla Morehead repeated the experiments in 2019, the differences between the groups were smaller and less consistent than in the original study, and the authors concluded that the evidence was not yet strong enough to justify banning laptops from lecture halls. They also pointed out that typed notes have practical benefits: they are easier to read, search and share, and students who review their notes before an examination may gain more from a complete record than from a brief handwritten summary. In their view, how students use their notes after a lecture may matter at least as much as how they produce them in the first place.

E
A separate line of research has looked inside the brain. The neuroscientist Audrey van der Meer and her colleagues in Norway recorded electrical activity in the brains of students who were writing words by hand or typing them. Handwriting was associated with more widespread connections between different brain regions, including areas involved in movement, vision and memory. The researchers suggested that the precise, varied movements needed to form each letter provide the brain with richer information than the repetitive action of pressing keys, which is almost identical whatever letter is typed.

F
Studies of young children point in a similar direction. Karin James, a psychologist at Indiana University, taught children who could not yet read to recognise letters in one of three ways: by writing them freehand, by tracing them, or by typing them. When the children were later shown letters while their brains were scanned, those who had practised freehand writing showed stronger activity in regions associated with reading in adults. James argues that the imperfect, variable letters children produce when writing by hand help them to learn what all versions of a letter have in common. Children who had only traced or typed the letters showed much weaker responses, even though they had spent the same amount of time practising.

G
What should schools conclude? Few researchers would recommend abandoning keyboards, which are essential tools in modern life and which can help pupils with physical difficulties to express their ideas. The evidence suggests rather that handwriting may play a particular role in the early stages of learning to read and in situations where the aim is understanding rather than recording. For older students, the most important factor may not be the tool at all, but whether they are actively thinking about what they write.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học giáo dục và khoa học thần kinh đã công bố.

passages.title: Saving the World's Languages
passages.text:
A
Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, but this impressive figure conceals a striking imbalance. More than half of the world's population speaks one of just two dozen major languages, such as Mandarin, Spanish, English and Hindi, while thousands of others are spoken by small communities, some numbering only a few hundred people. Roughly forty per cent of all languages are now considered endangered. In 1992, the linguist Michael Krauss warned that, unless action was taken, as many as ninety per cent of the world's languages could be lost or no longer learned by children by the end of the twenty-first century. The distribution is also geographically uneven: Papua New Guinea alone is home to more than eight hundred languages.

B
Languages rarely disappear because their speakers die out. Much more commonly, a community gradually shifts to a language that offers greater economic and social opportunities. Parents who have experienced discrimination, or who believe that their children will find better jobs in the national language, may stop speaking their own language at home. Schools, broadcasting and migration to cities all accelerate the process. The critical moment comes when a language is no longer passed from one generation to the next. A language may still have thousands of elderly speakers, yet if children are not learning it, its future is in serious doubt.

C
To track the situation, UNESCO publishes an atlas that classifies languages according to how threatened they are. A language described as vulnerable is spoken by most children, but only in certain settings, such as the home. One that is definitely endangered is no longer learned by children as a mother tongue, while a severely endangered language is spoken mainly by grandparents and older generations. At the extreme end of the scale, a critically endangered language has only a few speakers left, usually elderly people who use it partially and infrequently. The atlas is intended not simply as a record of decline but as a tool to encourage action.

D
Why should the loss of a language concern anyone other than its speakers? One answer is that each language represents a unique way of organising knowledge. Communities that have lived in the same environment for centuries often have detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, some of which are unknown to science. When the language disappears, much of this knowledge may disappear with it. Linguists add that every language reveals something about the range of possible human grammars, so that the loss of any single one narrows our understanding of how language itself works.

E
There are encouraging examples of decline being reversed. The most remarkable is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly for religious and scholarly purposes before being revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Today it has millions of native speakers. In Wales, a combination of legislation, Welsh-language television and bilingual education has helped to stabilise the number of speakers after a long period of decline, and the language is now visible on road signs and official documents throughout the country.

F
Some of the most influential methods were developed by indigenous communities themselves. In New Zealand during the early 1980s, Māori groups established ‘language nests’, preschools in which young children were looked after entirely in the Māori language by fluent older speakers. The model proved so successful that it was adopted in Hawaii a few years later and has since inspired similar programmes elsewhere. Its strength lies in recreating the natural conditions in which children have always acquired languages: daily, informal contact with adults who speak to them in that language.

G
Technology offers new tools as well. Recordings, online dictionaries and smartphone applications can help to document languages and make learning materials widely available, even to members of a community who have moved far from their homeland. Yet specialists caution against assuming that technology alone can save a language. A recording preserves a language much as a museum preserves an extinct animal; it does not keep it alive. Ultimately, the survival of a language depends on whether people choose to use it in their daily lives and, above all, whether they speak it to their children. Several communities now run online courses in their own languages, allowing younger members scattered across different countries to practise with fluent speakers.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu ngôn ngữ học và các chương trình phục hồi ngôn ngữ đã công bố.

passages.title: The Science of Remembering
passages.text:
A
Every student knows the experience of studying hard for an examination, performing reasonably well, and then discovering a few weeks later that almost everything has been forgotten. For a long time this was regarded as an unavoidable feature of human memory. Over the past century, however, psychologists have learned a great deal about how forgetting happens and how it can be slowed. Their findings point to techniques that are simple, inexpensive and remarkably effective, yet which are still used far less often than the familiar habit of last-minute revision.

B
The scientific study of memory is usually traced to the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, who published his research in 1885. To avoid the influence of meaning and prior knowledge, Ebbinghaus taught himself long lists of nonsense syllables, such as ‘dax’ or ‘bok’, and then tested how many he could recall after different periods of time. The results allowed him to draw what became known as the forgetting curve. Memory declined very steeply in the first hours after learning and then more gradually, so that a large proportion of the material was lost within a day unless it was reviewed.

C
Ebbinghaus also noticed something more encouraging. When he relearned a list after an interval, it took him less time than it had originally, and the material was then forgotten more slowly. Spreading out learning sessions over time, rather than concentrating them in a single block, produced much better long-term retention. This finding, known as the spacing effect, has since been confirmed in hundreds of experiments with learners of all ages, from young children memorising vocabulary to medical students learning anatomy, and it is one of the most reliable results in the whole of psychology. Its advantage is usually largest when material must be retained for months rather than days.

D
How long should the gaps between study sessions be? A large study published in 2008 by Nicholas Cepeda and his colleagues suggested that the answer depends on how long the information needs to be remembered. For a test only a week away, reviewing material after a day or two was most effective; for information that had to be retained for a year, intervals of several weeks produced the best results. Gaps that are too short add little, because the material is still fresh, while gaps that are too long mean that much of it has already been lost and must effectively be learned again.

E
A closely related principle concerns the way material is reviewed. Simply rereading notes is a popular strategy, but research suggests that it is much less effective than attempting to recall information from memory. In a study published in 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke asked students to read a short passage and then either read it again or write down as much as they could remember. On a test five minutes later, the students who had reread performed slightly better. After a week, however, those who had practised recalling the passage remembered substantially more. The effort of retrieval appears to strengthen memories in a way that passive review does not.

F
These ideas have been built into practical tools. In the 1970s, the German writer Sebastian Leitner proposed a system in which flashcards are stored in a series of boxes: cards answered correctly move to a box that is reviewed less often, while cards answered wrongly return to the first box for frequent practice. Computer programs have since automated the process. The Polish researcher Piotr Woźniak developed software that calculates the ideal moment to review each item, just before it is likely to be forgotten, and similar algorithms are now used by millions of language learners. Users of such programs often spend only a few minutes a day reviewing, yet are able to retain thousands of words.

G
Why, then, do so many learners continue to cram? Part of the answer is that spaced practice and self-testing feel harder than rereading, and people tend to interpret that difficulty as a sign that they are not learning. The psychologist Robert Bjork has described such challenges as ‘desirable difficulties’: conditions that slow down apparent progress during study but lead to stronger learning in the long run. Teaching students to recognise this may be as important as teaching them the techniques themselves.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học nhận thức về trí nhớ đã công bố.

passages.title: Teaching Children to Read
passages.text:
A
Few questions in education have provoked arguments as bitter as the apparently simple matter of how children should be taught to read. For much of the last century, teachers, researchers and politicians in the English-speaking world fought what came to be called the ‘reading wars’. On one side stood supporters of phonics, who believed that children should be taught explicitly how letters and groups of letters correspond to sounds. On the other were advocates of approaches that emphasised meaning, enjoyment and exposure to real books, and who argued that reading would develop naturally, much as speech does, if children were surrounded by stories.

B
The second view has an obvious appeal. It treats children as active learners, places stories rather than drills at the centre of the classroom, and promises to protect the pleasure of reading. In some versions, children were encouraged to work out unfamiliar words by looking at the pictures, considering what would make sense in the sentence, or recognising the shape of familiar words. Yet I believe this approach rests on a misunderstanding. Speech is something that humans have done for tens of thousands of years and that every child acquires without formal teaching; writing is a recent cultural invention, and very few children work out its code entirely on their own.

C
The scientific evidence, accumulated over several decades, points strongly in one direction. In 2000, a panel commissioned by the United States Congress reviewed a large body of experimental research and concluded that systematic instruction in phonics produced significant benefits, especially for young children and for those at risk of reading difficulties. Studies of the brain have reached a similar conclusion: skilled readers do not guess words from context but process the letters within them rapidly and automatically, a skill that depends on a secure knowledge of how spelling represents sound.

D
England offers a large-scale test of these ideas. Following an official review in 2006, schools were expected to teach systematic synthetic phonics, an approach in which children learn the sounds associated with letters and practise blending them together to read words. In 2012 the government introduced a short check for six-year-olds, in which each child reads forty words aloud to a teacher. Some of these are invented ‘alien’ words, included to ensure that children are decoding rather than recognising words they have memorised. The proportion of pupils reaching the expected standard rose from just over half in the first year to more than eighty per cent within seven years. The check has been held almost every year since, with only brief disruption during the pandemic.

E
Critics have raised reasonable objections. Some teachers complain that the check takes time away from other activities and that the invented words confuse able readers, who may try to turn them into real ones. Others point out that success in decoding does not guarantee that children understand what they read or that they will choose to read for pleasure, which surveys suggest is declining among older children. These concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but they are arguments for teaching more than phonics, not for teaching less of it.

F
In the United States, the debate was reignited in 2022 by a widely discussed series of radio programmes investigating popular classroom materials. The programmes argued that many schools had continued to teach children to guess words from pictures and context, methods that research had long since discredited, and that the consequences fell most heavily on children from poorer families, who were least likely to receive extra help at home. Since then, a number of states have passed laws requiring schools to base reading instruction on scientific evidence, and some publishers have revised their materials.

G
None of this means that stories and enjoyment should be pushed aside. Phonics teaches children how to unlock the words on the page, but understanding a text also depends on vocabulary, background knowledge and the habit of reading widely, and these are built through exactly the rich exposure to books that the other side of the reading wars always championed. The sensible conclusion is that phonics is necessary but not sufficient. A child who cannot decode will never become a confident reader; a child who can decode but has never been given a reason to read may not become one either.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ chính sách giáo dục và các nghiên cứu về dạy đọc đã công bố.

passages.title: Is a Four-Day Week the Future?
passages.text:
A
In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that by the early twenty-first century technological progress would allow people to work as little as fifteen hours a week. For several decades after his essay appeared, the trend seemed to be moving in his direction. Working hours in industrialised countries fell steadily, and the American car manufacturer Henry Ford had already shown in 1926 that a five-day, forty-hour week could be good for business, partly because workers with more free time were more likely to buy the products that factories made. Since the 1980s, however, the decline in working hours has largely stalled in many countries, and the standard five-day week has remained remarkably stable.

B
That stability is now being challenged. Between 2015 and 2019, the city council of Reykjavík and the national government of Iceland ran trials in which more than two thousand public employees reduced their weekly hours from forty to thirty-five or thirty-six, without any reduction in pay. Researchers reported that productivity and the quality of services were maintained or improved in most workplaces, while employees described lower levels of stress. Following the trials, trade unions negotiated agreements that gave a large majority of Iceland's workforce the right to shorter hours. Several other countries have since launched their own experiments.

C
The largest trial so far took place in Britain in the second half of 2022. Sixty-one companies, employing around 2,900 people, agreed to give staff a paid day off each week, or an equivalent reduction in hours, for six months, provided that output was maintained. The organisations involved ranged from small marketing firms to a fish-and-chip restaurant. The trial was analysed by researchers including Juliet Schor, a sociologist at Boston College, who had spent much of her career studying the causes and consequences of overwork. At the end of the six months, fifty-six of the companies chose to continue with the shorter week, and eighteen made the change permanent.

D
The results were striking. Company revenues remained broadly stable over the trial period, and many employers reported that staff had become more focused, cutting unnecessary meetings and reorganising their work more efficiently. Employees reported less burnout and better sleep, the number of sick days fell considerably, and fewer people left their jobs than in the equivalent period of the previous year. In Japan, Microsoft had reported similar gains from a shorter trial in 2019, claiming that sales per employee rose by around forty per cent during a month in which offices closed every Friday.

E
These findings are encouraging, but I think it would be unwise to conclude that every organisation should immediately adopt a four-day week. The companies that took part in the British trial volunteered to do so, and firms that expect a policy to succeed are naturally more likely to try it. Many were small, office-based businesses in which output is relatively easy to reorganise. It is far from clear that the same approach would work in a hospital, a school or a supermarket, where staff must be present to provide a service and where reducing hours may simply mean employing more people.

F
The form a shorter week takes also matters. Some employers have introduced what is known as a compressed week, in which staff work their usual hours over four longer days. This arrangement may suit some people, but it is a different proposition from genuinely reducing working time, and long days can lead to the very fatigue that a shorter week is supposed to prevent. In my view, the most persuasive results have come from trials in which total hours were actually reduced and in which employees themselves were involved in redesigning how work was done.

G
Keynes was wrong about the speed of change, but he may not have been wrong about its direction. The evidence so far suggests that a great deal of time at work is spent on tasks that add little value, and that many organisations could produce as much in four days as in five if they were willing to rethink their habits. Rather than a universal rule imposed by governments, the four-day week is perhaps best seen as an opportunity that employers in suitable sectors should be encouraged to test carefully for themselves.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các thử nghiệm tuần làm việc bốn ngày đã công bố.

passages.title: The Box That Changed the World
passages.text:
A
It is easy to overlook the steel shipping container. Millions of these plain metal boxes travel across the oceans every day, carrying everything from clothing and electronics to frozen food, yet few people give them a moment's thought. Economic historians, however, increasingly regard the container as one of the most important inventions of the twentieth century. By making it cheap and reliable to move goods across the world, it helped to create the global supply chains on which modern manufacturing depends, and it transformed the economies of port cities on every continent.

B
Before the container, cargo was handled in much the same way as it had been for centuries. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bales of every shape and size, and large teams of dockworkers loaded them into the hold of a ship piece by piece. The work was slow, physically exhausting and frequently dangerous. A ship might spend a week or more in port being loaded and unloaded, and theft was common, since goods passed through many hands. Moving cargo between ship and shore often accounted for a large share of the total cost of transporting it. Dockworkers were often hired by the day, and their employment was notoriously insecure.

C
The man most often credited with changing this was Malcom McLean, an American who had built up a successful trucking company. Frustrated by the hours his drivers spent waiting at ports while their loads were transferred to ships, he reasoned that it would be far more efficient to lift the entire body of a truck onto a vessel. In April 1956 a converted oil tanker called the Ideal X sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying fifty-eight metal boxes on its deck. McLean later calculated that the cost of loading had fallen from several dollars per tonne to just a few cents.

D
The idea did not spread immediately. Different companies built containers in different sizes, with incompatible fittings, so a box designed for one firm's ships could not easily be carried by another's cranes or trucks. Throughout the 1960s, engineers and international organisations negotiated common standards for the dimensions of containers and the corner fittings by which they are lifted and locked together. Once these were agreed, a container could move from a lorry to a train to a ship and back again anywhere in the world without its contents ever being touched. The standard length of twenty feet later gave the industry its basic unit of capacity, still used today to compare the size of ships and ports.

E
Demand from an unexpected source accelerated the change. During the Vietnam War, the United States military struggled to supply its forces through congested ports, and McLean's company won contracts to carry military cargo in containers. The operation proved so efficient that his ships, rather than return empty across the Pacific, began picking up goods from Japan on the way home. This trade helped to demonstrate the potential of containers for linking Asian factories with Western consumers, a connection that would grow enormously over the following decades.

F
The social consequences were severe for some communities. Traditional docks in the centres of cities such as London and New York, where narrow quays could not accommodate the huge cranes and storage areas that containers required, went into rapid decline. New ports were built on open land elsewhere, often far from the old waterfront neighbourhoods. Employment on the docks collapsed, since a single crane operator could now do work that had once required dozens of labourers, and whole districts that had depended on port work for generations faced long periods of unemployment.

G
Today the largest container ships can carry more than twenty thousand standard boxes and are longer than four football pitches. The cost of shipping has fallen so low that it is often cheaper to transport goods halfway around the world than to make them close to where they will be sold. This efficiency has a downside, however. When a single large ship ran aground in the Suez Canal in 2021, blocking it for six days, the disruption to global trade revealed how heavily the world economy had come to depend on a system that most people never notice.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử vận tải và thương mại quốc tế.

passages.title: Small Loans, Big Hopes
passages.text:
A
In 1976, Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at a university in Bangladesh, visited a village near his campus and met a group of women who made bamboo stools. Because they had no money to buy materials, they borrowed from traders who then insisted on buying the finished stools at a price so low that the women earned almost nothing. Yunus calculated that the total sum the women needed was tiny, the equivalent of less than thirty US dollars between more than forty people. He lent it to them from his own pocket, and they repaid him. From this modest beginning grew a movement that would eventually reach well over a hundred million people around the world.

B
The central problem Yunus had identified was that poor people, particularly in rural areas, had no access to ordinary banks. Lending small amounts is expensive for a bank, because the cost of assessing and administering a loan is much the same whatever its size. Moreover, poor borrowers usually have no property to offer as security, so banks have no way of recovering their money if a loan is not repaid. As a result, people with no other options turned to moneylenders, who often charged extremely high rates of interest. Moneylenders, by contrast, knew their borrowers personally and could rely on social pressure to recover what they were owed.

C
The bank that Yunus founded, which became an independent institution in 1983, developed an ingenious solution to the problem of security. Instead of requiring property, it lent to individuals who belonged to small groups, typically of five people. Members of each group did not guarantee one another's debts directly, but further loans to the group depended on everyone keeping up their repayments, so members had a strong incentive to choose reliable partners and to support each other. The bank reported repayment rates of more than ninety per cent, far higher than many conventional lenders achieved in the same regions.

D
From the start, the great majority of borrowers were women. Supporters of microfinance argued that women were more likely than men to spend additional income on their children's food, health and education, and that access to their own source of money could strengthen their position within the household. In 2006, Yunus and his bank were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, and by then microfinance institutions had spread across Asia, Latin America and Africa. For a time, the idea was celebrated as one of the most promising ways of ending poverty.

E
Doubts grew as the industry expanded. Some lenders, attracted by the reliable repayments, began to operate as profit-making businesses charging very high interest. In 2007, a Mexican microlender sold shares to investors and was criticised for charging annual rates that approached one hundred per cent. Three years later, in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, rapid growth in lending left many borrowers with loans from several institutions at once. Reports of aggressive debt collection led the state government to introduce strict regulations, and much of the local industry collapsed.

F
Researchers, meanwhile, set out to measure the effects of microcredit more rigorously. In 2015, a leading economics journal published the results of six randomised studies carried out in countries on four continents, in which some communities were given access to microloans while similar communities were not. The findings were consistent and sobering. Access to credit allowed some people to start or expand small businesses and gave households more flexibility in managing their money, but on average it did not lead to significant increases in income, nor to clear improvements in health or education. Effects also varied between individuals: borrowers who already ran a business tended to benefit more, while many others saw little change.

G
These results do not mean that microfinance has failed. Poor households often face irregular incomes and sudden expenses, and the ability to borrow, save and insure themselves safely can make their lives considerably less precarious. What the evidence does suggest is that small loans are not, by themselves, a reliable route out of poverty. Many specialists now argue that savings accounts, insurance and simple money-transfer services, increasingly delivered through mobile phones, may be as valuable to poor families as credit, and in some cases more so.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu về tài chính vi mô và các đánh giá tác động đã công bố.

passages.title: The Trouble with Open-Plan Offices
passages.text:
A
Walk into almost any modern office and you are likely to find the same arrangement: long rows of desks in a single large space, with few walls, few doors and little privacy. Open-plan layouts have become so common that it is easy to forget they were once a radical idea. Their supporters claim that removing walls encourages communication, breaks down hierarchies and sparks the kind of chance encounters from which new ideas emerge. Their critics argue that they are noisy, distracting and stressful. After more than a century of experiment, the evidence suggests that the critics have rather the stronger case.

B
Open offices are not a recent invention. In 1906, the American architect Frank Lloyd Wright designed an administration building for a mail-order company in which clerks worked together in a vast, light-filled hall. The arrangement was intended partly to make supervision easier, since managers could observe the whole workforce at once. Throughout the first half of the twentieth century, many large companies adopted similar layouts, often arranging desks in strict rows that resembled a factory floor more than a place for creative thinking.

C
A more humane version appeared in Germany in the 1950s, when a consulting group founded by the brothers Eberhard and Wolfgang Schnelle developed what they called the ‘office landscape’. Desks were grouped irregularly according to how teams actually worked together, and plants and movable screens were used to create a sense of separate areas within the larger space. The idea spread across Europe and the United States, and for a time it represented the most progressive thinking about how offices should be organised.

D
In the United States, the designer Robert Propst introduced a flexible system of movable panels and furniture in the 1960s, intending to give office workers more control over their surroundings. Companies soon discovered, however, that the panels could be used to pack employees into small, identical boxes as cheaply as possible. The result was the cubicle, which became a symbol of dull corporate life. Propst himself later expressed deep regret about the way his invention had been used, describing the crowded rows of cubicles that it produced in strongly critical terms.

E
The current fashion for completely open spaces is often justified by the claim that it increases collaboration. A study published in 2018 by Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban of Harvard Business School tested this directly. They gave employees at two companies wearable sensors that recorded face-to-face interactions before and after the companies moved from cubicles to open-plan offices. In both cases, face-to-face interaction fell by around seventy per cent after the move, while the use of email and instant messaging increased. Rather than talking more, employees seemed to withdraw, putting on headphones and communicating electronically to avoid being overheard.

F
Noise is a particular problem. Psychologists have found that overheard conversation is especially disruptive to tasks such as reading and writing, because the brain cannot help processing speech, even when it is irrelevant. A steady hum of machinery is relatively easy to ignore; a colleague discussing weekend plans a few metres away is not. Many workers in open offices report that they find it difficult to concentrate and that they postpone demanding work until the evening or until they can work from home.

G
Why, then, do open offices remain so popular with employers? The most honest answer is probably cost. Removing walls allows more people to be accommodated in the same space, and some companies have gone further by abolishing assigned desks altogether, so that employees must find a free place each morning. Such arrangements may make sense for staff who are frequently away from the office, but I suspect that savings on rent, rather than any genuine evidence about productivity, are usually the decisive factor.

H
None of this means that every employee should have a private office. Different kinds of work require different environments, and teams that genuinely need to cooperate closely can benefit from sharing space. The most sensible approach, in my view, is to offer a variety of settings: quiet rooms for concentrated work, open areas for discussion and small spaces for private conversations. The goal should be to let people choose the right environment for the task in hand, rather than forcing everyone into a single design that suits almost nobody.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ lịch sử thiết kế văn phòng và các nghiên cứu về môi trường làm việc đã công bố.

passages.title: Built Not to Last?
passages.text:
A
In a fire station in the Californian town of Livermore, a light bulb has been burning almost continuously since 1901. Hand-blown and fitted with a carbon filament, it has outlasted the building it was first installed in and has become a minor tourist attraction, with its own website and a webcam that allows visitors to watch it glow. For many people, the bulb is more than a curiosity. It seems to prove something that consumers have long suspected: that manufacturers are capable of making products that last for decades, but choose not to.

B
There is at least one well-documented case in which manufacturers deliberately shortened the life of their products. In 1924, the leading producers of light bulbs in Europe and the United States formed an agreement, later known as the Phoebus cartel, to limit the life of standard bulbs to around one thousand hours, at a time when many lasted considerably longer. Member companies were required to submit samples for testing, and those whose bulbs lasted too long were fined. The cartel collapsed in the 1930s, but it remains the most frequently cited example of what is now called planned obsolescence.

C
The phrase itself became popular during the Great Depression. In 1932, an American property dealer named Bernard London published a pamphlet arguing that the government should impose legal limits on the life of manufactured goods, forcing people to replace them and thereby creating employment. His proposal was never adopted, but the idea of encouraging people to replace goods more frequently soon found a more subtle form. In the 1950s, the industrial designer Brooks Stevens described the aim as instilling in the buyer the desire to own something a little newer and a little better sooner than was necessary.

D
Stevens was describing what is sometimes called psychological or perceived obsolescence. Rather than breaking, products simply come to seem out of date. The American car industry was a pioneer of this approach. In the 1920s, General Motors began introducing a new style of car every year, with changes to the shape, colour and decoration that had little to do with how well the vehicle performed. Fashion and consumer electronics have followed the same pattern, encouraging people to replace possessions that still work perfectly well.

E
Not every short-lived product is the result of a conspiracy, however. Making goods more durable usually makes them more expensive, and many consumers prefer a cheaper item that lasts a few years to a costly one that lasts a lifetime. The Livermore bulb, for instance, is extremely dim by modern standards; a bulb designed to last for a century would be far less efficient than one designed to produce bright light. Engineers constantly balance durability against price, performance and weight, and a product that fails relatively early may simply reflect those choices.

F
In recent years, attention has shifted from deliberate sabotage to the difficulty of repairing modern devices. Many smartphones and laptops are glued shut, use unusual screws or contain batteries that cannot easily be replaced. Spare parts and repair manuals may be available only to authorised dealers. In 2017, one major smartphone manufacturer admitted that software updates had slowed down older phones whose batteries had deteriorated; the company said this was intended to prevent unexpected shutdowns, but it was later fined in France and agreed to a large settlement in the United States.

G
Governments have begun to respond. In 2015 France made it an offence to shorten the life of a product deliberately, and in 2021 it began requiring certain electronic goods to display a score showing how easy they are to repair. The European Union has since adopted rules requiring manufacturers to make spare parts available for a number of years and to offer repairs at a reasonable price. Supporters of these measures argue that they will save consumers money and reduce the huge quantities of electronic waste produced each year.

H
Whether such laws will change the habits of consumers remains uncertain. A repair is only attractive if it is cheaper and more convenient than buying a new product, and many people enjoy owning the latest model. The debate about planned obsolescence, therefore, is not only about the behaviour of manufacturers. It also raises questions about what consumers value, and about whether a society that depends on constant consumption can find ways to make its possessions last longer.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử công nghiệp và các quy định về quyền sửa chữa đã công bố.

passages.title: The Puzzle of Tipping
passages.text:
A
Economists have long been puzzled by tipping. Standard economic theory predicts that people will not pay more than they have to, yet every year customers around the world voluntarily hand over billions in extra payments to waiters, taxi drivers and hairdressers. In the United States alone, restaurant tips are estimated to amount to tens of billions of dollars annually. Even more surprisingly, people tip in places they will never visit again, where the usual explanation, that a generous tip ensures good service next time, cannot apply. Tipping, it seems, is driven less by calculation than by social expectation.

B
The custom has a curious history. In the United States, tipping became widespread only in the decades after the Civil War, when wealthy Americans returning from Europe brought back the aristocratic habit of giving small sums to servants. At first, many Americans regarded the practice as undemocratic, since it seemed to create a class of people dependent on the generosity of their social superiors. In the early twentieth century several states actually passed laws banning tipping, though all of these had been repealed or abandoned within a couple of decades.

C
Supporters of tipping argue that it rewards good work and gives customers a way of expressing satisfaction. The research, however, suggests that the link between service and reward is surprisingly weak. The psychologist Michael Lynn, who has studied tipping for several decades, found that the quality of service, as rated by customers themselves, explains only a small fraction of the variation in the size of tips. Far more important are factors that have little to do with competence, such as the size of the bill, the weather and the mood of the customer.

D
Some of these factors are almost comically trivial. Studies have found that servers who introduce themselves by name, crouch beside the table when taking orders or draw a smiling face on the bill tend to receive larger tips. More troubling are findings that tips can be influenced by a server's appearance, age, gender and ethnic background. If tips reflect the prejudices of customers rather than the quality of work, then a system that is supposed to reward merit may in practice reinforce unfairness, and I find it difficult to see how such a system can be defended.

E
The consequences for workers are significant because in many places tips are not a bonus but a central part of their income. Under United States federal law, employers may pay staff who receive tips a basic wage of just over two dollars an hour, provided that tips bring their total earnings up to the general minimum wage. This means that a waiter's income can vary dramatically from one evening to the next, depending on the number and generosity of customers, and that the risk of a quiet night falls on the employee rather than on the business.

F
Not every country shares this approach. In Japan, tipping is generally not expected and may even cause confusion, since good service is regarded as part of the job rather than something to be paid for separately. In much of Europe, a service charge is included in the price or a small tip is optional. Some American restaurants have experimented with abolishing tips and raising menu prices instead. A well-known New York restaurant group adopted this policy in 2015, but reversed it several years later, partly because customers were reluctant to accept higher prices on the menu.

G
Recent technology has added a new twist. Payment screens in cafés and shops now routinely invite customers to add a tip of fifteen, twenty or twenty-five per cent, even for services such as buying a cup of coffee at a counter, where tipping was traditionally rare. Many consumers report feeling pressured by these prompts, particularly when the screen is turned towards them while the employee watches. The result, some economists argue, is a gradual increase in the number of situations in which a tip is expected.

H
In my view, the strongest case against tipping is not that it costs customers money, but that it disguises the true price of a service and shifts responsibility for paying workers from employers to the public. A system in which wages are set openly and prices include the full cost of labour would be both fairer to employees and clearer for customers. Old customs are difficult to change, however, and as long as most restaurants continue to rely on tips, individual customers who refuse to pay them will simply be penalising the staff.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ lịch sử tập quán tiền boa và các nghiên cứu hành vi người tiêu dùng đã công bố.

passages.title: How the Supermarket Was Invented
passages.text:
A
For most people in wealthy countries, the weekly visit to the supermarket is such a routine part of life that it is hard to imagine shopping any other way. Yet the supermarket is barely a century old. Until the early twentieth century, buying food was a slow, personal and often time-consuming activity. Customers handed a list to a clerk standing behind a counter, who then fetched each item from shelves the customer could not reach, weighed and wrapped it, and added up the bill. Shopping for a family could take an entire morning. Many basic foods, such as flour, sugar and biscuits, were sold loose from large containers rather than in branded packets.

B
The first important break with this system came in 1916 in Memphis, Tennessee, when a grocer named Clarence Saunders opened a store called Piggly Wiggly. Saunders allowed customers to walk through the aisles and select goods for themselves, using a basket to carry them to a cashier at the exit. Every product was marked with its price, so no clerk was needed to quote it. The design reduced the number of staff a store required and allowed it to charge lower prices. Saunders patented the layout and later franchised it to other shopkeepers, and within a few years there were hundreds of Piggly Wiggly stores across the United States.

C
Self-service was only one ingredient of the modern supermarket; size was another. In 1930, a former grocery manager named Michael Cullen opened a store in an old garage in New York, where he combined self-service with a very large range of goods, low prices and space for customers to park their cars. Cullen's idea was to sell enormous quantities at a small profit on each item, and his advertisements promised to save shoppers money at a time when the Great Depression made every cent count. Many historians regard his store as the first true supermarket.

D
Larger shops created a new problem: customers could buy only as much as they could carry in a basket. In 1937, Sylvan Goldman, the owner of a chain of grocery stores in Oklahoma, solved it by fixing two baskets to a folding frame on wheels. To his surprise, shoppers at first refused to use the new trolley. Men felt that pushing it made them look weak, while women complained that it reminded them of a baby carriage. Goldman eventually hired models to push trolleys around his stores, demonstrating how convenient they were, and the invention soon became universal.

E
The supermarket spread more slowly outside the United States. In Britain, wartime rationing and shortages delayed its arrival, and self-service stores did not become common until the 1950s. Even then, many customers were suspicious of the new system. Some were embarrassed to be seen carrying their own shopping, which they associated with poverty, and others missed the conversation and advice they had enjoyed with shop assistants. Shopkeepers, meanwhile, feared that allowing customers to handle goods freely would lead to an increase in theft.

F
Technology continued to transform the industry. On a summer morning in 1974, at a supermarket in the small town of Troy, Ohio, a cashier passed a packet of chewing gum over a scanner, the first time a product with a barcode had been sold in a shop. The system allowed prices to be read automatically and gave retailers detailed information about what was selling and when. Within two decades, barcodes were printed on almost every packaged product, and supermarkets could manage their stock with a precision that would once have been unimaginable. Early scanners were expensive, however, and many retailers were slow to install them until manufacturers had begun printing codes on their packaging.

G
The rise of the supermarket was not good news for everyone. Small independent grocers, unable to match the prices of large chains, closed in great numbers, and in many countries shopping moved from town centres to large stores on the edge of towns that could be reached only by car. Critics argue that this pattern has weakened local communities and encouraged unhealthy diets based on processed food. Today, the growth of online shopping and home delivery suggests that the supermarket itself may be about to undergo another transformation.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử ngành bán lẻ.

passages.title: Cooling the Urban Heat Island
passages.text:
A
On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. The phenomenon, known as the urban heat island, was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur meteorologist who kept careful records of temperatures in and around London. Howard noticed that the city was consistently warmer than the nearby fields, particularly at night, and he correctly suspected that the cause lay in the city itself. Two centuries later, as more than half of the world's population lives in urban areas and heatwaves become more frequent, his observation has acquired a new urgency.

B
Several factors combine to make cities warmer. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb a large proportion of the sunlight that falls on them and release the stored heat slowly after sunset. In the countryside, by contrast, plants release water vapour through their leaves, a process that cools the surrounding air in much the same way that sweating cools the human body. Cities have far less vegetation, so this natural cooling is largely lost. Tall buildings also trap heat and reduce the flow of air through streets, while vehicles, factories and air-conditioning units add heat of their own.

C
The difference is usually greatest at night. During the day, the countryside heats up too, but after sunset open fields lose heat rapidly to the sky. Urban areas, packed with materials that have absorbed heat all day, cool far more slowly. On calm, clear nights the centre of a large city may be as much as ten degrees warmer than its rural surroundings. This matters for health, because the human body relies on cooler night-time temperatures to recover from the stress of a hot day.

D
The consequences can be deadly. During the European heatwave of 2003, tens of thousands of people died, many of them elderly residents of cities who were unable to escape the heat in their apartments. Researchers have also found that the effects are unevenly distributed. In the United States, neighbourhoods with fewer trees and more paved surfaces, which are often home to poorer residents, can be considerably hotter than wealthier districts in the same city. The urban heat island, in other words, is not only an environmental issue but a question of social fairness.

E
Fortunately, many of the causes can be addressed. One of the simplest solutions is to make surfaces more reflective. A white or light-coloured roof reflects much more sunlight than a dark one and can be many degrees cooler on a sunny day, reducing the heat that passes into the building below. Several cities have experimented with reflective coatings on roads; in Los Angeles, some streets have been painted with a pale grey coating, and measurements suggested that their surfaces were noticeably cooler than those of untreated streets nearby.

F
Vegetation offers additional benefits. Trees provide shade and cool the air as they release water, and a street lined with mature trees can be several degrees cooler than a bare one. Green roofs, covered with soil and plants, help to insulate buildings and absorb rainwater that would otherwise run straight into drains. In the Colombian city of Medellín, a programme of planting trees and plants along busy roads and waterways created a network of green corridors, and the city reported that temperatures in these areas fell by around two degrees.

G
Such measures are not without difficulties. Trees require water, space and years of care before they provide significant shade, and in crowded districts there may be little room to plant them. Reflective surfaces can cause glare and, if poorly placed, may reflect heat onto pedestrians or nearby buildings. Planners therefore increasingly recommend combining several approaches, adapted to local conditions, rather than relying on a single technique. Schools in Paris, for example, have replaced asphalt playgrounds with planted areas and permeable surfaces that stay cooler on hot days.

H
The heat island will not disappear, since a city by its nature replaces fields and forests with buildings and roads. But the evidence shows that thoughtful design can reduce it significantly. As climate change brings longer and more intense heatwaves, the ability to keep cities cool may become one of the most important tasks facing urban planners in the coming decades.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu khí hậu đô thị và quy hoạch đã công bố.

passages.title: The Long Road to Bicycle Sharing
passages.text:
A
Today, more than a thousand cities around the world operate bicycle-sharing schemes, allowing residents and visitors to pick up a bicycle in one place and leave it in another for a small fee. The idea seems simple, yet it took several decades of experiments, failures and technological change before it worked reliably. The history of bicycle sharing is a useful reminder that a good idea is not enough on its own; it must also be designed in a way that takes account of how people actually behave.

B
The first scheme was launched in Amsterdam in 1965 by a group of young activists who wanted to reduce the number of cars in the city centre. They painted a number of ordinary bicycles white and left them unlocked on the streets for anyone to use free of charge. The experiment ended almost immediately. Many of the bicycles were stolen or thrown into canals, and the police removed the rest on the grounds that unlocked bicycles encouraged theft. Although it failed in practice, the White Bicycle Plan became famous as a symbol of an alternative way of organising city transport.

C
Copenhagen made a more durable attempt in 1995. Its scheme used specially designed bicycles with solid tyres and unusual parts that would be of little use to thieves, and they could be released from city-centre stands by inserting a coin, in the same way that shoppers release supermarket trolleys. The coin was returned when the bicycle was brought back. The system was popular, but because users remained anonymous, there was little to stop people from keeping bicycles for days or abandoning them far from the stands, and many were lost or damaged.

D
The solution to the problem of anonymity came with information technology. In the late 1990s and 2000s, cities began to introduce schemes in which users registered in advance and released bicycles with an electronic card. Because every journey could be linked to a particular person, users had a strong incentive to return bicycles on time and in good condition. The most influential of these systems opened in Paris in 2007. Operated by an advertising company in return for the right to use public advertising space, it provided around twenty thousand bicycles at stations spread across the city.

E
The Paris model was copied widely, but station-based systems are expensive to build. Each station requires a site, a payment terminal and a set of docks, and vehicles must constantly move bicycles from stations that have filled up to stations that have run out. In the middle of the 2010s, a new generation of companies, many of them based in China, offered an alternative: dockless bicycles fitted with GPS and electronic locks that could be found and unlocked using a smartphone app and left anywhere at the end of the journey.

F
Dockless bicycles spread with extraordinary speed, supported by huge sums of investment. Within a couple of years, millions had been placed on the streets of Chinese cities, often far more than anyone needed. Pavements became blocked, and photographs of enormous ‘bicycle graveyards’, where thousands of unwanted bicycles had been piled up by city authorities, circulated around the world. Several of the companies collapsed, leaving customers unable to recover their deposits, and many cities introduced strict limits on the number of bicycles that operators were allowed to provide.

G
What have bicycle-sharing schemes actually achieved? Research suggests that their benefits are real but sometimes different from what their supporters expected. Many trips made on shared bicycles replace journeys that would otherwise have been made on foot or by public transport, rather than by car, so the reduction in traffic is often modest. On the other hand, the schemes encourage physical activity, help people complete the short distance between a railway station and their final destination, and can make cycling seem normal in cities where it was previously rare.

H
The latest development is the electric bicycle, which allows riders to travel further and to climb hills without arriving exhausted. Many schemes now offer electric models alongside conventional ones, and they have proved especially popular with older users and commuters. Sixty years after the white bicycles disappeared from the streets of Amsterdam, the idea that inspired them has finally become part of everyday life in cities around the world.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử giao thông đô thị và các báo cáo về hệ thống xe đạp công cộng.

passages.title: The Garden City Idea
passages.text:
A
At the end of the nineteenth century, the industrial cities of Britain were crowded, polluted and often unhealthy. Millions of people had moved from the countryside in search of work, and many lived in cramped housing with little light or fresh air. At the same time, rural areas were losing population and struggling economically. It was against this background that a modest office worker named Ebenezer Howard, who earned his living recording speeches in Parliament, published a short book in 1898 proposing a new kind of settlement that would combine the advantages of town and country while avoiding the disadvantages of both.

B
Howard illustrated his argument with a famous diagram of three magnets. The town, he explained, offered jobs, entertainment and social life, but also high rents, polluted air and a separation from nature. The countryside offered beauty and clean air, but also low wages, isolation and a lack of amusement. A third magnet, which he called town-country, would draw people with the best of both: well-paid work and lively culture set in green surroundings. Howard did not regard this as an impossible dream but as a practical proposal that could be built with private money.

C
His plan was remarkably detailed. A garden city would be built on land purchased at agricultural prices and owned collectively by the community. It would be limited to around thirty thousand people, with homes, factories, shops and parks arranged in rings around a central garden, and it would be surrounded by a permanent belt of farmland. As the city grew and land values rose, the increase would benefit the whole community rather than private landlords, paying for public services and repaying the original investors. Once a city reached its planned size, new growth would take place in another garden city nearby.

D
Howard's ideas attracted influential supporters, and in 1903 work began on the first garden city at Letchworth, about fifty kilometres north of London. Its layout was designed by the architects Raymond Unwin and Barry Parker, who favoured cottages built in traditional styles, set back from tree-lined roads and grouped around shared green spaces. A second garden city followed at Welwyn after the First World War. Both towns still exist, and Letchworth continues to be managed by a foundation that reinvests income from its land in local projects. The town was intended to house factory workers as well as wealthier residents, with industry located at a distance from the homes.

E
Although only two true garden cities were ever completed, the movement's influence spread far beyond them. Garden suburbs, which adopted the leafy appearance of Howard's towns without their economic arrangements, appeared around many cities. In the United States, the planners Clarence Stein and Henry Wright designed a community at Radburn, New Jersey, in 1929, in which houses faced onto gardens and footpaths while cars were kept to separate roads at the back. After the Second World War, Britain's programme of new towns and its policy of protecting green belts around cities both drew directly on Howard's thinking. Similar ideas also shaped new settlements in Germany, Australia and other countries during the early twentieth century.

F
The American writer Lewis Mumford was among Howard's greatest admirers, declaring that the garden city and the aeroplane were the two great inventions to emerge at the beginning of the twentieth century. Not everyone agreed. In 1961, the journalist and activist Jane Jacobs attacked the garden city tradition in a widely read book, arguing that it was fundamentally hostile to cities. Busy streets, mixed uses and dense neighbourhoods, she claimed, were what made urban life safe and lively, and planners who tried to replace them with tidy, low-density layouts were destroying the very qualities that cities depend on.

G
Later critics added that low-density suburbs encouraged dependence on the car, since homes, shops and workplaces were often too far apart to reach on foot. Supporters reply that this was not what Howard intended: his garden cities were meant to be compact, self-contained towns served by railways, in which most people could walk to work. In recent years, interest in his ideas has revived, particularly his proposal that rising land values should be captured for the benefit of the community, which some housing experts see as a possible way of paying for new homes and infrastructure.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử quy hoạch đô thị.

passages.title: Learning from Nature's Designs
passages.text:
A
After almost four billion years of evolution, living things have found solutions to an enormous range of practical problems: how to stay clean, how to move efficiently through air and water, how to keep cool in a hot climate and how to build strong structures from very little material. Increasingly, engineers and designers are turning to these solutions for inspiration. The practice, known as biomimicry, was popularised in the late 1990s by the American writer Janine Benyus, who argued that nature should be seen not as a store of raw materials but as a source of knowledge. The idea itself is far older: inventors have studied birds for clues about flight for centuries.

B
One of the best-known examples began with a walk in the Swiss countryside in 1941. When the engineer George de Mestral returned home, he noticed that his clothes and his dog's fur were covered with the seed heads of burdock plants. Examining them under a microscope, he saw that each was covered with tiny hooks that caught on anything with loops, such as fabric or hair. It took him years of experiment to reproduce the effect with nylon, but the result, a fastener made from two strips, one of hooks and one of loops, was eventually patented and is now used on everything from shoes to spacecraft.

C
Some of the most valuable lessons concern surfaces. In the 1970s, the German botanist Wilhelm Barthlott discovered why the leaves of the lotus plant remain clean even in muddy water. Their surfaces are covered with microscopic bumps coated in wax, so that water droplets cannot spread out but instead roll off, collecting dirt as they go. This ‘lotus effect’ has since been copied in self-cleaning paints, glass and fabrics. Researchers have also studied the feet of geckos, which can climb smooth walls thanks to millions of tiny hairs, in the hope of developing adhesives that grip strongly but can be removed without leaving a mark.

D
Nature has also helped engineers to reduce noise and energy use. In the 1990s, Japan's high-speed trains created a loud boom whenever they emerged from tunnels, because the train pushed a wall of compressed air ahead of it. An engineer named Eiji Nakatsu, who was also a keen birdwatcher, noticed that the kingfisher dives from the air into water with barely a splash. When the front of a new train was redesigned to resemble the bird's long, narrow beak, the noise problem was largely solved, and the train used less electricity while travelling faster.

E
Buildings offer another field for imitation. In the Zimbabwean capital, Harare, the architect Mick Pearce designed an office and shopping complex that opened in 1996 without conventional air conditioning. Instead, he drew on the way some termite mounds are thought to regulate their internal temperature, using a system of chimneys and vents through which air circulates naturally, drawing cool air in at night and expelling warm air during the day. The building is reported to use only a small fraction of the energy consumed by comparable buildings of the same size.

F
Not every imitation of nature works as intended. In 2008, swimsuits inspired partly by the texture of shark skin attracted enormous attention when swimmers wearing them broke dozens of world records. Later research suggested that the suits' success owed more to the way they compressed swimmers' bodies and trapped air than to any shark-like quality, and the governing body of the sport banned the most advanced versions in 2010. The episode illustrates a common difficulty: it is easy to be inspired by a natural model, but much harder to understand exactly how it works. So many records fell in such a short period that some commentators described the suits as a form of technological doping.

G
Supporters of biomimicry argue that it can do more than produce clever products. Because natural systems tend to work at ordinary temperatures, use locally available materials and generate no lasting waste, they believe that imitating nature could help to make manufacturing far more sustainable. Critics caution that a product inspired by nature is not automatically environmentally friendly; a self-cleaning coating may still contain harmful chemicals. Nevertheless, as engineers face increasingly urgent pressure to save energy and materials, the four-billion-year research programme of evolution seems likely to remain a valuable source of ideas.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu về khoa học vật liệu, kỹ thuật và kiến trúc phỏng sinh học.

passages.title: Persia's Windcatchers
passages.text:
A
Approaching the old city of Yazd in central Iran, a traveller sees a skyline unlike any other: dozens of rectangular towers rising above the flat roofs of mud-brick houses. These structures, known in Persian as bâdgir, or windcatchers, were for centuries the main way of keeping buildings cool in one of the hottest and driest regions on earth. They required no fuel and had no moving parts, yet they could make the interior of a house bearable in summer temperatures that regularly exceed forty degrees. Today, as architects search for ways to reduce the energy consumed by air conditioning, these ancient towers are attracting renewed interest.

B
The basic principle is simple. A windcatcher is a tall tower with openings near the top that face the direction of the prevailing wind. Because wind speeds are higher well above the ground, where buildings and walls cause less obstruction, the tower can capture a steady flow of air even when the streets below are still. The air is pushed down a vertical shaft inside the tower and into the rooms below, creating a draught that cools the occupants. Many towers are divided internally by thin partitions, creating several shafts so that air can enter through one and leave through another.

C
Windcatchers also work when there is little or no wind. During the day, the sun heats the tower and the air inside it. Warm air is lighter than cool air, so it rises and escapes through the openings at the top, drawing air out of the house beneath. This upward movement, known as the stack effect, pulls in cooler air from courtyards or shaded areas at ground level to replace it. In this way, a windcatcher can act either as an inlet that brings fresh air into the building or as an outlet that removes hot air, depending on the conditions.

D
The cooling effect could be greatly increased with the help of water. In some houses, air descending from the tower passed over a pool or fountain in a basement room. As some of the water evaporated, it absorbed heat from the air, lowering its temperature before it flowed into the living areas. In others, the tower was connected to a qanat, an underground channel that carried water from distant mountains, and air was drawn along the cool tunnel before rising into the house. Families often moved to these lower, cooler rooms during the hottest hours of the day.

E
The materials used in traditional buildings contributed as well. Thick walls of mud brick absorb heat slowly during the day and release it slowly at night, so that the inside of a house remains cooler than the outside in the afternoon and warmer during the cold desert night. Windcatchers were also used to cool water stored in large underground reservoirs, which were often surrounded by several towers. In Yazd, the tower in the garden of a former governor's residence rises to more than thirty metres and is often described as one of the tallest in the world.

F
The design of a windcatcher reflected local conditions. In places where the wind blew consistently from one direction, towers had openings on a single side. Where winds were more variable, builders constructed towers with four or even eight sides, so that air could be caught whichever way it was blowing. The height and size of a tower also indicated the wealth of the family who owned it, and a grand windcatcher was a symbol of social status as much as a practical device.

G
With the spread of electricity and mechanical air conditioning in the twentieth century, many windcatchers fell into disuse, and some were demolished. Air conditioners were cheap to install and easy to control, and they worked regardless of the weather. However, they also consume large amounts of electricity, much of it generated from fossil fuels, and as more buildings install them, they add to the very heat that they are designed to remove, since each unit releases warm air into the street outside.

H
Modern architects have begun to adapt the principles of the windcatcher using new materials and technology. Some office buildings and schools in Europe now have rooftop units that capture wind and expel stale air without fans, and several projects in the Middle East have included tall ventilation towers inspired directly by the traditional design. Such systems are rarely powerful enough to replace air conditioning entirely in extreme climates, but they can reduce the need for it considerably, demonstrating that solutions developed centuries ago may still have something to teach us.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu kiến trúc bản địa và nghiên cứu về thông gió tự nhiên.
