passages.title: Japan's Bullet Train
passages.text:
A
On the first day of October 1964, nine days before the opening of the Tokyo Olympic Games, a sleek blue-and-white train left Tokyo for Osaka. Travelling at up to 210 kilometres per hour, it covered the distance of more than five hundred kilometres in about four hours, a journey that had previously taken well over six. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen, as the new line was called, was the world's first high-speed railway, and its trains soon became known abroad as bullet trains. Six decades later, Japan's high-speed network carries hundreds of millions of passengers a year and remains a source of national pride.

B
The project was far from certain to succeed. In the 1950s, many experts in Japan and elsewhere believed that railways belonged to the past and that the future of transport lay with cars and aircraft. The corridor between Tokyo and Osaka, however, was home to a large part of Japan's population and industry, and the existing line was becoming dangerously overcrowded. Shinji Sogō, the president of Japanese National Railways, argued strongly for an entirely new line, while the chief engineer, Hideo Shima, brought the technical expertise needed to build it. Part of the cost was covered by a loan from the World Bank.

C
A crucial decision was to build a completely separate line. Japan's existing railways used a narrow gauge, the distance between the rails, which limited the speed at which trains could safely travel. The Shinkansen was built to the wider standard gauge used in much of Europe and North America, and it shared no tracks with slower trains. The line was designed with gentle curves, avoided level crossings with roads entirely, and used many tunnels and viaducts to maintain a smooth path through Japan's mountainous terrain.

D
Safety has been the system's most remarkable achievement. In its entire history, no passenger has been killed in a collision or derailment of a Shinkansen train. This record is particularly impressive because Japan experiences frequent earthquakes. The network uses an early warning system that detects the first, weaker vibrations of an earthquake, which travel faster than the more destructive waves that follow, and automatically cuts power to the trains so that they begin braking before the strongest shaking arrives. In 2004, a train derailed during a powerful earthquake in central Japan, but none of the passengers on board was injured.

E
The trains are also famous for their punctuality. According to the railway company that operates the original line, the average delay per train is typically less than a minute, including delays caused by bad weather and natural disasters. Such reliability depends on careful organisation at every stage. At the terminal stations, teams of cleaners board each train as soon as it arrives and prepare it for its next journey in a matter of minutes, turning the seats to face the direction of travel and removing every trace of litter.

F
The Shinkansen transformed the economic geography of Japan. Cities along the route became closer in practical terms, making it possible to travel between them for a meeting and return on the same day, and the railway competed so successfully with domestic flights that on some routes air travel declined. Critics, however, point out that the network has also concentrated economic activity in the largest cities, drawing people and businesses away from smaller towns that the trains pass through without stopping.

G
The success of the Shinkansen inspired other countries to build high-speed lines of their own. France opened its first line between Paris and Lyon in 1981, and networks were later built in Spain, Germany, Italy, South Korea and Taiwan. China now has by far the largest high-speed network in the world, much of it built within the last two decades. Japan, meanwhile, is constructing a new line between Tokyo and Nagoya that will use magnetic levitation, allowing trains to travel at around five hundred kilometres per hour.

H
Not every high-speed project has been a success. In some countries, lines have cost far more than expected or carried fewer passengers than forecast. Yet the original Shinkansen showed that, where large cities are separated by a few hundred kilometres, a fast, frequent and reliable railway can compete with both the car and the aeroplane, a lesson that many countries are still learning today.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử đường sắt cao tốc Nhật Bản.

passages.title: Letting Nature Take Over
passages.text:
A
For most of the twentieth century, nature conservation meant protecting what was left: drawing boundaries around nature reserves, managing them carefully and preventing further damage. In recent decades a bolder idea has gained ground. Rewilding aims not simply to preserve surviving habitats but to restore natural processes on a large scale, often by bringing back species that have disappeared and then allowing ecosystems to develop with as little human interference as possible. Its supporters see it as a hopeful response to the loss of wildlife; its critics regard it as romantic, unpredictable and sometimes dangerous.

B
The most famous example comes from Yellowstone National Park in the United States, where grey wolves, eliminated by hunting in the early twentieth century, were reintroduced in the mid-1990s. Over the following years, scientists reported a series of changes. Elk, the wolves' main prey, became less numerous and appeared to avoid open valleys where they were vulnerable, allowing trees such as willow and aspen to recover along rivers. The story of how a single predator could reshape an entire landscape spread widely and became the defining example of rewilding. Visitors also gained new opportunities to watch wolves in the wild, bringing additional income to towns near the park.

C
The reality, as is often the case, turned out to be more complicated. Later studies suggested that the recovery of trees was patchy and that other factors, including drought, hunting by humans and the growing number of bears and cougars, had also influenced the elk population. Some ecologists argued that the popular account had exaggerated the wolves' role. None of this means that the reintroduction was a mistake, but it does show the danger of telling simple stories about complex systems, and I believe that rewilding projects should be honest about how uncertain their outcomes are.

D
In Europe, where very little truly wild land remains, rewilding has often taken a different form. At Knepp, a large estate in southern England, the owners abandoned intensive farming in 2001 after years of financial losses on heavy clay soil. Instead, they allowed hedges and scrub to spread across former fields and introduced free-roaming herds of hardy cattle, ponies, pigs and deer, which graze, trample and root in ways that mimic the animals that once lived wild in the region. Within two decades, the estate had become home to rare species that had almost vanished from Britain, including turtle doves and nightingales. Purple emperor butterflies, rarely seen elsewhere in the country, also became common.

E
Not every experiment has gone smoothly. In a nature reserve in the Netherlands, large populations of deer, cattle and horses were allowed to grow without the presence of predators. During harsh winters, when food was scarce, thousands of animals starved, and pictures of dying animals caused public outrage. The authorities eventually decided to reduce the herds by shooting some of the animals. The episode raised difficult questions about whether people have a responsibility to intervene when animals suffer in a landscape that humans themselves have created. Supporters had expected the animals to regulate their own numbers, as wild herds might have done in prehistoric times.

F
Rewilding also raises social questions. Farmers may fear that reintroduced predators will attack their livestock, and people who live in rural areas can feel that decisions are being imposed on them by outsiders who do not depend on the land for a living. These concerns are entirely reasonable, and projects that ignore them are unlikely to last. The most successful schemes have generally involved local communities from the start, offered compensation for any losses and created new sources of income, such as wildlife tourism, to replace those that have been lost. In several countries, the return of large animals has been allowed only after lengthy public consultation.

G
Despite these difficulties, I remain convinced that rewilding has an important part to play. It cannot replace traditional conservation, and it will not suit every landscape, but in places where farming has become uneconomic or where natural processes have been severely disrupted, allowing nature greater freedom may produce richer and more resilient ecosystems than careful management alone. What matters is that each project is planned carefully, monitored honestly and adapted as evidence accumulates, rather than promoted with promises it cannot keep.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các dự án tái hoang dã và nghiên cứu sinh thái đã công bố.

passages.title: Forests Between Land and Sea
passages.text:
A
Along tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, grow some of the most unusual forests on earth. Mangroves are trees and shrubs that live in the zone between high and low tide, their roots submerged in salt water twice a day and their trunks rising from soft, airless mud. Few other trees could survive such conditions for more than a few days. Mangroves not only survive but flourish, forming dense forests that are found along the coasts of more than a hundred countries and that provide benefits extending far beyond the shoreline. The word is used both for the individual trees and for the forests that they form.

B
The first challenge is salt. Sea water contains enough salt to kill most land plants by drawing water out of their tissues. Different mangrove species have evolved different solutions. Some filter out almost all of the salt at their roots, allowing only fresh water to pass into the plant. Others absorb salt but get rid of it through special glands on their leaves, which can sometimes be seen covered in tiny salt crystals. A third group stores salt in older leaves, which are then shed, carrying the salt away with them.

C
The second challenge is a lack of oxygen. The waterlogged mud in which mangroves grow contains very little air, and roots, like other living tissues, need oxygen to function. Some species solve this problem with prop roots, which arch outwards from the trunk above the water, supporting the tree and taking in air through small pores in their surface. Others send up hundreds of pencil-like roots called pneumatophores, which stick vertically out of the mud around the tree and act as snorkels, allowing air to reach the roots buried below.

D
Reproduction presents a further difficulty, since a seed that falls into the sea may be carried away or drowned before it can take root. Many mangroves have overcome this by a remarkable strategy: their seeds begin to germinate while still attached to the parent tree. Each develops into a long, spear-shaped seedling, sometimes called a propagule, before dropping into the water. Propagules can float for weeks or even months, travelling long distances on ocean currents, and quickly put down roots when they reach a suitable muddy shore.

E
These forests are of enormous value to people. The tangle of roots slows the movement of water, reducing the height of waves and protecting coastal communities from storms and erosion. Sheltered waters among the roots serve as nurseries for many species of fish and shellfish, including some that are later caught far out at sea, so the health of mangroves directly affects the livelihoods of fishing communities. Mangroves also trap sediment carried by rivers, helping coastlines to build up rather than wash away.

F
In recent years, scientists have drawn attention to another benefit: mangroves are exceptionally effective at storing carbon. Because their roots grow in waterlogged mud where dead plant material decays very slowly, carbon can accumulate in the soil for thousands of years. Studies suggest that a hectare of mangrove forest may store several times as much carbon as a hectare of tropical rainforest, most of it below ground. When mangroves are cleared, much of this stored carbon is released into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

G
Despite their value, mangroves have been destroyed on a large scale. Over the past half-century, a significant proportion of the world's mangrove forests has been lost, cleared for coastal development, agriculture and, above all, ponds for farming shrimp. Many such ponds are abandoned after a few years, once disease or pollution makes them unproductive, leaving behind damaged land that is difficult to restore. Replanting projects have had mixed results, partly because seedlings are often planted in places where the conditions of water and soil do not suit them.

H
Experts now emphasise that successful restoration depends on understanding why mangroves disappeared from a particular place in the first place, and on restoring the natural flow of water that allows them to grow. Where this is done, mangroves can recover surprisingly quickly, often re-establishing themselves from seeds carried in by the tide. Protecting the forests that remain, however, is far cheaper and more effective than trying to replace them once they have gone.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu sinh thái học về rừng ngập mặn.

passages.title: The Disappearing Night
passages.text:
A
For almost all of human history, people looked up on a clear night and saw thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way stretching across the sky. Today, most people living in cities have never seen it. Researchers who mapped the brightness of the night sky in 2016 estimated that more than a third of humanity, including around four-fifths of North Americans, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Artificial light at night has transformed our environment so gradually that few people notice what has been lost, yet I would argue that it is one of the most widespread and least discussed forms of pollution.

B
The problem is growing quickly. Satellite measurements show that the area of the earth's surface that is artificially lit at night has been expanding by around two per cent a year. Satellites, however, underestimate the change, because they cannot detect much of the blue light emitted by modern white lamps. A study that relied instead on observations by tens of thousands of volunteers, who recorded how many stars they could see, concluded that the night sky was becoming brighter by nearly ten per cent each year, a rate at which the number of visible stars would halve in less than a decade.

C
The consequences for wildlife are serious. Many animals rely on natural light to navigate, find food or time their behaviour. Newly hatched sea turtles, for example, find their way to the ocean by heading towards the brightest horizon, which on an undeveloped beach is the sky above the sea; near towns, lights draw them inland, where they die from exhaustion or are killed by predators and traffic. Migrating birds, which often travel at night, can become disoriented by brightly lit buildings, and very large numbers die each year in collisions with them.

D
Insects may be affected most of all. Moths and other night-flying insects are drawn to artificial lights, where many circle until they die or are eaten. Because insects pollinate plants and form the base of many food chains, scientists have suggested that light pollution may be one of the factors behind the alarming decline in insect populations reported in many parts of the world. It is unlikely to be the main cause, but unlike some other causes, such as changes in climate, it could be reduced quickly and at relatively little cost.

E
Humans are not immune either. Our bodies follow a daily rhythm controlled partly by a hormone, melatonin, whose production rises in darkness and helps us to sleep. Exposure to bright light at night, especially blue light, suppresses melatonin and can disturb sleep. Researchers are still investigating how much the background glow of outdoor lighting, as opposed to the screens and lamps inside our homes, contributes to such effects, so firm conclusions about the health risks of light pollution would be premature.

F
Ironically, a technology that should have helped has in some ways made matters worse. Modern LED lamps use far less electricity than older bulbs, and many cities have replaced their streetlights in order to save energy and money. Yet because LED lighting is so cheap to run, many places now install more lights and leave them on for longer, cancelling out much of the saving. In addition, the cold, bluish-white light produced by many early LED streetlights scatters more widely in the atmosphere than the orange glow of older lamps, increasing the brightness of the sky.

G
What makes this form of pollution unusual is how easily it could be solved. Unlike chemical pollution, light disappears the moment it is switched off. Lamps can be fitted with shields so that light shines downwards, where it is needed, rather than sideways or up into the sky. Warmer colours can be chosen, and lights can be dimmed or switched off late at night when streets are empty. Some towns have adopted such rules for decades; one city in the American state of Arizona introduced restrictions on outdoor lighting as early as 1958 to protect the view from a nearby observatory.

H
In my view, governments should treat darkness as a resource worth protecting, in the same way that they protect clean air and water. Good lighting design need not make streets less safe; well-directed light can improve visibility while reducing glare. The night sky has inspired science, art and religion for thousands of years, and it would be a great loss if future generations grew up without ever seeing it.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu về ô nhiễm ánh sáng đã công bố.

passages.title: The Toad That Conquered Australia
passages.text:
A
In June 1935, a small consignment of toads arrived in the Australian state of Queensland from Hawaii. There were just over a hundred of them, and they had been brought for a clear purpose: to eat the beetles that were damaging the region's valuable sugar cane crops. Within a few months, the toads had bred, and thousands of their offspring were released into cane fields along the coast. It was one of the most confident experiments in biological control ever attempted, and it went badly wrong. Today, the descendants of those original toads number in the hundreds of millions and occupy an area larger than many countries. The beetle larvae were causing heavy losses to farmers, and few effective chemical treatments were available at the time.

B
The cane toad turned out to be almost useless for the task it had been brought to perform. The adult beetles lived high on the stems of the cane plants, where the toads could not reach them, and their young lived underground, feeding on the roots. The toads, meanwhile, ate almost anything else they could catch, including native insects, frogs and small animals. Some scientists had warned against the introduction even before it took place, but their objections were overruled by agricultural officials eager to find a solution to the beetle problem.

C
Several characteristics have made the cane toad an exceptionally successful invader. A single female can lay tens of thousands of eggs at a time, far more than most native frogs. The toads tolerate a wide range of conditions, from tropical wetlands to dry grasslands, and in Australia they have no natural predators adapted to deal with them. Most importantly, they are poisonous at every stage of life. Glands on the adult toad's shoulders produce a powerful toxin, and animals that try to eat one often die within minutes. They will also breed in almost any still or slow-moving water, from farm dams to garden ponds.

D
The toads have spread across northern Australia at an accelerating pace. In the early years, the invasion front advanced by around ten kilometres a year; by the beginning of this century it was moving more than five times as fast. Researchers led by the biologist Rick Shine discovered that toads at the leading edge of the invasion had longer legs than those in long-established populations and travelled further each night. Because the fastest toads reached new territory first and bred with one another, each generation at the front was faster than the last, a striking example of evolution occurring within a few decades.

E
The impact on native wildlife has been severe in some areas. Large lizards called goannas, freshwater crocodiles, some snakes and a cat-sized marsupial known as the northern quoll have suffered dramatic declines where toads have arrived, because they attack the toads as they would any other prey and are killed by the poison. In some places, populations of these predators fell by more than ninety per cent within a few years. Other species, however, have been less affected than expected, and some birds have learned to turn toads over and eat only the parts that are not toxic. Pet dogs that bite toads are also frequently poisoned.

F
Eliminating the toads from Australia is now considered impossible, so scientists have looked for ways to reduce the damage. One promising approach takes advantage of the fact that animals can learn to avoid food that makes them ill. Researchers fed young quolls small pieces of toad meat treated with a chemical that caused nausea but was not dangerous. Quolls that had been trained in this way were far less likely to attack live toads after being released, and they survived much longer than untrained animals.

G
Communities have also become involved. In many towns, volunteers organise evening events at which they collect toads from gardens and parks, and researchers have developed traps that attract adult toads using recorded calls or attract tadpoles using chemicals released by toad eggs. Such efforts cannot stop the invasion, but they can protect particular areas, such as islands or wildlife reserves, where vulnerable native species survive. The story of the cane toad has become a lasting warning about the risks of introducing species to new environments without understanding the consequences.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu sinh thái học về loài xâm lấn tại Úc.

passages.title: A Vault for the World's Crops
passages.text:
A
On a remote Arctic island, about a thousand kilometres from the North Pole, a narrow concrete entrance juts out of a snowy mountainside. Behind it, a tunnel leads more than a hundred metres into the rock, ending in three chambers where the temperature is kept at eighteen degrees below zero. Stacked on shelves inside are boxes containing well over a million packets of seeds, sent from almost every country in the world. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, which opened in 2008, is often described as a ‘doomsday vault’, but its purpose is more practical than that dramatic name suggests.

B
Over thousands of years, farmers developed an enormous variety of crops. A single species such as rice or wheat exists in many thousands of local varieties, each adapted to particular soils, climates, pests and diseases. During the twentieth century, much of this diversity began to disappear as farmers around the world switched to a small number of high-yielding modern varieties. The older types might produce less, but they contain genes that could prove vital in the future, for example to help crops survive droughts, resist new diseases or cope with a changing climate. From the 1960s onwards, agricultural scientists warned that this loss of genetic diversity could threaten the world's food supply.

C
The idea of collecting and preserving seeds is far older than Svalbard. In the 1920s and 1930s, the Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov led expeditions across five continents, gathering hundreds of thousands of seeds for an institute in Leningrad, now St Petersburg. During the long siege of the city in the Second World War, staff guarded the collection while the population starved; several of them died of hunger rather than eat the seeds in their care. Vavilov himself, who had fallen out of favour with the Soviet authorities, died in prison in 1943.

D
Today, around seventeen hundred seed banks exist around the world, but many are vulnerable. Some have been damaged by floods, fires or equipment failures, and others by war. Svalbard was designed as a back-up for all of them. Seed banks send duplicate samples of their collections to the vault, where they are stored under what is known as a ‘black box’ arrangement: the depositor keeps ownership of the seeds, and only the depositor can ask for them to be returned. The location was chosen because it is geologically stable, high above sea level and naturally cold, so that the seeds would remain frozen even if the cooling equipment failed.

E
Preparing seeds for long-term storage is a careful process. After being collected, they are cleaned and checked for disease, and then dried until they contain very little moisture, since water in the seeds would form ice crystals that destroy their cells when frozen. The dried seeds are sealed in airtight foil packets and placed in cold storage. Even under these conditions, seeds slowly lose their ability to germinate, so seed banks periodically test samples by trying to grow them. When the proportion that germinates falls too low, fresh plants are grown in order to produce a new supply of seeds.

F
The vault proved its value sooner than expected. In 2015, an international agricultural research centre that had been based near Aleppo in Syria became the first organisation to withdraw seeds from Svalbard, after the civil war made it impossible to maintain its collection there. Using the duplicates it had deposited, the centre re-established its collection at new sites in Lebanon and Morocco and grew fresh seeds, some of which it later sent back to the vault to replace those it had taken out. It was the first time that any seeds had left the vault since its opening.

G
The vault has not been free of problems. In 2017, unusually warm weather caused melting snow and rain to enter the entrance tunnel. No seeds were affected, but the incident attracted worldwide publicity, and the facility was later improved with waterproof walls and new drainage. Some scientists also point out that frozen seeds preserve diversity only as it existed when they were collected; crops grown in farmers' fields continue to adapt to changing conditions, which is why many experts argue that seed banks should complement, rather than replace, the conservation of traditional varieties on farms.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu về ngân hàng hạt giống và đa dạng di truyền cây trồng.

passages.title: The Return of the Beaver
passages.text:
A
Few animals change their surroundings as dramatically as the beaver. Using only their teeth, beavers fell trees, build dams across streams and create ponds and wetlands where previously there was only a narrow channel of running water. For this reason, ecologists describe them as ecosystem engineers. In Britain, the Eurasian beaver was hunted to extinction several centuries ago for its fur, its meat and a substance from its glands that was used in medicine and perfume. Now, after an absence of around four hundred years, beavers are returning to British rivers, and their arrival is provoking both enthusiasm and concern. Its close relative, the North American beaver, is far more numerous and is a national symbol of Canada.

B
A beaver's teeth are remarkable tools. The front teeth never stop growing and are coated on the front with a hard, orange-coloured enamel that contains iron, while the back of each tooth is softer. As the animal gnaws, the softer material wears away more quickly, keeping the teeth sharp like a chisel. A single beaver can cut through a small tree in a matter of minutes. The branches provide food, since beavers eat bark, leaves and other plants, as well as material for building.

C
Beavers build dams to raise the level of water around their homes, which helps protect them from predators. Many families live in a lodge, a dome-shaped mound of sticks and mud built in or beside the water. The entrances are underwater, so that predators on land cannot easily get in, while inside, above the water level, there is a dry chamber where the beavers rest and raise their young. A small gap at the top of the lodge, where the sticks are not packed tightly with mud, allows fresh air to enter. In autumn, beavers store branches on the bottom of the pond close to the lodge, so that they can feed during winter when the surface is frozen.

D
The ponds and wetlands that beavers create can bring substantial benefits. Researchers studying a population living in an enclosure in the south-west of England found that the series of dams the animals built reduced the peak flow of water downstream during heavy rain, lowering the risk of flooding in nearby towns. The dams also trapped soil washed from surrounding farmland, along with some of the fertilisers and other pollutants carried with it, so that the water flowing out was cleaner than the water flowing in. The wetlands became home to many more species of plants, insects and amphibians than before.

E
The return of the beaver to England began unofficially. In 2008, a small group of beavers was discovered living wild on a river in Devon. Nobody knew exactly where they had come from, and the government initially proposed removing them. After local protests, it agreed instead to a five-year trial in which the animals were monitored closely. When the trial ended in 2020, the government allowed the beavers to remain permanently, the first time that an extinct native mammal had been officially accepted back into the wild in England.

F
Not everyone has welcomed them. Farmers have complained that beaver dams can flood valuable fields, block drainage ditches and damage crops, and that the animals sometimes fell trees in orchards and gardens. Landowners worry about who will pay for the damage. Supporters argue that most problems can be managed with relatively simple measures, such as protecting particular trees with wire mesh or installing pipes through dams so that water levels remain within acceptable limits, and that dams can be removed where necessary.

G
The debate reflects a broader question about how much space people are willing to give to wildlife in a crowded country. Beavers cannot be confined to nature reserves, since they move along river systems in search of new territory, and they will inevitably come into contact with farmland and homes. Their supporters argue that the benefits they bring, from cleaner water to reduced flooding, far outweigh the costs, provided that farmers receive advice and compensation. Whether that argument persuades the people who live alongside them is likely to determine how far the beaver's return can go. Similar arguments have taken place in Scotland, where beavers have had legal protection since 2019.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu sinh thái học và các dự án tái thả hải ly ở Anh.

passages.title: When the Plains Blew Away
passages.text:
A
On the afternoon of 14 April 1935, residents of the southern Great Plains of the United States saw a vast black cloud approaching from the north. Within minutes, day turned to night as a wall of dust, hundreds of metres high, swept across towns and farms. People caught outdoors could not see their own hands, and many feared that the world was ending. The storm, remembered as Black Sunday, was the worst of hundreds that struck the region during the 1930s, a decade in which a large area of farmland in parts of five states became known as the Dust Bowl. Families sealed their windows and doors with wet cloths, but fine dust still found its way onto every surface inside their homes.

B
The disaster had its roots in the decades before. When settlers arrived on the southern plains in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, they found land covered with deep-rooted native grasses that had held the soil in place for thousands of years, despite periodic droughts and strong winds. During the First World War, high prices for wheat and the arrival of tractors encouraged farmers to plough up millions of hectares of this grassland. For a time the strategy seemed to work: rainfall was relatively good, harvests were large and many farmers prospered.

C
Then, in the early 1930s, the rain stopped. Crops withered, and with the grass gone, nothing protected the exposed, dried-out soil. The strong winds of the plains lifted the fine topsoil into the air and carried it away in enormous clouds. Some storms carried dust hundreds of kilometres; in May 1934, a storm dropped dust on cities on the east coast, and ships far out in the Atlantic Ocean reported dust settling on their decks. On the plains, drifts of soil buried fences and machinery, and fields that had produced wheat became barren.

D
The human consequences were severe. The drought coincided with the Great Depression, and falling crop prices had already left many farmers deeply in debt. Families struggled with respiratory illnesses caused by breathing dust, which doctors called dust pneumonia. Hundreds of thousands of people eventually left the region, many travelling west to California in search of work as agricultural labourers. Their experiences were recorded in photographs taken for the federal government and in John Steinbeck's novel The Grapes of Wrath, which shaped how later generations understood the period. Many of those who stayed behind depended on government relief to survive.

E
The federal government responded with a range of programmes. A key figure was Hugh Hammond Bennett, a soil scientist who had been warning for years about the dangers of soil erosion. According to a frequently told story, while Bennett was giving evidence to members of Congress in Washington in the spring of 1935, a dust storm from the plains darkened the sky outside, dramatically confirming his argument. Whether or not the timing was quite so convenient, Congress soon passed legislation creating a permanent agency devoted to soil conservation, with Bennett as its first head.

F
The new agency promoted farming methods designed to keep soil in place. Farmers were encouraged to plough along the contours of the land rather than in straight lines, so that furrows would catch water instead of channelling it away, and to plant strips of different crops to break the force of the wind. Some land was returned to grass. Between 1935 and 1942, a programme of tree planting created long belts of trees across the plains to act as windbreaks. Because individual farmers could not afford to change their methods alone, the government paid many of them to do so. Many of these windbreaks still stand today.

G
When the rain returned at the end of the decade, the storms subsided, and conservation methods, along with improved irrigation, helped to prevent a disaster on the same scale when severe droughts struck again in later decades. Historians continue to debate how far the Dust Bowl was caused by drought and how far by human decisions, but most agree that the destruction of native grassland turned a natural drought into an ecological catastrophe. Today, as some agricultural regions face increasing risks of drought, the lessons of the 1930s about the importance of protecting soil remain highly relevant.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử môi trường và nông nghiệp Hoa Kỳ.

passages.title: How Sea Turtles Find Their Way
passages.text:
A
On summer nights along the beaches of Florida, tiny loggerhead turtles dig their way out of nests buried in the sand and scramble towards the sea. For those that survive the dash across the beach and the first dangerous hours in the water, an extraordinary journey lies ahead. Young loggerheads from Florida swim out into the Atlantic Ocean and spend years drifting and feeding in the vast circular current system that flows around the North Atlantic. Many years later, the females return to nest on the same stretch of coast where they themselves hatched. How they manage to do this has puzzled scientists for decades.

B
For much of the twentieth century, almost nothing was known about where young turtles went after leaving the beach. The American biologist Archie Carr, a pioneer of sea turtle research, referred to this mysterious period in their lives as ‘the lost years’. Carr and his colleagues attached metal tags to thousands of nesting females in order to track their movements, and these studies confirmed that females return repeatedly to the same nesting areas. But tags revealed only where a turtle had been caught, not how it had travelled, and the young turtles were too small to tag at all.

C
The first stage of the journey is now reasonably well understood. Hatchlings emerging from the nest head towards the brightest horizon, which on a natural beach is usually the open sky over the sea rather than the darker vegetation inland. Once in the water, they swim directly into the waves, which near the shore generally travel towards the beach, so that by heading into them the turtles move out to sea. Further offshore, where waves are a less reliable guide, the turtles appear to switch to a different and more remarkable sense.

D
That sense is the ability to detect the earth's magnetic field. The field varies from place to place in both its strength and the angle at which its lines meet the earth's surface, so that different locations have slightly different magnetic signatures. In a series of experiments, the biologist Kenneth Lohmann and his colleagues placed young turtles in a tank of water surrounded by coils of wire that could reproduce the magnetic conditions found at different points in the Atlantic. The turtles swam in directions that, in the real ocean, would have kept them safely within the current system rather than allowing them to drift into colder, more dangerous waters.

E
These results suggested that turtles possess a kind of magnetic map that allows them to work out where they are, not merely a compass that tells them which way is north. Further evidence came from a study of nesting sites. The earth's magnetic field changes slowly over time, so the magnetic signature of a particular beach gradually shifts along the coast. In a study published in 2015, J. Roger Brothers and Lohmann found that loggerhead nesting sites in Florida had moved in ways that matched these changes, which suggests that females remember the magnetic signature of the beach where they hatched and use it to find their way back.

F
Magnetic navigation is probably not the whole story. As turtles approach the coast, they may use other cues, such as the smell of particular beaches or the shape of the shoreline, to locate their nesting sites precisely. Scientists also do not yet understand exactly how turtles sense magnetic fields; several possible mechanisms have been proposed, but none has been confirmed. What is clear is that their ability to navigate across thousands of kilometres of open ocean is among the most impressive achievements in the animal world.

G
This research has practical importance, because all species of sea turtle face serious threats. Artificial lighting near beaches draws hatchlings away from the sea, and many conservation groups now persuade coastal towns to switch off or shield lights during the nesting season. Turtles are also caught accidentally in fishing nets and harmed by plastic waste. Understanding how turtles navigate may help to identify the routes and feeding areas that most need protection, and some researchers have even raised concerns that strong artificial magnetic fields, such as those produced by undersea cables, could interfere with their sense of direction. On some beaches, volunteers now patrol the sand during the nesting season.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu về định hướng của rùa biển đã công bố.

passages.title: The Cleverness of Crows
passages.text:
A
For much of the twentieth century, the phrase ‘bird brain’ was used as an insult, reflecting a widespread belief that birds were capable of little more than simple, instinctive behaviour. That view has been overturned by research on a family of birds that includes crows, ravens, rooks and jays. Over the past three decades, scientists have shown that some of these birds can make and use tools, solve complex problems, remember individual human faces and plan for the future. In some tasks, their performance rivals that of great apes, the animals usually regarded as the most intelligent after humans.

B
The most celebrated tool users are the crows of New Caledonia, a group of islands in the south-west Pacific. In 1996, the biologist Gavin Hunt reported that these birds manufacture two distinct kinds of tool. They strip twigs and shape the ends into hooks, and they cut the edges of tough pandanus leaves into stepped or tapered strips. The crows use these implements to extract insect larvae from holes in dead wood. Remarkably, the design of the leaf tools varies from one area to another, which some researchers interpret as evidence that the techniques are passed on and refined over generations, a basic form of culture.

C
A captive New Caledonian crow named Betty made headlines in 2002. Researchers at the University of Oxford, including Alex Kacelnik, had placed a small bucket of food at the bottom of a tube and offered the crows a straight piece of wire and a hooked one. When her companion flew off with the hooked wire, Betty took the straight piece, bent it into a hook by wedging one end against a surface, and used it to lift the bucket out. At the time, the behaviour appeared to show an astonishing capacity for improvisation. Later studies found that wild crows often bend twigs in similar ways, suggesting that Betty may have been drawing on a natural tendency rather than inventing an entirely new technique.

D
Other experiments have been inspired by an ancient fable in which a thirsty crow drops pebbles into a jug until the water rises high enough for it to drink. Nathan Emery and his colleagues gave rooks a tube of water with a worm floating out of reach; the birds dropped stones into the tube until they could reach their reward. Later studies with crows found that they preferred to drop heavy objects rather than light ones, and solid objects rather than hollow ones, suggesting that they understood, at least to some extent, which objects would raise the water level most effectively.

E
Crows also appear to be capable of combining objects to create something new. In 2018, a team including Auguste von Bayern presented New Caledonian crows with food placed in a box, too far away to reach with any of the short sticks available. Several of the birds solved the problem by fitting two or more sticks together to create a longer tool, a feat previously observed only in humans and great apes. Because the crows had never been trained to do this, the researchers argued that the birds were able to imagine the solution before carrying it out.

F
Some of the most entertaining research concerns the relationship between crows and people. At the University of Washington, the biologist John Marzluff and his students captured and released wild crows while wearing a particular rubber mask. For years afterwards, crows on the campus scolded and dive-bombed anyone wearing that mask, even if the person wearing it had never handled a crow, while ignoring people in other masks. The number of crows reacting to the mask increased over time, indicating that birds which had never been captured had learned from others which face to fear.

G
How can birds with brains the size of a walnut achieve such feats? Part of the answer is that bird brains are organised very differently from those of mammals. Research published in 2016 found that the neurons in the brains of crows and parrots are packed far more densely than in mammal brains, so that a crow's brain may contain as many neurons as the much larger brain of some monkeys. Size, it seems, is a poor guide to intelligence, and the study of crows has forced scientists to reconsider what it takes to think.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu về nhận thức của loài quạ đã công bố.

passages.title: The Hidden Language of Elephants
passages.text:
A
Elephants live in complex societies. Females and their young stay together in close family groups led by an older female, the matriarch, while adult males often live alone or in loose bachelor groups. Members of a family may become separated by several kilometres as they search for food and water, yet they manage to coordinate their movements, meet up again at particular places and respond to one another's distress. For a long time, it was unclear how they did so. The answer, it turned out, lay largely in sounds that human beings cannot hear. Elephants can live for sixty years or more, and the bonds between members of a family may last for decades.

B
The discovery was made in 1984 by Katy Payne, an American researcher who had previously studied the songs of humpback whales. While watching elephants at a zoo in the United States, she noticed a faint throbbing sensation in the air, similar to the feeling she remembered from standing near a church organ as its deepest notes were played. Suspecting that the elephants were producing sounds too low for humans to hear, she returned with recording equipment. When the recordings were played back at higher speed, they revealed a rich variety of calls far below the range of human hearing.

C
Such sounds, known as infrasound, have an important advantage: low-frequency sound waves lose energy much more slowly than high-frequency ones as they travel through the air. Elephants' deep rumbles can therefore carry over distances of several kilometres. Researchers have found that the range is greatest in the early evening and at night, when the air near the ground is cooler and calmer, and some scientists believe that elephants time many of their long-distance calls to take advantage of these conditions. The calls also carry information about the identity, age and emotional state of the caller, so that listeners can recognise relatives from far away.

D
Elephants may also communicate through the ground. The biologist Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell noticed that elephants sometimes froze, lifted one foot or pressed their trunks to the ground, as if listening. Her research suggested that the powerful rumbles of elephants produce vibrations that travel through the earth, possibly even further than sound travels through the air, and that elephants detect these vibrations with sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks. This could allow them to sense distant calls, or even the movement of other herds, without hearing anything at all.

E
The vocal abilities of elephants are not limited to rumbles. Researchers in Kenya, including Joyce Poole, have described elephants that imitated sounds they had heard, which is rare among mammals. One young female living near a busy road appeared to reproduce the noise of passing trucks, and a male kept in captivity with Asian elephants imitated the chirping calls of his companions rather than the sounds typical of African elephants. Such imitation suggests that elephants, like humans, parrots and some whales, are capable of learning new sounds rather than relying only on calls they are born with. Scientists regard this kind of vocal learning as a sign of unusually flexible intelligence.

F
Recent research suggests something even more remarkable. In 2024, a team led by Mickey Pardo analysed hundreds of rumbles recorded from wild African elephants and found that some calls appeared to be addressed to particular individuals. When the researchers played back a call that had originally been directed at a specific elephant, that elephant responded more strongly than to calls directed at others. The scientists concluded that elephants may address one another with something like names, an ability previously known in only a very small number of animals, including humans and dolphins.

G
Understanding elephant communication has practical value. Wildlife managers use recordings to estimate the number of elephants in dense forests where they are hard to see, and some projects have experimented with playing elephant calls to discourage herds from raiding crops. At the same time, the research raises concerns. Human noise from roads, mining and machinery may interfere with elephants' ability to hear one another over long distances, potentially disrupting family groups that depend on keeping in contact. Researchers have also built up large libraries of recordings to help them interpret what different calls mean.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu về giao tiếp của voi đã công bố.

passages.title: Stronger Than Steel
passages.text:
A
Few natural materials have attracted as much scientific attention as the silk of spiders. Weight for weight, the strongest spider silk is stronger than steel, and it can absorb far more energy before breaking than the synthetic fibres used in bulletproof vests. It is also remarkably elastic, stretching considerably without snapping, and it is light, biodegradable and well tolerated by the human body. Engineers have long dreamed of producing it in large quantities for uses ranging from surgical stitches to lightweight cables, but the dream has proved extraordinarily difficult to achieve.

B
Spiders do not produce a single kind of silk. A typical orb-weaving spider, which builds the familiar circular web, has several different glands, each producing silk with particular properties. Dragline silk, which forms the frame and spokes of the web and serves as a safety line when the spider drops from a height, is especially strong. The spiral that catches insects is made from a much stretchier silk coated with sticky droplets, while other glands produce silk for wrapping prey or protecting eggs. Each type is suited to a different job, and a single web may combine several of them. Some species can produce as many as seven different kinds.

C
The process by which spiders turn liquid into solid fibre is as impressive as the silk itself. Inside the spider's glands, the silk proteins are stored as a thick, concentrated liquid. As this liquid flows along a narrow tube towards the spinnerets, the openings at the rear of the spider's body, water is gradually removed and the chemical conditions change, becoming more acidic. Finally, as the spider pulls the silk out, using its legs or the weight of its own body, the proteins line up in long chains and lock together into a solid thread. The whole process takes place at ordinary temperatures and uses only water as a solvent.

D
Why not simply farm spiders, as silkworms have been farmed for thousands of years? The difficulty is that most spiders are territorial and, when kept together in large numbers, tend to eat one another. A rare demonstration of what is possible came in 2012, when a cape woven from the golden silk of more than a million spiders went on display at a museum in London. The spiders had been collected in Madagascar, carefully harnessed so that their silk could be drawn out, and then released. The project took years and showed clearly that natural spider silk could never be produced cheaply on an industrial scale.

E
Scientists have therefore turned to genetic engineering. By identifying the genes that spiders use to make silk proteins, researchers have been able to insert them into other organisms, including bacteria, yeast, plants and silkworms, which then produce the proteins. One of the most publicised experiments, at the start of this century, involved goats that had been modified to produce silk proteins in their milk. The proteins could then be extracted and purified, but turning them into a fibre with the properties of natural silk proved much harder than producing the proteins themselves. Silkworms, which already spin large quantities of silk, have been a particular focus of this research.

F
The central problem lies in spinning. The extraordinary strength of spider silk depends not only on its chemical composition but on the precise way the proteins are arranged as the fibre forms, and reproducing the conditions inside a spider's narrow ducts has proved extremely difficult. Early artificial fibres were often weaker and more brittle than the natural material. In recent years, however, researchers have made progress by designing spinning devices that imitate the gradual changes in acidity and water content that occur inside the spider.

G
Several companies now produce materials based on spider silk proteins, and a number of products have reached the market, including clothing and cosmetics. Medical applications appear especially promising, because the material is strong, flexible and unlikely to be rejected by the body, which makes it attractive for stitches, artificial ligaments and scaffolds on which new tissue can grow. Large-scale industrial uses, such as cables or protective clothing, remain further away. After decades of effort, the humble spider still produces, effortlessly and in its own body, a material that human technology can only partly imitate.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu khoa học vật liệu về tơ nhện đã công bố.

passages.title: The Secrets of Hibernation
passages.text:
A
Winter presents warm-blooded animals with a serious problem. Keeping the body at a constant high temperature requires a great deal of energy, yet in many parts of the world food becomes scarce precisely when the weather turns cold. Some animals respond by migrating to warmer regions; others grow thicker coats or store food. A smaller number adopt a more extreme strategy. They shut down most of their bodily activity and enter a state known as hibernation, in which they may remain for weeks or months, surviving on the fat they accumulated during the previous summer and autumn. Animals that hibernate include certain bats, hedgehogs, marmots and many species of ground squirrel.

B
Hibernation is far more than a long sleep. In a hibernating ground squirrel, the heart, which normally beats hundreds of times a minute, may slow to just a few beats, and breathing may pause for long periods. Most remarkably, body temperature falls to close to that of the surrounding environment. In some small hibernators, it drops to only a few degrees above freezing, and the Arctic ground squirrel, which lives in Alaska and northern Canada, has been recorded with a body temperature slightly below zero, apparently without its blood freezing. By reducing their metabolism in this way, hibernators can cut their energy use dramatically.

C
Curiously, few hibernators remain in this state continuously. Every week or two, they warm up to their normal body temperature for a period of several hours before returning to hibernation. These periodic arousals consume a large proportion of the energy an animal uses over the whole winter, and scientists have long puzzled over why they happen. One theory is that animals need to restore some functions of the brain or the immune system that cannot operate at low temperatures; another is that they need to sleep, since hibernation itself does not appear to provide the benefits of normal sleep. During each arousal, the animal shivers intensely to generate heat.

D
Bears are something of a special case. Their body temperature falls by only a few degrees during the winter, so some scientists prefer to describe their state as a form of winter dormancy rather than true hibernation. Yet bears achieve something remarkable in their own way. For several months they neither eat, drink nor pass waste, and females give birth to cubs and feed them with milk during this period. Even more surprisingly, bears emerge in spring having lost very little muscle strength or bone density, despite months without movement, whereas a human confined to bed for the same length of time would suffer serious weakening.

E
Hibernation is not limited to cold climates. The fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar, a small primate, hibernates for up to seven months during the dry season, when food is scarce. Because the tropical temperature remains relatively high, the lemur's body temperature rises and falls with the temperature of its tree hollow, sometimes by more than twenty degrees in a single day. It was the first primate known to hibernate, and its discovery challenged the assumption that hibernation was primarily a response to cold rather than to a lack of food.

F
Medical researchers have taken a keen interest in hibernation. If doctors could induce a similar state in humans, they might be able to protect patients who have suffered serious injuries or strokes by reducing the demand for oxygen in their tissues until treatment is possible. The ability of bears to avoid muscle and bone loss has attracted attention from researchers studying conditions such as osteoporosis. Space agencies have even considered whether astronauts on very long missions might one day be placed in a hibernation-like state, which would reduce the amount of food, water and space they require.

G
Such ideas remain speculative. Humans are not natural hibernators, and the biological mechanisms that allow animals to survive extreme cold and inactivity are still only partly understood. Researchers have identified some of the genes and chemical signals involved, and in laboratory experiments they have been able to induce a hibernation-like state in mice, which do not normally hibernate. Whether similar techniques could ever be applied safely to people is a question that may take many years to answer. Many experts remain doubtful that it will ever be possible.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu sinh lý học về ngủ đông đã công bố.

passages.title: The World Inside Us
passages.text:
A
Each of us carries around a vast population of microscopic organisms. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and other microbes live on our skin, in our mouths and, above all, in our intestines, where tens of trillions of them form what scientists call the gut microbiome. For most of the twentieth century, bacteria were regarded mainly as causes of disease, to be eliminated wherever possible. Today, researchers increasingly see the microbes in our gut as partners, essential to our health, and the study of the microbiome has become one of the fastest-growing fields in biology.

B
A frequently quoted claim holds that bacterial cells in the human body outnumber human cells by ten to one. This figure, based on rough estimates made in the 1970s, was repeated for decades in textbooks and articles. In 2016, however, a team of researchers including Ron Milo recalculated the numbers using more accurate data on the volume of the colon and the number of red blood cells in the body, and concluded that the ratio is closer to one to one. Even so, the bacteria in our bodies contain far more genes than we do, which greatly expands the range of chemical tasks that the combined human and microbial system can perform.

C
Those tasks are numerous. Gut bacteria break down dietary fibre that our own enzymes cannot digest, producing substances that nourish the cells lining the colon and help to regulate inflammation. Some bacteria manufacture vitamins, including vitamin K. The microbiome also plays a key role in training the immune system, helping it to distinguish between harmless substances and genuine threats. Experiments with mice raised in completely sterile conditions, without any microbes, have shown that such animals develop abnormal immune systems and are more vulnerable to some infections.

D
Our microbial communities begin to form at birth. Babies born naturally are first colonised by bacteria from their mothers, while those born by caesarean section initially acquire different microbes, many of them from the skin and the hospital environment. Breast milk contains complex sugars that babies cannot digest but that feed particular beneficial bacteria. Over the first few years of life, the microbiome becomes more diverse and stable, shaped by diet, environment and contact with other people and animals. Courses of antibiotics, especially in early childhood, can disturb this process, sometimes for months.

E
Some of the most intriguing research has linked the microbiome to body weight. In one experiment, the biologist Jeffrey Gordon and his colleagues took gut bacteria from pairs of human twins in which one twin was obese and the other was not, and transferred them into mice raised without microbes. Mice that received bacteria from the obese twins gained more fat than those that received bacteria from the lean twins, even though both groups ate the same food. The results suggested that gut microbes can influence how much energy is extracted from food and stored in the body.

F
The way people live also appears to shape their microbes. Studies by Justin and Erica Sonnenburg and others of the Hadza, a community of hunter-gatherers in Tanzania, found that their gut microbiomes are considerably more diverse than those of people in industrialised countries, and that they change with the seasons as the Hadza diet shifts between foods such as meat, berries and honey. Some researchers suspect that modern diets low in fibre, together with widespread use of antibiotics, have reduced the diversity of microbes in the West, with possible consequences for health.

G
Turning such findings into medical treatments has proved more difficult than early enthusiasm suggested. One clear success is the treatment of a serious and recurrent intestinal infection by transferring gut bacteria from a healthy donor, which has cured large numbers of patients for whom antibiotics had repeatedly failed. Evidence for many other interventions is weaker. Probiotic supplements are widely sold, yet their benefits for healthy people remain uncertain, and a study led by Eran Elinav found that taking probiotics after a course of antibiotics actually delayed the return of patients' original gut bacteria.

H
Researchers also warn that much of the evidence comes from studies in mice, whose biology differs from ours in important ways, and that it is often difficult to tell whether changes in the microbiome cause disease or are caused by it. The microbiome is unquestionably important, but scientists are only beginning to understand how to influence it safely and effectively.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu y sinh học về hệ vi sinh vật đường ruột đã công bố.

passages.title: Why We Laugh
passages.text:
A
Laughter is one of the most familiar of human behaviours, yet it has received surprisingly little scientific attention compared with emotions such as fear or anger. Most people assume that we laugh mainly because something is funny, and that laughter is therefore closely connected with jokes and humour. Over the past few decades, however, research by psychologists, neuroscientists and animal behaviourists has suggested a rather different picture, in which laughter is less about comedy than about relationships with other people. Babies begin to laugh at around three or four months of age, long before they can speak or understand a joke.

B
Some of the most influential evidence came from the American psychologist Robert Provine, who spent years listening to people laughing in everyday settings such as shopping centres and university campuses. Provine and his students recorded more than a thousand episodes of natural laughter, noting what had been said immediately beforehand. To their surprise, only a small minority of laughs followed anything resembling a joke. Most came after ordinary remarks, such as greetings or comments about mutual friends. Provine also found that speakers laughed considerably more than their listeners, which suggested that laughter was being used to signal friendliness rather than simply in response to something amusing.

C
Laughter is also overwhelmingly social. Provine estimated that people are around thirty times more likely to laugh when they are with others than when they are alone, and much solitary laughter occurs in response to television or other media, which create a kind of artificial company. Laughter is also highly contagious, which is why television comedies have long used recorded laughter. Hearing someone else laugh activates regions of the brain involved in preparing facial movements, so that we are primed to join in, often before we know what the joke was. In an extreme case in 1962, an outbreak of laughter spread among pupils at schools in what is now Tanzania and lasted for months, forcing several schools to close.

D
Humans are not the only animals that laugh. Chimpanzees, gorillas and other great apes make breathy, panting sounds when they play or are tickled, and an analysis of these sounds by Marina Davila-Ross and her colleagues found that they become more similar to human laughter in species more closely related to us. The researchers concluded that laughter probably evolved from a play signal used by the common ancestors of humans and apes millions of years ago. Even rats appear to have a form of laughter: the neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp discovered that rats produce high-pitched chirps, too high for humans to hear, when they are tickled, and that they actively seek out the hand that tickles them.

E
The neuroscientist Sophie Scott has studied how people perceive different kinds of laughter. Her research shows that listeners can usually tell the difference between spontaneous laughter, which is triggered involuntarily, and deliberate laughter produced to be polite or to show agreement. The two kinds sound different and are processed by different networks in the brain. Interestingly, people who are closely acquainted tend to laugh together more spontaneously, and Scott has suggested that shared laughter may help couples and friends to manage tension and recover from disagreements.

F
Laughter may also bind groups together through its effects on the body. In a series of experiments led by the evolutionary psychologist Robin Dunbar, participants who watched comedy videos in a group were able to tolerate more pain afterwards than those who watched documentaries. Dunbar argued that laughing triggers the release of endorphins, natural chemicals that reduce pain and create a sense of wellbeing, and that this response may have helped early humans to form social bonds within larger groups than other primates could manage.

G
Popular claims about the health benefits of laughter should be treated with some caution. Laughter can reduce stress and raise people's mood, and it certainly does no harm, but some of the more ambitious claims, for example that it strengthens the immune system or significantly extends life, are not well supported by evidence. What does seem clear is that laughter is an ancient and powerful social signal, and that understanding it helps to explain why spending time with others feels so important to us. Laughter clubs and laughter yoga classes have nevertheless become popular in many countries.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học và khoa học thần kinh về tiếng cười đã công bố.

passages.title: Training in Thin Air
passages.text:
A
When the Olympic Games were held in Mexico City in 1968, at an altitude of more than two thousand metres, the results surprised many observers. In events lasting only a few seconds, such as sprints and jumps, athletes performed exceptionally well; the American long jumper Bob Beamon set a world record that stood for more than twenty years. In longer races, however, many favourites struggled badly, and several endurance events were won by athletes from Kenya and Ethiopia who had grown up at high altitude. The Games prompted a wave of scientific interest in how altitude affects the body and whether athletes from lower regions could benefit from training there. One Australian distance runner collapsed after finishing his race and had to be given oxygen.

B
The explanation lies in the air itself. At high altitude, air pressure is lower, so each breath contains fewer molecules of oxygen. For sprinters and jumpers, the thinner air offers less resistance, which helps them, while their short efforts depend relatively little on oxygen supplied by the lungs. Endurance athletes, by contrast, rely on a continuous supply of oxygen to their muscles, and at altitude their bodies cannot deliver enough of it, so they tire more quickly and must slow down.

C
Over a period of weeks, however, the body adapts. The kidneys respond to the reduced oxygen by releasing more of a hormone called erythropoietin, usually known as EPO, which stimulates the production of red blood cells. Because red blood cells carry oxygen around the body, an athlete who returns to sea level with a higher concentration of them should, in theory, be able to deliver more oxygen to the muscles and perform better. This is the basic idea behind altitude training, and it is also why artificial EPO has been banned as a performance-enhancing drug.

D
Living and training at altitude has a significant drawback. Because less oxygen is available, athletes cannot train as hard as they would at sea level, and the loss of training intensity may cancel out the benefits of their increased red blood cells. In the 1990s, the American researchers Benjamin Levine and James Stray-Gundersen tested a solution. They divided a group of runners into three groups: some lived and trained at sea level, some lived and trained at altitude, and a third group lived at about 2,500 metres but travelled down to a lower altitude for their hardest training sessions. Only the third group significantly improved their race times.

E
The approach, known as ‘live high, train low’, has since been widely adopted. Because not every athlete can relocate to the mountains, some sleep in special tents or rooms in which the oxygen content of the air is reduced to simulate altitude, while training normally during the day. Such devices allow athletes to gain some of the benefits of altitude without leaving home, although scientists disagree about how effective they are, and some sporting authorities have debated whether their use is fair. Their popularity has grown steadily since the 1990s.

F
Not everyone responds equally. Studies have found that some athletes produce large increases in red blood cells after a period at altitude, while others show little or no change, possibly because of genetic differences. Altitude can also cause problems: poor sleep, headaches, dehydration and reduced appetite are common, and athletes who ascend too quickly may suffer from altitude sickness. Coaches therefore usually recommend gradual adjustment and careful monitoring, and many advise that a stay of at least three weeks is needed for meaningful benefits. Because dry mountain air increases the loss of fluid from the body, athletes are also advised to drink more water than usual.

G
The success of East African runners is sometimes explained simply by the altitude at which they live, but the reality is more complex. Many Kenyan and Ethiopian champions come from regions where children traditionally run long distances to school, and running has become a major route to wealth and status, creating intense competition from an early age. Training towns such as Iten in Kenya, at around 2,400 metres, now attract athletes from all over the world. Altitude may help, but it is only one ingredient in a combination of factors that includes culture, opportunity and an enormous amount of hard work.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu khoa học thể thao về tập luyện độ cao đã công bố.

passages.title: Why Are So Many Children Short-Sighted?
passages.text:
A
Short-sightedness, known medically as myopia, used to be a relatively uncommon condition. Today it is spreading at a pace that has alarmed eye specialists around the world. In several cities in East Asia, including Seoul, Shanghai and Taipei, studies have found that between eighty and ninety per cent of young people leaving school are myopic. Rates are rising in Europe and North America as well, though less steeply. One widely cited projection suggests that by 2050 around half of the world's population could be affected. I believe that this trend deserves far more public attention than it currently receives.

B
Myopia occurs when the eyeball grows too long from front to back, so that light from distant objects is focused in front of the retina rather than on it. As a result, faraway things appear blurred. Glasses or contact lenses can correct the blurring easily, which may explain why the problem is often regarded as a minor inconvenience. Yet severe myopia significantly increases the risk of serious eye diseases later in life, including detachment of the retina and glaucoma, which can lead to permanent loss of sight. A rise in severe myopia today may therefore mean a rise in blindness in the decades ahead. In some people, the eye continues to lengthen well into early adulthood.

C
Genes undoubtedly play a part, since children with two myopic parents are more likely to become myopic themselves. But genetic change cannot explain an increase that has occurred within two or three generations. Something in the way children now live must be responsible. For many years, the main suspect was close work, especially reading. It seemed natural to assume that children who spent long hours studying would damage their eyesight, and the pressure of intensive education systems in East Asia appeared to fit this explanation.

D
A different factor has since emerged as more important: time spent outdoors. In an influential study, researchers compared children of Chinese descent living in Sydney with children of similar background in Singapore. Only around three per cent of the Sydney children were myopic, compared with nearly thirty per cent of those in Singapore. The two groups read for similar amounts of time, but the children in Sydney spent many more hours outside each week. Later studies in other countries produced similar results, suggesting that being outdoors protects children's eyes regardless of how much they read.

E
The leading explanation is light. Even on a cloudy day, light outdoors is many times brighter than typical indoor lighting. Bright light is thought to stimulate the release of dopamine in the retina, a chemical that helps to slow the growth of the eyeball. Children who spend most of their days indoors, at school and at home, may simply not receive enough bright light to keep their eyes growing normally. Close work may still contribute to the problem, but the evidence suggests that it matters less than once believed.

F
This understanding has already been put into practice. In southern China, a trial added an extra forty-minute outdoor class to the school day in a group of schools, and after three years the proportion of children who had developed myopia was noticeably lower than in schools without the extra class. In Taiwan, where rates of myopia among children had been rising for decades, the authorities encouraged schools to ensure that pupils spent around two hours a day outside, and the long upward trend began to reverse. Researchers are also testing eye drops and special lenses that may slow the progression of myopia in children who already have it. Low doses of atropine, a long-established medicine, are among the treatments being studied.

G
The solution, in principle, is remarkably simple and cheap. Yet persuading schools and parents to give children more time outside is not easy, particularly in education systems where every hour of the day is devoted to academic work and where parents worry about safety. In my view, outdoor time should be treated not as a distraction from learning but as an essential part of children's health, in the same way that physical exercise and a balanced diet are. The cost of failing to act may be measured, decades from now, in millions of people with serious visual impairment.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu nhãn khoa và dịch tễ học đã công bố.
