passages.title: The Humble Pencil
passages.text:
A
Few objects are as ordinary as the pencil. Billions are made every year, and most people have used one since early childhood without giving it a second thought. Yet the pencil is the product of centuries of experiment, accidental discovery and international rivalry. Its story involves a remarkable mineral deposit in the north of England, a war between European powers and a long series of improvements by craftsmen and engineers, many of whose names have been forgotten.

B
The story begins in the sixteenth century, when a large deposit of an unusual black mineral was discovered at Borrowdale, in the hills of Cumbria. The material was soft enough to leave a dark mark on almost any surface, and local shepherds reportedly used it to mark their sheep. People at the time believed it was a form of lead, which is why we still speak of pencil ‘lead’ today, although the substance was actually graphite, a form of carbon that contains no lead at all. The Borrowdale graphite was unusually pure and solid, so it could be cut into sticks and used directly for writing and drawing. No deposit of comparable purity has ever been found anywhere else in the world.

C
Because graphite was so soft and dirty to handle, early users wrapped the sticks in string or sheepskin. Later, craftsmen began inserting them into hollowed-out pieces of wood. The mineral also became extremely valuable for another reason: it could be used to line the moulds in which cannonballs were cast. As a result, the mine at Borrowdale was closely guarded, and at times it was opened for only a few weeks each year to prevent prices from falling. Laws were passed making the theft of graphite a serious crime. Smuggling nevertheless continued, and stolen graphite was sold on a thriving black market in nearby towns.

D
Other countries had no deposit of comparable quality, and when war cut France off from English graphite in the 1790s, the French government asked an inventor named Nicolas-Jacques Conté to find an alternative. His solution, patented in 1795, was to grind impure graphite into a powder, mix it with clay and water, shape the mixture into thin rods and fire them in a kiln. The process had a crucial advantage. By changing the proportion of clay, manufacturers could control the hardness of the finished lead: more clay produced a harder lead and a lighter line, while less clay produced a softer, darker one.

E
Conté's method remains the basis of pencil manufacturing today. The grades printed on pencils reflect it: ‘H’ stands for hard and ‘B’ for black, so that a 4H pencil makes a faint, precise line suitable for technical drawing, while a 6B is soft enough for shading. The familiar HB pencil lies in the middle of the range. Modern factories make the casing by cutting grooves into thin slabs of wood, laying the leads into the grooves and gluing a second slab on top before the sandwich is cut into individual pencils. Cedar is a popular choice of wood because it is soft enough to sharpen easily without splintering. Some artists keep a dozen grades or more.

F
In 1858, an American named Hymen Lipman received a patent for a pencil with an eraser attached to one end. Today the eraser is usually held in place by a small metal band called a ferrule, which is squeezed tightly around the wood. Interestingly, many pencils sold in Europe still have no eraser, partly because some teachers believe that children who cannot easily rub out their mistakes will think more carefully before writing. American pencils, by contrast, almost always have one.

G
The colour of the pencil also has a history. In the 1890s, a European manufacturer introduced high-quality pencils painted yellow, a colour then associated with luxury, and the design became so successful that competitors copied it. In North America, yellow remains by far the most common colour for wooden pencils. Despite the arrival of computers and tablets, the pencil has survived because it is cheap, reliable, needs no power and can be erased, qualities that make it valued by artists, architects and schoolchildren alike. Some modern pencils are even made from recycled newspaper or plastic instead of wood.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử công nghệ và đồ dùng văn phòng.

passages.title: From Bitter Drink to Chocolate Bar
passages.text:
A
Chocolate is one of the world's favourite foods, eaten in enormous quantities as bars, sweets and drinks. For most of its history, however, it looked and tasted nothing like the sweet, smooth product we know today. The cacao tree, from which chocolate is made, originated in the tropical forests of South America, and its seeds were first used thousands of years ago by peoples living in what is now Mexico and Central America. The transformation of those bitter seeds into a mass-produced treat took place only in the nineteenth century, through a series of inventions in Europe. Its scientific name, Theobroma, comes from Greek words meaning ‘food of the gods’.

B
The Maya and later the Aztecs prepared cacao as a frothy drink, often flavoured with chilli peppers, vanilla or flowers and served without sugar. It was a drink of great prestige, associated with religious ceremonies, feasts and the nobility, and cacao seeds were so valuable that the Aztecs used them as a form of money. Records from the period list prices in cacao beans, and archaeologists have even found counterfeit beans, made by filling empty shells with mud, which suggests how valuable genuine ones were.

C
Spanish explorers encountered chocolate in the early sixteenth century, and at first many found the bitter drink unpleasant. Once it had been sweetened with sugar and flavoured with spices such as cinnamon, however, it became fashionable among the Spanish nobility, and during the seventeenth century the habit spread to France, Italy and England. Chocolate remained expensive, largely because cacao had to be shipped across the Atlantic, and in London fashionable chocolate houses became meeting places for the wealthy, much as coffee houses were. Some doctors of the period even recommended it as a medicine.

D
Before cacao can become chocolate, it must go through a lengthy process, much of which still takes place on the farms where it is grown. The large pods are cut from the trees and split open, and the seeds, surrounded by a sweet white pulp, are piled together and left to ferment for several days. Fermentation is essential, since it develops the chemicals that later produce the characteristic flavour of chocolate. The beans are then dried, usually in the sun, before being sold and shipped to factories, where they are roasted, cracked open and separated from their shells. The remaining pieces, called nibs, are ground into a thick paste.

E
The modern chocolate industry was born when manufacturers learned how to change that paste. In 1828, the Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten patented a press that squeezed out much of the fat, known as cocoa butter, leaving a solid that could be ground into a fine powder. Cocoa powder mixed more easily with water and was cheaper to make. Equally important, the fat that had been removed could be added back to ground cacao in larger quantities, and in 1847 a company in Bristol, England, used this technique to produce what is often considered the first solid chocolate bar intended for eating. Other manufacturers soon followed.

F
Switzerland contributed two further breakthroughs. In 1875, after years of experiments, Daniel Peter succeeded in making milk chocolate by combining chocolate with condensed milk, which contained less water than fresh milk and so did not spoil the mixture. A few years later, Rodolphe Lindt invented a machine that stirred and heated chocolate continuously for many hours, a process known as conching, which made it far smoother and more pleasant to eat. By the end of the century, chocolate had become affordable for ordinary people in Europe and North America.

G
Today the industry is global, but its foundations remain fragile. Most of the world's cacao is grown not in the Americas but in West Africa, much of it by smallholder farmers who earn very little from their crop. Prices are volatile, the trees are vulnerable to disease and changing weather, and investigations have repeatedly found children working on cacao farms in dangerous conditions. Several large companies have promised to improve conditions and pay farmers more, but campaigners argue that progress has been slow, and that consumers rarely consider the long journey their chocolate has made. Two countries, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, together produce more than half of the world's supply.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử thực phẩm và ngành ca cao.

passages.title: The Frozen Water Trade
passages.text:
A
In the early nineteenth century, the idea that anyone would pay for frozen water seemed absurd to most people. Ice formed naturally on the ponds and lakes of New England every winter and melted away every spring, and nobody imagined that it could be harvested, stored and sold in the tropics. Yet within a few decades, ice from Massachusetts was being shipped to the Caribbean, South America, India and China, and the ice trade had become a major industry employing thousands of people. Its story is a remarkable example of how persistence and practical invention can create a market where none existed before. His achievement eventually earned Tudor the nickname ‘the Ice King’.

B
The man most responsible was Frederic Tudor, the son of a wealthy Boston family. In 1806 he sent a ship loaded with ice to the Caribbean island of Martinique, believing that people in hot climates would be eager to buy it. The venture was a failure. Much of the cargo melted before it could be sold, local people did not know what to do with ice, and there were no proper buildings in which to store it. Tudor lost a great deal of money, and over the following years his debts grew so large that he was imprisoned more than once. He nevertheless refused to give up.

C
Tudor's eventual success depended on solving the problem of melting. Through years of trial and error, he found that sawdust, a waste product available almost free from timber mills, was an excellent insulator. Ice packed in sawdust in the hold of a ship, or stored in thick-walled buildings known as ice houses, could last for months. He also built ice houses at his overseas markets and set about creating demand, offering free ice to bar owners so that they could serve cold drinks and encouraging hospitals and wealthy households to use it for preserving food.

D
Another key innovation came from one of Tudor's suppliers, Nathaniel Wyeth, who in the 1820s invented a horse-drawn device for cutting ice. Instead of being hacked out in irregular lumps, ice could now be cut into large blocks of uniform size. Uniform blocks could be packed tightly together with little space between them, which reduced melting, and they could be loaded and unloaded far more quickly. Harvesting became a highly organised activity, carried out by large teams of workers on frozen lakes during the coldest weeks of winter. A single large lake could yield many thousands of tonnes of ice in one winter.

E
The most astonishing achievement of the trade was the shipment of ice to India. In 1833, a ship carrying around 180 tonnes of ice left Boston for Calcutta, a voyage of some four months that crossed the equator twice. Remarkably, about two-thirds of the cargo survived the journey. The ice was a sensation among the British residents of the city, and for decades afterwards regular shipments from New England supplied ice to India, where it was valued not only for cooling drinks but also for treating patients suffering from fever.

F
At home, the trade transformed the American diet. Ice allowed fresh meat, fish, milk and vegetables to be stored for longer and transported over greater distances, and by the middle of the century many ordinary households had an icebox, a wooden cabinet lined with metal in which a block of ice kept food cool. The meat-packing industry in particular depended on ice to send products from the Midwest to cities on the east coast in refrigerated railway wagons. Ice also made cold drinks and ice cream available in summer, luxuries that had once been enjoyed only by the very rich.

G
The trade eventually fell victim to the very demand it had created. Natural ice depended on the weather, and in unusually warm winters the harvest failed, causing shortages and sharp rises in prices. As cities grew, concern also increased about pollution in the lakes from which ice was cut. Meanwhile, engineers were developing machines that could manufacture ice artificially and, later, refrigerators that kept food cool without ice at all. By the early twentieth century, the frozen water trade was in rapid decline, but the habits of refrigeration it had established were permanent.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử thương mại thế kỷ 19.

passages.title: The Glassmakers of Murano
passages.text:
A
For several centuries, the finest glass in Europe came from a small island in the lagoon of Venice. Murano's glassmakers produced goblets, chandeliers, beads and mirrors of a quality that no one else could match, and their work was sought after by kings, popes and wealthy merchants across the continent. The industry made Venice rich, and the Venetian authorities went to extraordinary lengths to protect it. Today, Murano glass remains famous throughout the world, but the island's ancient craft faces challenges its founders could never have imagined. Glassmaking skills were often passed from one generation to the next, and some workshops on the island can trace their history back for centuries.

B
Glassmaking had been practised in Venice since at least the tenth century. In 1291, however, the government of the Republic ordered that most of the city's glass furnaces be moved to Murano. One reason was safety: glassmaking requires furnaces that burn day and night at very high temperatures, and in a city built largely of wood, the risk of fire was a constant concern. Another reason, many historians believe, was to concentrate the glassmakers in one place where their activities, and their valuable technical secrets, could be more easily controlled. Murano soon became home to dozens of furnaces and a thriving community of craftsmen.

C
The glassmakers of Murano enjoyed an unusual position. They were among the most respected citizens of the Republic, and their daughters were permitted to marry into noble families, a privilege rarely granted to craftsmen. At the same time, they were not free to leave. Venetian law forbade glassmakers to practise their craft outside the Republic, since a skilled worker who moved abroad could take valuable knowledge with him. Those who left were threatened with severe punishment, and their families who remained behind could also suffer the consequences.

D
Murano's reputation rested on a series of technical innovations. In the fifteenth century, Angelo Barovier developed a method of producing an almost perfectly clear glass, known as cristallo, by using carefully purified ingredients. Clear glass allowed craftsmen to produce thin, elegant vessels and, later, mirrors of exceptional quality. Glassmakers also perfected decorative techniques such as millefiori, in which slices of multicoloured glass rods are arranged to form patterns resembling a field of tiny flowers, and filigree, in which fine threads of white or coloured glass are embedded within clear glass. Such techniques were often closely guarded within individual families.

E
The making of a blown-glass vessel follows a sequence that has changed little over the centuries. A mixture of sand and other minerals is melted in a furnace until it becomes a glowing liquid. The glassmaker collects a lump of molten glass on the end of a long metal tube, known as a blowpipe, and blows into it to form a bubble. The vessel is then shaped with simple tools while it is repeatedly returned to the heat of the furnace to keep it workable. Finally, the finished object is cooled very slowly in a special oven, since glass that cools too quickly is likely to crack. An elaborate piece may require the work of a master and several assistants over many hours.

F
Despite the Republic's efforts, Murano's monopoly could not last for ever. In the seventeenth century, the French minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, determined to end France's dependence on expensive Venetian mirrors, persuaded several Murano glassmakers to move to Paris. The workshop they helped to establish soon produced mirrors of comparable quality, and in the 1680s it supplied the glass for the famous Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. Over the following century, glass industries in Bohemia, England and elsewhere also grew, and Venice gradually lost its dominant position.

G
Today Murano's furnaces face new difficulties. Cheap imitations, many produced in factories abroad and sold to tourists as genuine Murano glass, have undercut local workshops, and in 1994 a certification mark was introduced to help buyers identify authentic pieces. Rising energy costs have also hit an industry whose furnaces must burn continuously; in 2022, some workshops were forced to shut their furnaces temporarily as gas prices soared. Many glassmakers worry, too, that fewer young people are willing to undertake the long apprenticeship needed to master the craft. Others, however, remain optimistic.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử thủ công và nghề thủy tinh Venice.

passages.title: The Bayeux Tapestry
passages.text:
A
In a museum in the small Norman town of Bayeux hangs one of the most famous works of art of the Middle Ages: a strip of cloth about seventy metres long and half a metre high that tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066. In a series of vivid scenes, it shows the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings and the battle itself, in which William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English king Harold Godwinson. For historians, it is an extraordinary source of information about the eleventh century; for ordinary visitors, it is a gripping story told almost like a modern comic strip. It has become one of the most widely reproduced images of medieval Europe.

B
Despite its name, the Bayeux Tapestry is not strictly a tapestry at all. In a true tapestry, the design is woven into the fabric on a loom. The Bayeux work is an embroidery: its images were stitched onto panels of plain linen using wool dyed in a limited range of colours, including shades of red, yellow, green and blue. The panels were then joined together to form a single continuous piece. The work is remarkable not only for its size but for the skill of its needlework, which manages to convey movement, emotion and detail with simple stitches.

C
Nobody knows exactly who made it or where. Most historians believe that it was commissioned by Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, who was William's half-brother and who appears prominently in several scenes. Because of features of its style and the spelling of some of the Latin words that run above the images, many experts think that it was made in England, possibly by embroiderers in Canterbury, within a few years of the conquest. English needlework was famous throughout Europe at the time, and it is quite possible that the embroiderers themselves were English women working for their new Norman rulers.

D
The scenes contain a wealth of detail about everyday life. They show ships being built and loaded, horses being transported across the sea, food being cooked and served, and soldiers wearing armour of interlocking metal rings. Hundreds of human figures appear, along with horses, dogs and other animals. Above and below the main story run decorative borders filled with mythical creatures, scenes from well-known fables and images of ordinary activities such as ploughing and hunting. One scene even depicts a comet passing overhead, which observers at the time interpreted as a sign of coming disaster.

E
Historians must use the work with care, however, because it was made to tell a particular version of events. It presents the Norman claim that Harold had sworn an oath to support William as the next king of England, and that by taking the throne himself he had broken his promise. From this point of view, the invasion was a just punishment. English sources from the period tell a rather different story, and the tapestry is best understood as a piece of political storytelling rather than a neutral record.

F
One of its most famous images has also become a subject of debate. The scene of Harold's death is usually said to show him being struck in the eye by an arrow, an episode that has become part of popular history. Close examination has suggested, however, that the arrow may have been added or altered during later repairs, and that Harold may instead be the figure shown being cut down by a mounted knight. Because the cloth has been repaired many times over the centuries, it is not always easy to know which details are original.

G
The tapestry's survival is itself remarkable. For centuries it was kept in Bayeux Cathedral and displayed to the public once a year. During the French Revolution it was nearly cut up to cover military wagons, and it was saved only when a local official intervened. In the Second World War, German officials took a close interest in it and moved it to Paris in 1944. Its final scenes are missing; the story breaks off in the middle of the English retreat, and nobody knows how the original ending looked. Today it is displayed behind glass in carefully controlled light to prevent further damage.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử trung cổ và nghiên cứu về tấm thảm Bayeux.

passages.title: The Invention of Nothing
passages.text:
A
Of all the numbers we use, zero may seem the least interesting. It represents nothing, after all, and young children learn to write it without difficulty. Yet zero was one of the hardest ideas in mathematics to develop, and for thousands of years many sophisticated civilisations managed without it. Its gradual acceptance, spread over more than a millennium and across several continents, transformed arithmetic, made modern science possible and, eventually, laid the foundations for the digital computer. The idea of treating nothing as a quantity also troubled many thinkers, some of whom regarded it with deep suspicion.

B
The first need for something like zero arose from the way numbers are written. In a positional system, such as the one we use today, the value of a digit depends on where it stands: the 2 in 205 means two hundred, while in 25 it means twenty. Such a system requires some way of marking an empty position, otherwise 205 and 25 would look the same. Around three hundred years before the common era, scribes in ancient Babylon began to use a pair of small slanted marks to show that a position was empty. This was a placeholder, however, not a number: the Babylonians never wrote it on its own or used it in calculations.

C
On the other side of the world, the Maya of Central America independently developed a symbol for zero, often drawn as a shell. They used it in their elaborate calendar, which counted the days that had passed since a starting point thousands of years earlier, and their positional number system allowed them to record very large quantities. Because the Maya had no contact with Asia or Europe, their achievement had no influence on the development of mathematics elsewhere, but it shows that the concept arose more than once in human history. Maya inscriptions record dates spanning many centuries.

D
The decisive step was taken in India. Indian mathematicians had used a dot to mark an empty position for some time, and in the seventh century the astronomer Brahmagupta went further, treating zero as a number in its own right. In a book written in 628, he set out rules for calculating with it: adding zero to a number leaves the number unchanged, and subtracting a number from itself produces zero. He struggled with division by zero, a problem that troubled mathematicians for centuries afterwards, but his work marked the moment when ‘nothing’ became something that could be counted and calculated. His treatment of negative numbers, which he described in terms of debts and fortunes, was equally influential.

E
Indian numerals, including zero, spread westwards through the Islamic world. In the ninth century, the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote a book explaining how to calculate with the Indian system. When his work was later translated into Latin, his name was transformed into ‘algorismus’, from which comes the modern word ‘algorithm’. The Sanskrit word for zero, meaning ‘empty’, was translated into Arabic as ‘sifr’, which eventually gave English both ‘zero’ and ‘cipher’.

F
Europe was slow to adopt the new numbers. In 1202, the Italian mathematician Leonardo of Pisa, known today as Fibonacci, published a book introducing the system to European readers and demonstrating its usefulness for merchants. Calculations that were laborious with Roman numerals became far simpler. Yet resistance was considerable. In 1299, the city of Florence banned the use of the new numerals in official financial records, partly because they were thought to be easier to alter fraudulently: a zero could be changed into a six or a nine with a single stroke of a pen. Old habits were slow to change.

G
Over the following centuries, the advantages of the system proved overwhelming, and by the sixteenth century it was used across most of Europe. Zero went on to play a central role in algebra, in the development of calculus and in the coordinate systems that allow equations to be represented as graphs. Today it lies at the heart of digital technology, in which every piece of information is ultimately stored as a pattern of ones and zeros. The symbol that the Babylonians used merely to fill a gap has become one of the most important ideas humanity has ever had.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử toán học.

passages.title: Navigating Without Instruments
passages.text:
A
The islands of Polynesia are scattered across a vast triangle of the Pacific Ocean, with Hawaii at its northern point, New Zealand in the south-west and Easter Island in the east. The distances between them are enormous; some groups of islands lie thousands of kilometres from their nearest neighbours. Yet by around eight hundred years ago, almost every habitable island within this triangle had been settled, making it one of the last regions on earth to be reached by human beings. How the ancestors of the Polynesians found these tiny specks of land in such an immense ocean has long fascinated scholars. Their ancestors are thought to have come originally from island South-East Asia, moving gradually eastwards over thousands of years.

B
For much of the twentieth century, many Western scholars doubted that such voyages could have been made deliberately. In 1956, the historian Andrew Sharp argued that the islands had been settled largely by accident, by canoes blown off course by storms or carried by currents while their crews were fishing or travelling between nearby islands. In his view, navigation without instruments was simply too unreliable for voyagers to find distant islands on purpose and then return home. His argument was influential, although it angered many Pacific Islanders, whose oral traditions described planned voyages of discovery.

C
Evidence against the accidental theory gradually accumulated. In the early 1970s, researchers used computers to simulate thousands of drifting voyages, taking into account winds and currents. Hardly any of the simulated canoes reached Hawaii, New Zealand or Easter Island by chance, suggesting that these remote islands could only have been settled by people who were sailing in a chosen direction. Archaeologists also found that the settlers had brought with them the plants and animals they needed to establish new communities, including pigs, dogs, chickens and crops such as taro, which hardly seemed consistent with accidental arrivals.

D
The most dramatic test came in 1976. A group of enthusiasts in Hawaii built a replica of a traditional double-hulled voyaging canoe, which they named Hōkūleʻa, and set out to sail it to Tahiti, more than four thousand kilometres to the south, without compass, charts or other modern instruments. Since no Hawaiian still possessed the knowledge needed, they recruited Mau Piailug, a master navigator from a small island in Micronesia, where traditional methods had survived. After about a month at sea, the canoe reached Tahiti, where it was greeted by a crowd of thousands. The route was the same one described in Hawaiian traditions.

E
Traditional navigators rely on a detailed knowledge of the sky. They memorise the points on the horizon where particular stars rise and set, so that a star rising in a known position can be used to hold a course; as one star climbs too high to be useful, the navigator switches to another rising at the same point. During the day, the sun serves a similar purpose. Navigators also learn which stars pass directly overhead at particular islands, which helps them judge how far north or south they have travelled.

F
The ocean provides further clues. Large swells, generated by distant weather systems, travel in consistent directions for long periods, and an experienced navigator can feel the pattern of several swells through the movement of the canoe, even at night or under cloud. Near land, swells bend around islands and bounce off them, creating patterns that reveal an island's position before it can be seen. Clouds tend to gather above islands, and some seabirds, which fly out to sea to feed during the day and return to land at dusk, indicate the direction of land to those who know their habits.

G
The success of Hōkūleʻa inspired a revival of traditional voyaging across the Pacific. One of the Hawaiian crew members, Nainoa Thompson, studied with Mau Piailug and in 1980 navigated the canoe to Tahiti and back himself, becoming the first Hawaiian in centuries to make such a voyage using traditional methods. Since then, voyaging societies have trained new generations of navigators, and Hōkūleʻa has sailed around the world. For many Pacific Islanders, the revival has become a powerful symbol of cultural pride, demonstrating the skill and courage of the people who first explored the ocean.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu nhân học và lịch sử hàng hải Thái Bình Dương.

passages.title: The Birth of Paper Money
passages.text:
A
Most of the money in our pockets has almost no value as a physical object. A banknote is simply a piece of printed paper or plastic, worth a few cents to produce, yet people accept it in exchange for goods and services worth many times that amount. The idea that a piece of paper could stand in for valuable metal was a revolutionary one, and it emerged first not in Europe but in China, more than a thousand years ago. It is so familiar today that few people stop to consider how strange it really is.

B
The origins lie in practical necessity. In the province of Sichuan, in south-western China, the main currency during the tenth and eleventh centuries consisted of coins made of iron rather than copper. Iron coins had little value individually, so even modest purchases required large quantities of them, and carrying enough money to buy expensive goods was extremely difficult. Merchants began leaving their coins with trusted dealers in exchange for written receipts, which could then be passed from person to person as payment. In effect, the receipts were circulating in place of the coins themselves. A string of a thousand iron coins could weigh several kilograms, making large transactions especially awkward.

C
At first, these receipts were issued by private merchants, but problems soon arose. Some issuers printed more receipts than they could honour, and when holders demanded their coins, the dealers could not pay. In 1023, the government of the Song dynasty took control of the system, establishing an official office to issue the notes. This is often regarded as the beginning of government-issued paper money. To prevent forgery, the notes were printed with elaborate designs in several colours, and severe penalties were announced for anyone caught copying them. Each note was valid only for a fixed period, after which it had to be exchanged for a new one.

D
Paper money reached its greatest extent under the Mongol rulers of China in the thirteenth century. Kublai Khan made paper currency the main form of money throughout his empire and required merchants to accept it. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited China during this period, described the system with astonishment, explaining to European readers how notes made from the bark of the mulberry tree were accepted everywhere as if they were gold or silver. Many of his readers found the account hard to believe.

E
The system, however, contained a dangerous temptation. Because paper money cost so little to produce, governments facing heavy expenses, especially for wars, were inclined to print more of it. As the quantity of notes grew far faster than the quantity of goods available, prices rose and the notes lost their value. Inflation of this kind contributed to the economic difficulties of the later Mongol period, and the Ming dynasty, which followed, eventually abandoned paper money in favour of silver during the fifteenth century. Similar episodes of runaway inflation have occurred many times since, in countries all over the world.

F
Europe came to paper money much later. In the 1660s, a bank in Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, began issuing notes. Sweden's currency at that time included enormous copper plates, some weighing several kilograms, which were very inconvenient to carry, and the bank's notes offered an attractive alternative. Unfortunately, the bank repeated the mistake made in China centuries earlier: it issued far more notes than it could support with its reserves, and within a few years it collapsed. Its founder, Johan Palmstruch, was held responsible and was sentenced to death, although the sentence was later reduced.

G
Over the following centuries, banknotes became normal across Europe and the rest of the world, usually backed by a promise that they could be exchanged for gold or silver. During the twentieth century, that link was gradually broken, and today most currencies have value simply because governments declare them legal and people trust that others will accept them. As payments increasingly move to cards and mobile phones, paper money itself may become less common, but the central idea that emerged in Sichuan a thousand years ago remains the basis of modern economies: money is ultimately a matter of trust. Some countries, including Sweden, are already moving rapidly towards a largely cashless economy.

— Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử kinh tế và tiền tệ.
